News.title: Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
News.content:
Video shows the moment a deadly massive flash flood and mudslide hit the Nepal-Tibet border.

At least 31 people have been killed, and hundreds of tourists are missing.

The first two video clips have been edited by the BBC with white flashes, due to the distressing content.

Other clips show bridges being torn apart by the floodwater as people run to find cover.

Follow the story live.

News.title: Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children
News.content:
As a jury trial kicked off last week in an Oakland, California, federal court, state lawyers argued the tech company knew that millions of 11- and 12 year-old users were on Instagram and Facebook over the years, yet "did little to keep them off" the platforms.

Although the trial had only gone on for five days, state lawyers relied heavily on information found in millions of internal Meta documents provided in the case. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.

One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use." Still, the states argued, Meta targeted young users.

"The trial did not go well for Meta," Bonta said on Wednesday.

Meta maintained throughout the brief trial that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for its youngest users, pouring resources into testing and research, and building new features.

"We're always working on teen safety," head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said during an hour of court testimony on Tuesday.

The case was settled and court adjourned before he could reappear before a jury.

Before Mosseri's testimony, a former researcher at Meta, George Volichenko, appeared and with lawyers went over various internal communications he had been a part of regarding Meta's work on safety.

Volichenko said he struggled to understand when he was at the company in 2022 why the team he worked on wasn't given more freedom to better test and implement new safety features.

One of those was "quiet mode", which muted notifications for teen users during the night. His team knew such a feature would be much more widely adopted if Meta turned it on by default.

He recalled his manager telling him he "shouldn't worry too much about the adoption figures being low, because the team exists partially to protect the company against the upcoming lawsuits".

As part of the Wednesday settlement, however, a feature called "night mode", which blocks notifications between midnight and 6am, will now be on by default - meaning they will be turned on automatically. The settings are also designed only to be turned off by a parent or guardian.

"The framework we've negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms", C J Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said.

Other features for teen users being implemented as part of the deal include:

A default two-hour daily time limit (cumulative across Instagram and Facebook) that teens can only turn off with a parent's permission.

Likes will be hidden, on teen's profiles and those that they interact with.

"School mode", or a mute on notifications between 08:00 and 15:00 during school days.

Prompts noting when a teen has hit 15 minutes of continual use. Then notifications when cumulative use has hit 60 and 90 minutes.

The ability to choose a feed that is not driven by an algorithm.

The ability to turn off autoplay for videos and content.

Extreme make-up filters will no longer be accessible.

As for the new daily time limit for teen users, that will be reduced to one hour of total daily use should other social media platforms like TikTok, Snap and YouTube also agree to implement new restrictions for young users.

Bonta urged such platforms to do so, saying the settlement with Meta "is a good blueprint" for other companies to follow.

Should they not, he suggested on Wednesday that his office would now be "more focused" on bringing changes to the entire social media industry.

Meta also said TikTok and YouTube should implement the same safety features for their younger users.

"Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta's Mahoney said.

YouTube and TikTok have been contacted for comment.

District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb called the Meta deal a "monumental public health victory".

He added: "The safety features Meta is required to install will fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook."

News.title: Rocky Horror star Tim Curry dies at 80
News.content:
Born in Warrington in 1946, Curry's first acting job after university was in the original London production of groundbreaking rock musical Hair in 1968.

In 1973, a fellow cast member, Richard O'Brien, asked Curry to audition for his new musical, and cast him in the role of the flamboyant lingerie-clad "sweet transvestite" Dr Frank-N-Furter.

Curry first put his stamp on the character of the riotous scientist on stage in the upstairs theatre at London's Royal Court in 1973.

The show's popularity snowballed and resulted in a big-screen adaptation, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and O'Brien.

It was not an immediate hit at cinemas but became a fan favourite and holds the record for the longest-running theatrical release in film history.

Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played the role in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".

In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".

"Being compared to you has been one of the greatest compliments I've ever received, even though it's a comparison no one could ever hope to live up to," he wrote in the letter.

The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's deliver of the famous line from the musical, "Don't dream it, be it".

News.title: Murder arrests after fire kills two including child near Middlesbrough
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people died in a house fire including a child, police have confirmed.

The blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a 48-year-old woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said the two victims were yet to be formally identified.

The men, aged 23 and 31, have been arrested on suspicion of murder and are in police custody, the force said.

Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area and encourage anyone who has concerns, or who may have information, to approach our officers."

Patrols have been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said earlier.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California, and landed in Birmingham shortly before midday.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

There did not appear to be a police presence as Harry and his family left the airport, a source told the BBC.

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

Though not confirming the family's arrival in the UK, a spokesman for the Sussexes did say their chickens were staying in California, but they were bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them.

The chickens, which the couple rescued, have regularly featured on Meghan's Instagram account and also appeared in her Netflix programme.

News.title: New thunderstorm warnings for parts of UK as rain set to continue
News.content:
The Met Office has issued fresh warnings for thunderstorms that will bring more wet weather to parts of the UK on Thursday.

The first warning is valid from 02:00 BST with thunder and heavy rain due to move across south-east England in the early hours of Thursday morning.

A second comes into force at 06:00 BST for a wider area of England and Wales. This will last through to 22:00 and may become slow moving in the afternoon and evening.

Downpours could bring localised flash flooding and travel disruption - with the wettest areas potentially seeing 75mm (3in) of rain. Large hail, lightning and gusty winds could accompany the showers and it will feel rather humid for many.

Spells of rain are set to continue over the weekend - a bank holiday for England, Wales and Northern Ireland - accompanied by windy conditions in the south.

News.title: Stourbridge fires that razed 19 homes were accidental, say investigators
News.content:
Two fires that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge were started accidentally in fields where farming machinery was in use, according to West Midlands Fire Service.

Investigators established agricultural equipment was being used in the vicinity of fields immediately before the fires were first reported. The service would not confirm the type of machinery.

The first fire started in a field near Racecourse Lane at about 13:27 BST on 13 August, while a second began shortly afterwards in a field near Quarry Park Road.

The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alert to millions of people across England and Wales, warning them against "any activity that could start a fire".

News.title: US designates Palestine Action a terrorist group
News.content:
The US has imposed sanctions on Palestine Action, designating it as a terrorist group.

The US Department of the Treasury said it had "taken action" against the UK-based group, which it accused of supporting "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020".

Supporting Palestine Action became illegal in the UK in 2025 after the government banned it under anti-terror legislation.

The group's co-founder Huda Ammori responded in a social media post, saying: "As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical."

In a statement to the BBC, Ammori said the group's actions had "always been about saving lives", adding the ban should be a "wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and democracy".

Announcing the move in a statement on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear.

"Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated."

The sanctions imposed include freezing any assets belonging to the group that are either based in the US or in the control of US citizens.

The US ban on the group is part of a wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration against what it says are far-left terror organisations around the world.

The Department of Treasury accused Palestine Action of having supported "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government".

Palestine Action, which used so-called direct action tactics against Israeli-linked arms companies in the UK, has been facing an ongoing legal battle to get its UK ban overturned.

In June, Court of Appeal judges ruled the UK government made a "justified and proportionate" interference on freedom of expression rights.

But Palestine Action has since been given permission to challenge the decision at the Supreme Court.

More than 2,000 people are facing potential trial after being arrested for protesting against the ban by allegedly declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group during mass demonstrations.

Separately, four of its members were jailed in June for a break-in at a defence firm that caused more than Â£1m worth of damage, with one person sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

News.title: Nepalese authorities say 33 UK nationals missing after flash floods
News.content:
Thirty-three people from the UK are among hundreds feared missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.

Flooding and mud slides hit the Rasuaw region in the morning on Wednesday, killing at least 157 people in Nepal and three in Tibet, according to Chinese state media.

Nepal police said 579 tourists are missing - including 466 who are foreign nationals, from 28 different countries.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is in touch with local authorities and "will do everything we can" to support British nationals affected, urging those in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

The UK Foreign Office said it is working closely with Nepalese authorities "following concerning reports of British nationals who are missing" and has encouraged Brits to follow local guidance and "remain alert to the changing situation".

According to Nepal police, 113 of the missing tourists are Nepalese, and 54 are from the US.

Excursion company Alpine Eco Trek, which offers guided expeditions and tours in Nepal, confirmed to the BBC that it has not been able to establish contact with a group of 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash, and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

The company said it had made attempts to charter a rescue helicopter, and will continue to help with ongoing rescue efforts on Thursday.

According to the company's travel logs, shared with the Press Association, the age of the missing British citizens ranges from 13 to 65.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he is "deeply concerned" by news of the flash flooding, and wrote on social media: "All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home".

In a joint statement with Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland, the UK embassy in Nepal urged British nationals in Nepal to "exercise caution in affected areas".

News.title: King and Queen to visit the Caribbean in autumn tour
News.content:
King Charles III and Queen Camilla will travel to the Caribbean later this year, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The royal pair will travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with the King also visiting the Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip.

The tour - planned for 27 October to 4 November - will "celebrate the communities, cultures and nature within the Commonwealth family," the palace said on Wednesday.

It marks the first time the King has visited the Caribbean since 2021, when he travelled to Barbados to see the country officially removed Queen Elizabeth II as its head of state and become the world's newest republic.

The monarch, who was the Prince of Wales at the time, acknowledged the "appalling atrocity of slavery" the Caribbean island suffered during a speech he made.

He also visited Antigua and Barbuda in 2017 following the widespread devastation caused by Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and made official visits to Guyana in 2000 and the Bahamas in 1973.

He travelled across the Atlantic Ocean earlier this year when he visited Bermuda in May, where he is also head of state.

The trip marked his first royal visit as monarch to a British overseas territory and came after a state visit to the US.

News.title: Boy, 15, arrested over stabbing at Brent Council HQ
News.content:
On Wednesday, one man who works in the area told BBC London the stabbing "felt normal".

"These things happen every single day here, in London and in the area. It's not a big surprise," he said.

"You see things like this happen all the time. You read the news and every single day there's something going on. If it's in Harrow, or Wembley, or Neasden, or Willesden or wherever, it doesn't come as a surprise."

However, one woman who lives in the area said the stabbing "came as a shock".

"I've never felt unsafe around here and it's a bit concerning," she said.

Student Demi said he felt "uneasy" after the stabbing.

"It's not really an unsafe area," he said. "It's a bit out of the ordinary.

"These things happen, unfortunately, but it's a bit strange to have it happen here."

Kate, another local resident, said: "Usually we feel very safe. We're fortunate living in this area because there are lots of security patrols and there are always people around.

"Stabbings are terrible tragedies, but it could happen anywhere, and I know there are areas of London that have to deal with that every day.

"I still feel safe. We're fortunate to live here with so much security; I wish that everyone lived in such an area."

News.title: Call with couple in Iran prison 'enormous relief'
News.content:
The family of an East Sussex couple detained in Iran say they have spoken to them for the first time in three months.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges, which they both deny, and are being held in Evin prison.

Lindsay's son, Joe Bennett, said hearing his mum's voice was "an enormous relief" and encouraged the government to visit the couple as the UK embassy in Iran reopened last week after closing due to ongoing security concerns in the region.

A Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) spokesperson confirmed staff had returned to the embassy and said the pair's health and welfare was a "top priority".

Bennett, who lives in Folkestone, said the 12-minute phone call was their first official conversation since the couple ended their hunger strikes.

He said his mother told him she and her husband were "slowly rebuilding their strength" after losing a substantial amount of weight.

"Just hearing mum's voice properly again was an enormous relief," he added.

"We only had 12 minutes, but after everything that has happened, those 12 minutes meant a great deal."

Bennett said his mother and her partner had remained "mentally resilient" and "determined to return home".

Bennett claimed the conversation was "monitored" and conducted with an interpreter present, limiting what could be discussed.

He is now calling for the UK Government to take "swift action" to arrange an urgent consular visit and ensure the couple receive appropriate medical care.

He also hopes to meet with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and for the government to use all available diplomatic and legal channels to secure their release.

He said the family was particularly concerned the couple did not receive a full medical assessment following their hunger strikes.

News.title: Inquest begins into death of Jason Arday
News.content:
An inquest has begun into the death of Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row.

He was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, days after resigning from his post.

His appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Senior coroner Dr Julian Morris said on Wednesday: "The various reports have given me reason to suspect that Professor Arday died an unnatural death 12 days ago."

He told London Inner South Coroner's Court: "It therefore follows that I must open an investigation."

The Metropolitan Police said at the time that Arday's death was being treated as unexpected and was "not believed to be suspicious".

Arday was found "unresponsive" by family members at his home in Battersea, the inquest heard on Wednesday. Despite resuscitation efforts he was pronounced dead, the inquest was told.

The 41-year-old had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

He said controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The claims emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Such scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

After his death, his family issued a statement saying they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former Cambridge professor before his death.

Arday's memoir is due to be published in the UK on Thursday. The publisher, Simon & Schuster, announced on Monday that the book will be released as planned, with his family saying: "It is only right that we honour his wishes."

News.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
News.content:
People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get Â£30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced.

Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets.

To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said.

HMRC said its customer service had "vastly" improved over the past two years, with average call waiting times now 11 minutes and more of its services being delivered online or through its app.

In January 2025, the Public Accounts committee accused HMRC of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels" in a highly critical report., external

The MPs' report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system".

Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London.

"Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP.

"So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

"I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a Â£30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay.

"And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance."

The HMRC said 80% of customer interactions now took place digitally, reducing the time spent on the phone to advisers, who were there to deal with vulnerable or digitally excluded customers or those with particularly complex problems.

A spokesperson said: "Our customer service performance has improved significantly with average call wait times now around 11 minutes.

"Overall customer satisfaction is at around 80% with more people than ever using our digital services, including millions using the HMRC app."

Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses if Reform wins power.

He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises.

The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU.

Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans".

News.title: Yellow warnings remain in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid until 22:00 BST, and was amended on Wednesday morning to cover northern and eastern Wales, as well as north-west England, the Midlands and parts of eastern and southern England.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

Another Met Office yellow warning is in place for Thursday, when more thunderstorms are expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged people would find the increase "difficult" but highlighted his move to cut VAT from electricity bills, which he said would help from October.

He said the government would "continue to look... at how we get energy prices down in the long term".

As well as the VAT cut, the government said the warm homes discount would take Â£150 off bills for six million households this winter.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government must "put cheap energy first", saying while it had promised to cut bills by Â£300 they had "gone up by nearly Â£400 instead".

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said Burnham needed to "wake up to the scale of the challenge" and make bold changes to lower bills.

Reform UK treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick said households faced a "difficult period ahead" and said Labour's "net zero ideology" is driving up bills.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed in, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use proceeds to help those struggling with bills.

Longer term, he said Burnham should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting," he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

He said the gap between gas and electricity bills meant it would be cheaper for households to transition to heat pumps.

The FBI is investigating another cyberattack in the United States’ water sector, this time involving a small developer of water utility technology.

The breach at the Kansas firm was apparently not part of a suspected Iranian-affiliated campaign against water plants in Minnesota and other states starting in July but highlights growing threats to water infrastructure.

Both the company and the FBI have confirmed the breach at Micro-Comm in Olathe, Kansas, which had not been previously reported. Responsibility was claimed by Barracuda, a relatively new ransomware group that says it is motivated by profit and is not government sponsored.

On August 6, the group published what it claimed was nearly 850,000 corporate files comprising roughly 644 gigabytes of data. Micro-Comm manufactures programmable logic controllers (PLCs), computerized devices used to manage machinery within critical infrastructure networks, specifically wastewater processing facilities.

The incident at Micro-Comm underscores the challenges of defending local American water systems and third-party vendors against increasing cyberattacks aimed at computer systems embedded across the nation's critical infrastructure.

The breach occurred amid a spate of late July hacks directed at PLCs in Minnesota and at least six other states. Cybersecurity experts believe those intrusions formed part of an ongoing Iranian-linked cyber campaign.

On July 30, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a warning that hackers were actively targeting PLCs from U.S.-based Rockwell Automation, France's Schneider Electric, and Germany's Siemens.

CISA subsequently noted on August 19 that threat actors were utilizing AI to streamline attacks on Siemens systems. The company later stated it was coordinating with CISA and affirmed that its products are safe.

Dixon Land, a spokesperson for the FBI’s Kansas City field office, said in an email that the bureau was in communication with Micro-Comm regarding the incident and coordinating with additional law enforcement entities. CISA referred inquiries to Micro-Comm.

Jim Cote, a co-owner of the firm, stated in an interview that the business identified the intrusion on July 31.

Cote noted that the documents released by the hackers did not include sensitive material such as customer passwords and credentials, which remain stored by clients, or information concerning Micro-Comm's capability to remotely access its hardware.

In an August 8 newsletter to clients, the business reported experiencing a limited malware attack, adding that any sensitive details contained within the files were encrypted. Micro-Comm stated the breach was "in no way related to water system hacks currently being reported on the news."

Cote added that the FBI advised the firm that the security breach was an opportunistic attack rather than one specifically targeting Micro-Comm, though the business advised customers to update passwords as a precautionary measure.

According to internet-monitoring platform Censys, approximately 200 deployments of the company's SCADAview CSX systems across U.S. states remain accessible via the internet.

An index of files compiled by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch lists references to specific public-sector clients, including local municipalities and a U.S. military facility, along with staff names and technical product details such as diagrams.

Tom Hegel, a senior threat researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, observed that while the document leak does not indicate any water facility suffered operational disruption, the exposed data could assist malicious actors over time.

News.title: Carabao Cup draw LIVE: Man City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Man Utd learn third round ties
News.content:
The Carabao Cup third round draw takes place this evening ( PA Archive )

The Carabao Cup gathers pace tonight when the third round ties are decided to complete the Premier League’s involvement in the competition.

So far the nine Premier League teams in Europe have sat out as the second round edges towards completion, but holders Manchester City, Arsenal, who lost to City in last season’s final, Manchester United, Aston Villa, Liverpool, Bournemouth, Sunderland, Brighton and Crystal Palace will all learn their third-round opponents tonight.

There has already been a pre-draw, with those aforementioned teams set to be separated in order to avoid a clash in Uefa competitions. Of the eight teams in the Champions League and Europa League, six were drawn at home with Arsenal and Aston Villa heading on the road.

The draw will be completed before Chelsea face Luton and Fulham face AFC Wimbledon tomorrow evening to conclude the second round.

News.title: Teen receives life sentence after pleading guilty to murdering 10-year-old cousin
News.content:

A teenager has been sentenced to life in prison after pleading guilty on Wednesday to the 2022 murder of his 10-year-old cousin in Wisconsin.

According to the criminal complaint, Carson Peters-Berger, now 18, persuaded Iliana “Lily” Peters to leave a trail and explore the surrounding woods as she was riding her bicycle home from her aunt's house in Chippewa Falls on April 24, 2022.

Her father reported the fourth-grade student missing around 9 pm on Sunday after she failed to return home.

The two homes were about a six-minute walk apart.

The young girl's body was discovered the following day.

An autopsy determined she had been beaten, strangled, and sexually assaulted.

Peters-Berger, who was 14 at the time of the homicide, was arrested the day after Peters' body was located. He was charged as an adult.

Relatives of Iliana “Lily” Peters comfort each other as they pray together at a vigil for the 10 year-old girl at Valley Vineyard Church in Chippewa Falls ( AP )

At the time of his arrest, prosecutors said the eighth grader admitted in statements to law enforcement that “his intention was to rape and kill the victim from the get-go” when they left the house together and headed down the walking trail.

Chippewa County Judge Steven Gibbs accepted the guilty plea on Wednesday and handed down the life sentence.

Under a plea agreement, two additional charges, first-degree sexual assault causing great bodily harm and first-degree child sexual assault involving a child under 13, were dismissed.

Peters-Berger's attorneys, Michael Cohen and Alicia Linzmeier, did not respond to emails requesting comment.

His defense team had previously tried to transfer the case to juvenile court, where proceedings are confidential, arguing he would not receive necessary mental health treatment within the adult justice system.

However, the judge refused, stating the severe nature of the offenses warranted trial as an adult. A state appeals court also affirmed keeping the case in adult court.

President Donald Trump has still not picked a replacement for his outgoing press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, just days before she leaves the White House.

“I have never had so many job applications in my life,” Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One last Friday. “They all want that job.”

Trump is still mulling over his options, administration officials told CBS News, but the clock is ticking. Leavitt’s last day is expected to be Friday.

For now, top Trump officials will lead White House press briefings on a rotation, according to the sources.

Several names both inside and outside the administration have been floated since Trump announced earlier this month that Leavitt would leave her post to spend more time with her family, but two of CBS News’ sources said there are no front-runners yet.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has still not picked a replacement for his press secretary Karoline Leavitt days before she leaves the White House ( AFP via Getty Images )

One name that has been suggested is Scott Jennings, a conservative commentator for CNN who is constantly making headlines by sparring with his panelists.

Jennings, a former staffer for Mitch McConnell, became an early favorite for the role, CNN reported Thursday, citing multiple sources familiar with the matter.

Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles, who CBS News says is involved in the search for the new press secretary, recently met with Jennings at a Washington, D.C. steakhouse, according to two of CNN’s sources.

Earlier this month, when Jennings’ fellow panelists on CNN NewsNight asked if he’d be up for the role, he said, “I don’t know.”

open image in gallery Conservative commentator Scott Jennings reportedly became an early favorite for the role, but when asked if he’d be up for it, he said, ‘I don’t know’ ( Getty Images Courtesy of the Rainey Center )

Katie Miller, the wife of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, has also been floated as a potential replacement.

Miller has worked in politics before as a press person for the Homeland Security Department and former Vice President Mike Pence. She currently hosts The Katie Miller Podcast, which several administration officials have made appearances on, including Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

There was also speculation that Trump’s former personal attorney, Alina Habba, could be on the White House’s list, but she has put those rumors to rest.

“Flattered by the Kalshi odds, but I’m not in the running for any job. However, if I’m getting a new one, I’d love for one of these anonymous sources to let me know first,” she wrote on X on August 19. “Fake news remains the undefeated champ…well…until I come at them.”

open image in gallery Several names already inside Trump’s press team have also been floated, including White House Communications Director Steven Cheung ( Pool/Getty Images )

Several names already inside Trump’s press team have also been floated, including White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly.

It’s unclear who Trump is seriously considering for press secretary as he has thrown out multiple names that could fill the role.

When asked by a reporter last Friday who he would want to replace Leavitt, Trump said, “Maybe you.”

“How about Scott Jennings, sir?” another reporter asked. “Scott Jennings is good,” Trump replied.

“I don’t know. Maybe Margo,” Trump added, referring to his communications advisor Margo Martin.

News.title: Tottenham vs Charlton LIVE: Savio gets goal and assist on debut as Spurs dominate Carabao Cup clash
News.content:
'We need more time' says Tottenham head coach after Brentford loss

Tottenham cruised into the third round of the Carabao Cup after a 5-1 victory over Charlton Athletic on Wednesday night.

Roberto De Zerbi’s men brushed off the weekend’s chastising defeat to Brentford with a dominant performance against the Championship club to book their place in the next round of the league cup.

Mikey Moore’s strike found the back of the net to break the deadlock and less than four minutes later Dominic Solanke hooked in the second.

Kevin Danso came off the bench to nod in a third goal with his first touch before Tottenham’s new signing, Savio, made his debut and collected a goal and an assist to cap off an impressive night for De Zerbi and his men.

Lloyd Jones headed in a consolation goal for Charlton but they head out of the cup and can focus on their league campaign.

News.title: PC Andrew Harper’s killers ‘to be excluded from early release scheme’
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Pc Andrew Harper’s killers will be excluded from the early release scheme and will remain in prison, reports say.

Offenders serving sentences for specific categories of manslaughter will no longer qualify for early discharge, including Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, according to The Telegraph.

Andy Burnham previously promised to do "everything possible" to ensure the pair were not freed from custody, following widespread condemnation of the scheme.

However, the Prime Minister declined to confirm this specific change relating to "unlawful act" manslaughter earlier this month, telling reporters it was "speculation".

He ordered a review into the policy, which is being conducted by Justice Secretary Alex Norris and is expected to be published when Parliament returns from summer recess in September.

Mr Norris was asked by Mr Burnham “to develop a plan to maximise public safety and minimise the early release of prisoners”.

Police chiefs have since been told Mr Norris will introduce secondary legislation to amend the Sentencing Act, according to the newspaper.

Bowers and Cole, two of Pc Harper’s three killers, were passengers in the car that dragged the police officer down a country road after he got caught in a strap attached to the vehicle as they fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019.

Pc Andrew Harper and his widow Lissie Harper ( Thames Valley Police/PA )

Under the scheme’s current rules, they would be released next year, halfway through their 13-year sentences.

Labour’s early release scheme started in September 2024 with the aim of easing overcrowding in jails.

It allows certain prisoners to be released after serving 40% of their fixed-term sentence, rather than the usual 50%.

The 2026 Sentencing Act, which became law earlier this year, allows for an expansion of the early release scheme by reducing the threshold from 40% of a fixed-term sentence to a third.

Since becoming Prime Minister, Mr Burnham has excluded rapists and child sex offenders from being eligible for the scheme.

Unlawful act manslaughter is when a person causes the death of another while committing a separate illegal act.

A Government spokesperson said: “The death of Pc Andrew Harper was a horrific crime.

“Our thoughts are with his family and friends, and we share the anger from the police community that we are in this position.

“The Prime Minister has asked the Justice Secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of Pc Harper.

“Thanks to tireless campaigning by Andrew’s family, Harper’s Law means that anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime now gets a mandatory life sentence.

“This Government has gone further by introducing a presumption that anyone convicted of murdering a police, prison or probation officer is handed a whole-life order.”

Two Dodgers fans who say they were subjected to excessive force and wrongly ejected from Dodger Stadium in 2024 are asking a judge to let them tell jurors about the 2011 parking lot attack on San Francisco Giants fan Bryan Stow.

Luis Ortiz and Joanna Maria Iniguez allege in a Los Angeles Superior Court lawsuit that security guards removed them from the stadium after they objected to how two other fans who ran onto the field were treated.

Filed in January 2025, the lawsuit accuses the Dodgers of assault, battery, false imprisonment, civil rights violations and negligent hiring, retention and supervision. The trial is scheduled for Nov. 2.

open image in gallery The lawsuit accuses the Dodgers of assault, battery, false imprisonment, civil rights violations and negligent hiring, retention and supervision ( Jayne Kamin-Oncea-Imagn Images No file chosen Add Video From your media library Open library )

On Monday, the plaintiffs' attorney filed court papers with Judge Upinder Kalra stating his opposition to a team pretrial motion to exclude any evidence regarding the attack on Stow.

In 2011, Stow was attacked in one of the venue's parking lots. A Los Angeles Superior Court jury in 2014 awarded about $18 million in damages to Stow while attributing 75 percent of the liability to the two assailants who beat him into a coma, 25 precent to the team, and none to former Dodgers owner Frank McCourt.

"The fact that security at Dodgers games has increased to the point that it currently exists, largely as a result of the Bryan Stow incident, is clearly relevant evidence," the plaintiffs' lawyer contends in his court papers.

The outgrowth of substantially increased security by the Dodgers in response to its alleged lack of same during the Stow beating is relevant to prove that the Dodgers' alleged zero-tolerance policy includes permitting its security personnel to "run roughshod" over even minor encounters with patrons like Ortiz and Iniguez, the pair's lawyer further states.

In their previous court papers, Dodgers attorneys denied the plaintiffs' allegations and said any damages they suffered was due to the "reckless, negligent or improper conduct of plaintiffs themselves."

Ortiz and Iniguez attended the game between the Dodgers and the San Diego Padres on Oct. 5, 2024, at Dodger Stadium. Both saw security guards apprehend two other fans who ran onto the field and believed the pair were being handled too harshly, according to the suit, which further states that Iniguez made an obscene finger gesture toward the guards.

When a female guard subsequently approached the plaintiffs and told them they would have to leave the venue, they protested that they had done nothing wrong and were only being ejected because they objected to the treatment of the fans who went onto the field, the suit states.

The guards then forcibly removed Ortiz and Iniguez from their seats and both suffered shoulder injuries, according to the suit, which further states Iniguez suffered injuries to her arm, wrist, elbow and hand.

Ortiz and Iniguez have suffered lost income as well as emotional distress due to their injuries, the suit states. The suit does not indicate any relationship between the plaintiffs or say if they went to the game together.

News.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after mosquito imported on plane
News.content:
Five airport workers in Frankfurt have been infected with malaria and one has died after being bitten by a stowaway mosquito, health officials have said.

The employees are thought to have been infected in early July, but their diagnosis was delayed due to a lack of travel history to malaria-endemic regions, according to the Robert Koch Institute, Germany’s federal agency responsible for disease control.

It is believed that they were bitten by mosquitoes which arrived at the airport on a plane, most likely from Africa, where 95 per cent of global malaria cases are found.

The five surviving airport workers – who are all male and are said to work in different parts of the facility and in different jobs – are undergoing medical care.

Traps have now been installed across the airport in an attempt to catch any remaining mosquitoes and analyse their origin, according to an airport spokesperson.

It is not the first time that Frankfurt Airport, Germany’s busiest travel hub, has recorded a case of malaria, according to the Robert Koch Institute, which added that there was another incidence in 2023.

More than 610,000 people die of malaria every year, the overwhelming majority children under five in Africa who are unable to quickly access treatment.

The disease, which is caused by a parasite carried by infected mosquitoes, is largely curable if treated early with antimalarials.

In Britain and Europe, there are thousands of imported cases of malaria every year reported in returning travellers from Africa and Asia – but local transmission is exceedingly rare.

Of the 5,000 or so cases recorded in Europe every year, typically just five are caught locally – either from an airport or from a non-infected European mosquito picking up the disease from a sickened person and spreading it to others.

Early symptoms include fever, headaches, and chills, which can quickly develop into multi-organ failure.

Vaccines were made available for the first time in 2024 and are licenced for use in young children in Africa, although they are thought to be only between 30 and 50 per cent effective at preventing the disease.

News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”

News.title: The five best coastal places to retire in the UK
News.content:
How equity release can help you purchase a seaside property

UK homeowners aged 55 or over may be able to use equity release in two main ways: either to help fund the purchase of a second home, or to buy a new home and release equity from that property as part of the same legal transaction. Seeking professional advice is key to understanding which option may be right for you.



The most popular equity release product is a lifetime mortgage. A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home. It will reduce the value of your estate and could affect your entitlement to means-tested benefits. There is no obligation to make monthly repayments with a lifetime mortgage, although you can choose to make some if you wish. Instead, the full amount plus interest is only repaid when the last homeowner dies or enters permanent long-term care, and this is usually done with the sale of the home.



You must always seek professional help when considering equity release. Make sure your adviser is looking at products from lenders that are members of the Equity Release Council. The Equity Release Council, the industry trade body, requires its members to offer plans that comply with its product standards.

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.
