World.title: Govt. increases SCT beneficiaries in Chama
World.content:
Chama Assistant Community Development Officer, Charity Mpundu, has disclosed that the number of beneficiaries under the Social Cash Transfer (SCT) programme has increased from about 900 to over 10,000.

In an interview with the media, Ms. Mpundu said the increase has enabled more vulnerable people in the district to benefit from Government’s social protection programmes.

She said the beneficiaries include elderly people, persons with disabilities and female-headed households, among other categories of people with social needs.

Some beneficiaries who spoke to ZANIS, said the money received under the SCT programme has helped them meet household needs, particularly in rural areas where economic activities are largely dependent on farming.

One of the beneficiaries, Umoza Kumwenda, an elderly man, thanked Government for introducing the programme.

Mr Kumwenda said the K1,200 he receives, helps him purchase essential household goods and meet his basic needs while awaiting the next payment.

Another beneficiary, Tasiya Goma, commended Government for the initiative, describing it as an important intervention in supporting elderly and vulnerable people in society.

Ms Goma said the programme is particularly important in Chama because most households depend on farming, which does not always provide a regular source of income throughout the year.

World.title: Zambia: 'I Became Protective' - A Cancer Survivor's Fight to Fix Zambia's Health System
World.content:
"Once you go through something as traumatic as a cancer diagnosis, you automatically become protective of the next person," said Karen Nakawala, a Zambian broadcaster and cervical cancer survivor.

Nakawala knows that trauma firsthand. In 2019, her life changed when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer.

The diagnosis forced Nakawala to confront the disease she would later dedicate much of her life to talking about publicly. After treatment, she converted her experience into advocacy, determined to help other women recognize the importance of early screening and seeking care.

During her own treatment, she said she saw gaps throughout the healthcare system, with many women falling through the cracks, a realization that pushed her from patient to advocate. "I believe that cancer healthcare solutions should be culturally grounded given our diverse culture and should be rooted in those who live it," she said.

Through her journey, she created Teal Sisters Foundation, an organization that has become a platform for women to access information, share their experiences, and seek support without judgment. Her private Facebook community, initially created as a safe space where women could speak openly about their health without being judged, has grown to more than 137,000 members. The women-only Facebook community aims to boost access to cervical cancer screening, prevention and treatment in Zambia.

Cancer is an increasing burden in Zambia.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer indicates that cervical cancer is still the most prevalent form of cancer in the country, with 4,730 estimated new cases in 2024. It was also the most prevalent form of cancer causing death and accounted for 2,769 cancer-related deaths in the same year. Breast cancer was the second most prevalent form of cancer among women, with 1,555 estimated new cases and 730 deaths.

Zambia has the third-highest burden of cervical cancer in the WHO African Region after Eswatini and Malawi

There is also a huge shortage of specialists in the country. Ministry of Health data shows that Zambia has just six oncologists serving a population of about 20 million people. To help close this gap, Zambia has, since 2006, invested in training nurses to play a greater role in cervical cancer prevention and care, including screening, treatment and vaccination.

Against this backdrop, the reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging unit at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital takes on particular significance.

For years, patients needing radiotherapy faced a major gap in the country's cancer-care system. Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital was shut down in 2020 for a major upgrade. Its closure left patients with fewer treatment options and forced them, in some cases, to seek care outside the country. Nearly 1,000 patients were left waiting for radiotherapy during the interruption, with about 600 referred to India for treatment, according to health authorities.

Nakawala described the six-year gap as "the worst period in Zambia's cancer healthcare space."

She said the country lost many women to breast and, in particular, cervical cancer, some diagnosed at early stages that could have been treated with good outcomes had radiotherapy been available. Those who could afford it traveled outside the country for treatment, she said, at "an astronomical out-of-pocket spend for families." That gap, she said, has left a large backlog of patients now waiting for treatment, placing pressure on the newly reopened unit.

Zambian Cancer Society/LinkedIn The opening of the refurbished radiotherapy and imaging section of the Cancer Diseases Hospital, Lusaka

Zambia's reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging cancer treatment facility at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital pushed for better women's cancer care in Africa. The facility was upgraded and commissioned by President Hakainde Hichilema in August, 2026. It can now treat up to 60 patients a day.

For patients, the restoration of the service means that specialised cancer treatment can once again be accessed closer to home, reducing the delays, travel and financial pressure associated with seeking care abroad. The hospital's upgraded radiotherapy services include external beam radiotherapy, treatment planning and brachytherapy, supported by advanced imaging equipment.

"The first thing that comes to mind is the relief that patients and their caregivers feel," said Nakawala. "It is always better to receive treatment close to home where you are surrounded by loved ones."

Cancer treatment can be isolating, she said, and travelling abroad can deepen that isolation when patients cannot afford to take a caregiver with them. The reopening of the radiation unit therefore brings hope while potentially shortening treatment delays and reducing cancer mortality in the country.

Still, she cautioned that 60 patients a day "is not enough, but it is a positive step forward," and that treatment capacity should grow once the unit is fully operational. However, the government must ensure that there is a solid plan for servicing and reinvesting so that we get uninterrupted optimal operation and services, which will be much to the benefit of both government and patients, she added.

Hichilema said that the installation of advanced cancer treatment equipment at the Cancer Diseases Hospital in Lusaka is a major step towards positioning Zambia as a regional centre for cancer diagnosis and treatment. He said Zambia is now the third country in Africa, after South Africa and Egypt, to have the equipment, which will allow patients to access specialised cancer treatment locally rather than travelling abroad, including to India.

The reopening comes at a critical time for Zambia, where the burden of cancer continues to place pressure on an already stretched health system. The burdens of breast cancer, cervical cancer, and HIV are overlapping among women in low- and middle-income countries.

Nakawala said the six-year closure exposed how centralized cancer treatment has been in Zambia. Even when cancer was caught early, she said, most deaths during that period were driven by lack of access and delayed treatment, worsened whenever machines broke down, and treatment was interrupted - sometimes never resuming. She pointed to several consequences of the resulting gaps in services: late-stage diagnosis, as patients often wait to seek care until pain and side effects become advanced; higher mortality tied to delayed or absent treatment; and a heavier financial burden on the country, since sending patients abroad for treatment costs more than treating them at home.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in sub-Saharan Africa, with an estimated 129 000 new cases in 2020.

Yet survival remains far lower than in high-income countries, with five-year survival estimated at around or below 50% in the region. The burden is expected to grow sharply, with the number of women diagnosed each year projected to nearly double by 2040. The African Breast Cancer – Disparities in Outcomes (ABC-DO) study found that 50% to 90% of women in different African countries are diagnosed when the cancer has already reached an advanced stage, when treatment is more difficult, and the chances of cure are lower.

According to the study, inadequate treatment access and late diagnosis are responsible for the poor outcomes. Many women recognise changes in their breasts and seek medical help, but face long waits before receiving a diagnosis and starting treatment.

WHO Africa Zambia steps up cervical cancer screening with HPV testing

In the study, half of women in Zambia and Namibia and three-quarters in Uganda reported having breast symptoms for more than six months. Survival at three years was just 46% among women in Zambia and Uganda, compared with 58% among Black women in Namibia and South Africa and 36% in Nigeria. The study estimates that more than one-third of breast cancer deaths in sub-Saharan Africa could be prevented through earlier diagnosis and timely access to high-quality treatment.

Nakawala attributed the same regional shortfall in equipment behind those numbers. "38% of countries in sub-Saharan Africa have no radiotherapy equipment at all," she said, "and 60-70% of women are diagnosed at a late stage."

She said five in ten women diagnosed with breast cancer in sub-Saharan Africa will not survive five years, compared with nine in ten who survive in high-income countries. She listed stigma, lack of awareness and information, financial constraints, distance, and limited access to screening and timely treatment as the biggest barriers keeping women from care.

"In Zambia, cervical cancer is the number one killer of women, yet it is highly preventable. It is followed by breast cancer, which, if caught early, can be treated with good outcomes," said Nakawala.

Breast cancer can also be treated with good outcomes when detected early.

Breast cancer, she said, is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women in Africa, with cases expected to double by 2040.

Zambia's ambition to become a regional centre of excellence in cancer care will therefore require more than a single upgraded facility. She said decentralization is essential so the burden doesn't fall entirely on the newly upgraded Lusaka unit. She added that two additional centres are under construction in Ndola to serve the northern region and in Livingstone to serve the south.

Beyond radiotherapy, Nakawala said government needs to work more closely with civil society organizations to raise awareness and share information with women, particularly given the gap created by years without radiation treatment. She called for greater investment in women's health and more equitable access to care. She said that Zambia should align more closely with the World Health Organization's Global Cancer Initiative to speed up early detection and diagnosis and improve survival.

She also pointed to the role of groups like the Africa Breast Cancer Council, of which she is a member, in helping governments strengthen advocacy, stakeholder engagement, and community efforts to reduce stigma by sharing best practices across member countries.

Nakawala argued that geography should not determine whether a woman survives cancer.

"No one single person should be disadvantaged because of their geographical location. We are all entitled to good healthcare services regardless of geography," she said.

She said that when the world talks about universal healthcare, it must reach beyond urban areas to everyone, which is why decentralizing cancer care matters so much. For Zambia and the wider region, that means bringing cancer services closer to the people who need them through greater investment, training and decentralisation.

"Let us all be intentional when it comes to cancer," Nakawala said. "Governments and international communities should support advocacy programmes which are centred on prevention and early diagnosis."

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Vows Arrests Over Anti-Migrant Violence

President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators of violence against foreign nationals will be arrested and prosecuted once police have gathered sufficient evidence. He rejected claims that the government tolerates xenophobia. Ramaphosa also denied that South Africa had been isolated by other African leaders over the recent violence. He said the country remained a respected pan-African actor. He said the government had engaged African leaders on migration and that regional cooperation was needed to address the underlying causes of migration, including insecurity and poor governance.

Nigeria Launches Manhunt After Mass Abductions

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who attacked four villages in Niger State. The attackers killed more than 40 people and abducted an unverified number of residents. Local officials said that as many as 500 people may have been taken. A video released by the kidnappers appeared to show some of the captives alive in a forest. Survivors have fled to neighbouring states and Benin. Others are receiving treatment for injuries. The attacks, which also involved improvised explosive devices, come amid growing insecurity in the region and concerns over the spread of jihadist groups along Nigeria's north-western border areas.

Anger Mounts After Deadly Guinea Landfill Collapse

Two days after a deadly landfill collapse in Guinea, rescuers are using giant excavators to search for victims. Anger is growing among residents who said that they had repeatedly warned authorities about the landfill's dangerous condition and urged its closure. At least 31 people have died, and more than 20 were injured after a landfill collapsed in Conakry's Dar es Salam neighbourhood following heavy rain. Hundreds of displaced residents are sheltering at a school, and dozens of households remain at risk. The site has been linked to previous deadly collapses and severe pollution. The government plans to replace it with a new landfill, which has been underway since 2022.

ICC Clears Libya Case for First Trial

The International Criminal Court has confirmed 17 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity against former Libyan security official Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri. This paves the way for the first Libya-related case to reach trial since the ICC opened its investigation 15 years ago. El Hishri is accused of torture, rape, murder, enslavement and other abuses against Libyan and migrant detainees at Tripoli's Mitiga prison. Survivors and rights groups said that the case could expose the wider system of migrant detention and exploitation in Libya, including alleged links to European migration-control policies. They called for further investigations into the responsibility of European officials.

Close 

Interpol Arrests 58 in Global Cybercrime Operation

Interpol said 58 people linked to organised West African cybercrime networks have been arrested in a global operation targeting romance and investment scams across 22 countries and six continents. Operation Jackal IV, conducted between November 2025 and June 2026 and identified 263 suspects. It uncovered fraud involving cryptocurrency, email compromise, money laundering and sextortion, including the targeting of minors. In South Africa, police arrested 39 people, raided seven sites, and seized $2.67 million. They also blocked 257 bank accounts linked to a syndicate. Interpol said the operation highlights the growing global reach of networks such as Black Axe and the importance of international cooperation in disrupting their finances. Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world.

World.title: South Africa: Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court - South African News Briefs - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court

Self-proclaimed political fixer Brown Mogotsi’s alleged escape plot is set to return to court on 1 September, reports EWN. The case was postponed after the State could not produce a report from Correctional Services to prove his alleged attempt to break free. Mogotsi allegedly planned to disguise himself in a Correctional Services uniform and walk out of the Johannesburg Magistrates Court cells. He was removed from a police van before being taken to court and placed in leg irons, with security also tightened. Mogotsi has been in custody since May after failing to secure bail over allegations that he provided false addresses.

Gauteng Health Probes Bribery Allegations

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Gauteng Department of Health is investigating allegations that officials may be accepting bribes from patients in exchange for appointments, access to medical files and the collection of medication outside normal procedures, reports SABC News. Department spokesperson Steve Mabona condemned bribery, corruption and preferential treatment in public healthcare. He said that the allegations are serious enough to warrant an investigation into whether officials are soliciting or accepting payments from patients.

Biko Family Seeks Testimony From Apartheid Spy

The reopened inquest into the 1977 death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko could examine the role of former apartheid spy Craig Williamson, reports EWN. Biko’s family is seeking to have him subpoenaed. The family says Williamson’s previous evidence that Biko was under surveillance could help answer questions about what security forces knew before his death. Biko’s widow, Nontsikelelo, is also expected to testify about the surveillance operation. The family has requested more time to prepare her and review evidence from the original inquest and Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The court is expected to rule on the postponement request.

World.title: Former Texas high school teacher arrested after probe into inappropriate student relationship
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former Texas schoolteacher was arrested Tuesday amid allegations of inappropriate relationships with students, nearly one year after authorities began investigating her.

Holly Adams, who taught at Angleton High School near Houston, is charged with one count of tampering with evidence and two counts of purchasing or furnishing alcohol to a minor, the Brazoria County Sheriff's Office said.

The probe began after a student told school staff that Adams was having an inappropriate relationship with a former student, KTRK-TV reported.

TEXAS SUBSTITUTE TEACHER ACCUSED OF IMPROPER RELATIONSHIP WITH STUDENT, ALARMING PARENTS

The student told school officials that the victim FaceTime-called him over the summer from a bedroom in Adams' house and that the bed was covered in nude photos of her, according to the news outlet. Another image depicted Adams and the former student cuddling, the report states.

Adams reportedly invited students to her home to perform chores, and she allegedly admitted to speaking with three members of the school baseball team on Snapchat.

HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER WHO ALLEGEDLY HAD SEX WITH STUDENT IN CLOSET NOW FACES CHARGES INVOLVING MORE TEENS

Many female teachers who sexually abuse male students sometimes convice themselves that the relationship is legitimate, said Gail Saltz, MD, Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical College.

"They're more likely to be psychologically both grooming their victim, but also what's called self grooming," Saltz told Fox News Digital. "They are convincing themselves that what they are doing is having an intimate, romantic relationship that is benefiting the victim as well."

Saltz noted that the damage done to the male students is just as damaging as female victims.

"It is easily as damaging in terms of, you've been abused by an adult. And that adult took advantage of your trust," she said. "That violated boundaries that you weren't ready for."

Adams was taken to the Brazoria County Detention Center and released on a $26,000 bond the same day. She no longer works for the Angleton Independent School District, a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff's office.

World.title: Massachusetts high court blocks city from displaying Catholic saint statues honoring first responders
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Massachusetts' highest court has blocked a city from installing two towering Catholic saint statues honoring police officers and firefighters outside a new public safety headquarters, ruling the monuments could improperly signal government support for one religion.

The Aug. 20 ruling upheld an October 2025 lower court decision that temporarily blocked the city from installing two 10-foot statues of St. Michael the Archangel, the patron saint of police officers, and St. Florian, the patron saint of firefighters.

The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, which is representing the city of Quincy, told Fox News Digital the legal battle is not over.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

"This ruling is disappointing but is only preliminary," Joe Davis, senior counsel at Becket and lead attorney for the city of Quincy, told Fox News Digital. "Quincy chose these statues to honor the courage and sacrifice of its firefighters and police. The City should not have to hide public art simply because some people may think of religion when they see it. As the Court noted today, this is not the final word for these statues, and we will continue defending Quincy’s right to honor its heroes."

Critics contend that placing religious figures outside a government building would violate the Massachusetts Constitution's protections on religious neutrality.

The controversy began after The Patriot Ledger reported that Quincy planned to install the two statues outside its new public safety headquarters.

The statues were crafted by a sculptor in Italy and chosen by Quincy Mayor Thomas Koch.

AMERICA’S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

According to court documents, Koch said he did not pick the statues to advertise religion but to "honor, inspire and encourage our First Responders" as well as "boost morale" and "ensure [first responders’] lifesaving work would remain maximally effective."

Critics of the statues said the plan had not been publicly disclosed during the building approval process and raised constitutional concerns.

The legal battle started in May 2025, when faith groups and taxpayers sued the City of Quincy and Koch in Norfolk Superior Court, saying that the intended installation of the statues outside the city's new public safety headquarters violated the Massachusetts Constitution's protections on religious neutrality.

The plaintiffs are represented by the ACLU of Massachusetts, the national ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State, the Freedom From Religion Foundation and Cloherty & Steinberg LLP.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

The ACLU of Massachusetts wrote in its brief, "The statues, whose imagery is drawn directly from Catholic iconography, lack a predominantly secular purpose. The primary effect of permanently installing two new, oversized, overtly religious statues as the sole adornments on the City’s public safety building is to advance religion."

The National Fraternal Order of Police and Massachusetts Fraternal Order of Police, however, said in a brief that St. Michael is revered by people of various faiths, not just Christians.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

"First responders of all stripes, religious creeds, and political affiliations — and not just Catholics or Christians — cherish both saints for their symbolic importance to the profession," the brief states.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Koch, the mayor of Quincy, said, "Quincy’s firefighters and police put their lives on the line for this city every day, and these statues were chosen to honor their bravery, service, and sacrifice."

Koch added, "This decision is disappointing, but it is preliminary, and we will continue to fight for the ability to commemorate our first responders as the law permits."

In a statement, Jessie Rossman, legal director at the ACLU of Massachusetts, said, "Here in Massachusetts, our state constitution is clear: the government must remain neutral in matters of religion and must not elevate one faith above others. With today's landmark ruling, the Supreme Judicial Court affirms those principles, which are the essential foundation of a pluralistic society where people of all faiths and no faith can flourish."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As Quincy residents and taxpayers, our clients believe that installing these plainly religious statues would undermine those ideals," Rossman added. "We are proud to represent these courageous plaintiffs, and we look forward to continuing to litigate the merits of this case in Superior Court."

World.title: ‘Never give up a fight’: NYC mom shows her kids 5, 7 the scars from neck-slash attack as lesson in survival
World.content:
Alexis Rowan, 27, is just a week removed from a fight for her life — stitches out, a permanent scar as the nightmare’s lasting mark — yet more resolved than ever to live as an example of strength for the children she begged to come home to.

It was the fight over flight she learned from her mother, Tricia Rowan, a self-described descendant of boxing legacy.

"Get your daughter in MMA," Tricia Rowan, told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday. "That's what I'm signing my grandkids up for this fall."

NYC MOM SURVIVES NECK-SLASH ATTACK ON HIKING TRIP IN ARIZONA: 'I CAN’T DIE LIKE THIS'

Her daughter, Alexis, survived a death-defying, neck-slashing attack Wednesday, Aug. 19, in northern Arizona's Havasupai Indian Reservation, and they are using the moment to warn women, Americans, and even their kids/grandkids (5 and 7) of what "literal screaming for your life is; that is what fighting for your life" truly sounds like.

"She is a true example of what it means to make the noise so someone comes to your rescue," Tricia Rowan said. "Never just take anything laying down, like scream, fight and she did it. She's a warrior."

WITNESSES RECOUNT 'SCARY' NYC STABBING AFTER SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY YELLED 'ALLAHU AKBAR' DURING ATTACKS

Alexis Rowan admitted she needed nearly a week to rehear and rewatch the attack recorded on a nearby Ring camera, but she is resolute in using the moment now and not shielding her young children from the scars left by the shocking Arizona hiking-trail attack that nearly took her life.

"It's, you know, right there – and especially before like I had all the stitches in it," Alexis Rowan said. "So, of course, they look at me and it's the first thing they see."

THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN

"I like my kids to be aware like just like I was always raised: You have to be aware of your surroundings; I'm not going to sit and lie to them because things like this does happen in life.

"You see it on the news, you see anything, 'oh my God, that can never happen.' No, it could happen, so I always tell my kids: You have to pay attention.

JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS

"Living in New York City, always be aware, like pay attention from everywhere. Just be aware.

"Even though, yes, they are little," she continued, "but they need to be aware that things like this can happen.

"You can't panic. We have to think smart, make a decision... be aware."

FBI HEADQUARTERS WELCOMES UFC FIGHTERS FOR TRAINING SESSIONS AHEAD OF HISTORIC WHITE HOUSE MMA EVENT

The 27-year-old New York City mother was hiking through the Havasupai Reservation when she said a man came up behind her and slashed her neck after she asked him for directions to a gift shop.

Her fight versus flight sensed something was "not right."

The man, following her at a distance, led her to call home because she was afraid, telling the person on the line that she was not safe when he asked if she was.

ALASKA RUNNER HOSPITALIZED AFTER USING BEAR SPRAY TO FIGHT OFF BROWN BEAR ON ALASKA TRAIL

"As soon as I said, 'No,' the man came behind me and sliced my own neck," Rowan said, sharing a photo that showed the deep gash in her neck as Ring camera footage showed the blood flowing over her and her 60 pounds of hiking gear.

The attack became a blur, she said, as she feared she was bleeding to death.

"I was like, ‘I’m going to die. Like, I can’t die like this. Like, I have my kids to go home to. Like, they need me,’" Alexis Rowan recalled. "This is not the way I’m gonna die.

"All of these thoughts are like running through my head."

SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY SPAT ON WOMAN BEFORE TACKLING HER IN LATE-NIGHT STORE ATTACK NEAR UPENN CAMPUS

A woman from the nearby gift shop came outside after hearing the commotion, Ring camera footage obtained by Fox News Digital showed, frightening off the attacker and ushering her into the home to wait for help.

The Rowans called the woman who saved her life a hero. That woman in the gift shop wanted to remain anonymous. She personally knew the reservation member, and knew he was a dangerous man with an alleged history of preying on women in the reservation, perhaps why she initially came out of the door before briefly retreating.

Tricia Rowan said the instinct to fight had long been a central lesson in their family.

"It’s always about self-protection, self-awareness and never go down without a fight — whatever it takes — and always scream," she said. "I was so proud of the warrior that she was for screaming for her life."

‘HERO' MOM DIES AFTER USING LAST STRENGTH TO SAVE 4-YEAR-OLD SON FROM FLORIDA RIVER

The family said the scream that drew the woman outside was the difference between life and death. Tricia Rowan initially hesitated to release Ring camera footage with sound that captured her daughter’s cries, concerned about the trauma it could cause Alexis and her grandchildren. But she said she now believes the public needs to hear it.

"People got so numb to violence," Tricia Rowan said. "Until you hear that video of my daughter, that is what literal screaming for your life is. That is what fighting for your life is."

She said, Alexis, despite carrying heavy camping bags and suffering the sudden attack, "is a true example" of why people in danger should "make the noise so someone comes to your rescue."

The Rowans said their family has a history of resilience, including a line of strong women who raised children through adversity. Tricia Rowan said she also learned that a distant relative, John L. Sullivan, was a famed boxer — a fitting connection, she said, for a family now focused on teaching the next generation to defend themselves.

World.title: Wounded Marines relive the harrowing Kabul airport attack in explosive new Fox Nation documentary

Five years after the deadly explosion at Kabul International Airport in Afghanistan, Fox Nation takes an exclusive look at the harrowing incident and the ramifications it had on the U.S. military and American foreign policy.

"Ambush at Abbey Gate: The Afghanistan Withdrawal," a new 40-minute documentary, aims to uncover the mistakes made that led to the suicide bombing at Abbey Gate, a major entrance to Hamid Karzai International Airport.

Retired U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Tyler Vargas-Andrews, who lost his right and left leg in the explosion, spoke out about the terrifying experience with the show's host, Joey Jones.

GOLD STAR FATHER SAYS PRIOR AFGHANISTAN REVIEW SMELLED 'LIKE A COVER-UP' AS NEW LOOK EXAMINES MILLIONS OF DOCS

"Staff Sergeant Darren 'Taylor' Hoover was killed next to me," he said. "My whole abdomen, you know, had been ripped open. I took 150 ball bearings into my body, lost my left kidney. I lost 157 centimeters, large and small intestine."

Retired U.S. Marine Corps Cpl. Kelsee Lainhart was also hurt in the surprise attack, describing the ordeal as damaging several different parts of her body.

DOLLY PARTON'S ‘ALL-AMERICAN HEART’: HOW COUNTRY ICON FORGED SPECIAL BOND WITH US MILITARY

"Different shrapnel and ball bearings hit me in the blast," she said. "I have a ball bearing in my skull, a few other parts of my body, and then the shrapnel hit my vertebrae."

The incident killed 11 Marines, one sailor and one soldier on that fateful day in August 2021. Among the dead were 45 injured American service members, many with severe injuries. More than 160 Afghan civilians were also killed in the blast.

Vargas-Andrews vowed he and his fellow soldiers impacted by the Kabul attack would never let the memory of the day fade away. "We'll never be forgotten," he said. "[This] mentally wounded the entirety of the 'GWOT' [Global War on Terrorism] generation."

The documentary traces not only the Kabul attack itself, but also the injured soldiers' inspirations for joining the U.S. military, despite many criticizing the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan as an "absolute disaster," Jones said.

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

"I remember going up to my mom's room, and I was, like, 'Hey, I'm going to join the Marine Corps.'" Vargas-Andrews said. "I knew it was a place that I could hopefully go and become a man and help those less fortunate. And still to this day, enlisting in the Marine Corps is the best decision I've ever made in my life."

Former Army aviator Rep. Matt Van Epps, R-Tenn., recently blasted the Biden administration over the controversial U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

"The Biden-Harris administration absolutely failed to withdraw from Afghanistan, and it didn't have to be that way," Van Epps told Fox News Digital. "And it's important for the American people to remember what the Biden-Harris administration did in that abject failure, withdrawing from Afghanistan."

The congressman also introduced a resolution marking the fifth anniversary of the shocking bombing at Hamid Karzai International Airport.

To uncover more about the somber legacy of the Kabul bombing and America's tumultuous exit from Afghanistan, tune into "Ambush at Abbey Gate: The Afghanistan Withdrawal," now streaming on Fox Nation.

World.title: Commanders' Jayden Daniels deflects question on LSU cease-and-desist letter after social media trolling wave
World.content:
Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels’ cease-and-desist letter to LSU earlier this month over the use of his name, image and likeness completely backfired – at least in the eyes of football fans.

Daniels was taking a stand after what he viewed as a "disrespectful" move allowing current Tigers cornerback DJ Pickett to wear his No. 5, the number he wore at LSU, heading into the 2026 college season.

What transpired after releasing a statement on Instagram about why he filed the cease-and-desist letter against LSU ultimately backfired into a tsunami of social media trolling.

JAYDEN DANIELS WANTED ‘RESPECT’ FROM LSU. INSTEAD, HE STARTED AN UGLY FIGHT THAT WILL TARNISH HIS REPUTATION

The New York Mets, StubHub, Columbia’s football social page, and many more trolled Daniels with their own version of "respect" for the dual-threat quarterback. The Mets posted a final score of a victory against the Washington Nationals, which finished 4-1, saying, "Stopped at 4 out of respect for Jayden Daniels."

For StubHub, the ticket marketplace jokingly posted "we will no longer offer tickets in groups of 5. Out of respect for Jayden Daniels…"

Thousands of other social media users did the same, and Daniels himself hadn’t spoken to the media to give his reaction. At the end of his press conference on Wednesday following a joint practice against the Baltimore Ravens, Daniels’ final question was about the cease-and-desist letter and whether he had anything else to say.

"I posted the statement on Instagram and said everything I needed to say. So, appreciate y’all," Daniels replied, deflecting any sort of additional comment on the matter.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The move has simply blown up in his face and created a whirlwind of finger-pointing and trolling on social media. But while it’s not ideal heading into a season with that sort of distraction on the outside, Daniels has appeared calm and collected as he prepares for a new year.

Daniels noted being "locked in on training camp" in his statement regarding the cease-and-desist letter to LSU. But he still feels slighted by his former team that he won a Heisman Trophy with before heading to the NFL.

"I have been locked in on training camp and that's been my number one focus. I have a lot of gratitude for my time at LSU and I'm proud of what my teammates and I accomplished there," Daniels posted. "Obviously there are issues to be worked out between my team and LSU and my hope is that it will get done privately.

"My sole personal focus is on Commanders' football. I realize the business of football is unique and I trust this can all be resolved."

Daniels is hoping that him and his No. 5 Commanders jersey is on the field for the entirety of the 2026 NFL season after injuries took a toll in his sophomore campaign.

Daniels was the Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2024, leading the Commanders to the NFC Championship Game in shocking fashion after defeating the Detroit Lions on the road in the Divisional Round. But he only participated in seven games last year as the Commanders were unable to make it back to the playoffs.

World.title: Tap-to-pay charity scam can cost you thousands
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Tap to pay has become one of my favorite modern conveniences. I use it all the time. In fact, I rarely need to pull out a physical wallet anymore because contactless payments are accepted in so many places.

There's a security advantage, too. Mobile wallets can use tokenization or virtual card numbers, so your actual card number does not need to pass directly to a merchant during a transaction.

That makes what's happening with a tap-to-pay charity scam especially frustrating. Criminals are taking a technology designed to make paying easier and using a moment of distraction to turn a small donation into a potentially massive charge.

You may think you're giving $5 or $20 to a good cause. Then you check your account and discover hundreds or even thousands of dollars are gone. Here's how the scam works and what you can do to protect your money.

APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES

New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com .

How the tap-to-pay charity scam works

The setup can feel completely ordinary. You're leaving a store, walking through a busy shopping area or heading through a public event. Someone approaches you and claims to be raising money for a youth group, school fundraiser or another cause. They ask for a small donation. Maybe you agree to $5. Maybe you offer $20. Then they tell you they can accept tap to pay. That's when you need to pay very close attention.

The scammer enters a different amount

One version of the scam involves the solicitor entering a much larger amount into a smartphone or payment reader before you tap your phone or card. You think you're approving $20. The payment screen may actually say $2,000. If you tap without carefully checking that amount, you could authorize the larger transaction. Brentwood police warned in January 2026 about a version involving people approaching shoppers outside stores for small donations. Police said victims could be charged significantly more than expected after using tap to pay, Square or Cash App.

Some victims lost thousands of dollars

The numbers can get ugly fast. The Washington State Attorney General issued a warning after receiving reports involving solicitors near the Seattle waterfront. In one case, a person agreed to donate $15 and later discovered a $4,800 charge. Another person agreed to give $20 and later found a charge of nearly $5,000. Those examples show why you should never treat the final tap as a formality.

Never hand a stranger your unlocked phone

There's another risk worth keeping in mind. If someone claims the transaction failed and asks to take your phone to help, end the transaction. A scammer does not need to take your phone for the inflated-payment scheme to work. However, handing over an unlocked phone creates a much bigger security problem. Depending on your settings, that person may be able to reach email, messages, payment apps or financial information. I would never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger during any financial transaction.

Why tap-to-pay security may not stop this scam

Tap to pay itself remains a secure way to make legitimate purchases. The weakness here involves what you approve. If a scammer puts $2,000 on the payment screen and you authenticate that transaction, the payment system sees an approved purchase.

The criminal is counting on you to skip one very important step: reading the amount before tapping. We use contactless payments so frequently that the gesture can become automatic. Pull out the phone. Authenticate. Tap. Walk away. That routine gives a scammer an opening.

CyberGuy has previously covered how quickly mobile payment scams can turn into serious financial losses through services such as Venmo, Zelle and Cash App.

How to protect yourself from a tap-to-pay charity scam

You do not need to stop using tap-to-pay. I certainly don't plan to. Instead, change how you handle unexpected payment requests.

Keep your phone in your hands

Never give a stranger your unlocked phone to complete or troubleshoot a payment. If something supposedly went wrong with a transaction, cancel it and move on. When your financial information is involved, you should stay in control of your device from beginning to end.

Read the amount before you tap

This may be the single most important habit. Stop for a second and look at the amount displayed on the merchant's phone or payment terminal. Do this before your phone or card goes anywhere near the reader. If you agreed to donate $10, make sure the screen says $10. The FTC also recommends reviewing your financial statements after making donations to confirm you were charged only the amount you intended.

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

Avoid high-pressure donations

A legitimate cause will still exist five minutes from now. If someone tells you that you need to donate immediately, I would walk away. Scammers often rely on pressure because they do not want you thinking too carefully about the request. The FTC specifically advises people against letting fundraisers rush them into making a donation.

Research the charity yourself

Ask for the organization's name, then look it up independently. Do not rely on a website, QR code or social media account the solicitor hands you. Search for the charity yourself and check whether it is registered. Look for independent reviews and see how the organization says donations should be made. The FTC recommends researching unfamiliar charities before sending money.

Use the charity's official donation channel

If the cause sounds worthwhile, you can still donate. Go directly to the organization's official website after you have verified it. That gives you time to confirm who will receive your money without someone standing over you waiting for a tap.

Turn on bank and card alerts

I'm a big fan of account alerts because they can tell you the moment something happens with your money. Turn on notifications for card purchases and withdrawals. Also consider alerts for transfers or other significant account activity. If you intended to donate $20 and immediately get an alert showing $2,000, you can contact your financial institution right away.

Lock down your payment and banking apps

Check the security settings inside apps such as Venmo, Cash App, PayPal and your bank's mobile app. Enable Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a separate PIN when the app offers those protections. That creates another barrier if someone ever gets access to your unlocked phone.

What to do if you already fell for the scam

If you spot an inflated charge or realize you approved far more than you intended, move quickly. The sooner you respond, the sooner your bank can tell you what options are available.

1) Contact your bank or card issuer immediately

Call the bank or card issuer connected to the transaction. Explain exactly what happened. Tell them how much you agreed to pay and how much was actually charged. Ask whether the transaction can be stopped, disputed or reversed. If your banking app allows it, consider locking the affected card while you investigate. Brentwood police specifically advise suspected victims of this scam to contact their bank or card issuer immediately.

2) Save evidence of what happened

Take screenshots of the transaction and save any payment confirmations. Write down where the encounter happened and approximately what time it occurred. Also record the merchant name shown with the charge. Those details can help your bank or law enforcement investigate.

3) Check every financial account on your phone

If the scammer ever handled your unlocked phone, review the financial apps installed on it. Look for unfamiliar transfers or purchases. Then check whether anyone changed your email address, phone number or other account information. Continue watching those accounts over the following days because suspicious activity may appear later.

4) Change passwords if your phone left your hands

If a stranger had access to your unlocked device, change passwords for sensitive accounts that may have been exposed. I would start with your primary email account because criminals can use email to reset passwords elsewhere. Then secure banking and payment accounts. Use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available.

HOW FLORIDA RETIREE LOST $200K IN FAKE PAYPAL REFUND SCAM

5) Strengthen your phone security

Make sure your phone requires Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a strong passcode. Also protect sensitive apps when your device offers that option. The goal is to keep someone from turning a few seconds with your unlocked phone into access to your financial life.

6) Use strong antivirus software

Antivirus software will not reverse an inflated tap-to-pay transaction. However, it becomes much more relevant if the scammer convinced you to click a link, visit a website or download something. Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious software and warn you about dangerous links used in follow-up scams. I recommend running trusted security protection across your devices and keeping it updated. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

7) Reduce the personal information scammers can find

Fraudsters often come back for a second attempt. If they learn your name, phone number or other personal details, they can combine that information with data already available online to make the next scam more convincing. Data brokers and people-search sites can expose personal information about you. You can remove much of this information yourself. However, the process can take time and information may reappear. A data removal service can automate many of those removal requests and continue checking for your information. It cannot erase information a criminal already obtained. Still, reducing your online footprint gives scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

8) Consider identity theft protection

If someone gained access to sensitive information on your phone, you may want an additional set of eyes watching for signs of fraud. Identity theft protection services can monitor for suspicious activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places it should not. Some services also provide recovery assistance if your identity gets misused. That can be especially useful if you believe the incident exposed more than a payment card. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

9) Consider freezing your credit

A fraudulent tap-to-pay charge by itself does not automatically mean someone can open credit in your name. However, the situation changes if a scammer also obtained sensitive personal information that could be used for identity theft. In that case, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new credit account in your name.

10) Report the scam

If you lost money, report what happened. Contact local law enforcement when appropriate, especially if the amount is significant or the same solicitors appear to be targeting other people. You can also report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . If the person claimed to represent a charity, consider contacting your state attorney general or charity regulator as well.

The safest way to donate with your phone

I still like mobile wallets and I still plan to use tap to pay. The technology gives us convenience along with useful payment protections.

What changes for me is how I handle a stranger asking for a quick donation. I want to know exactly who is getting my money before I approve anything.

If I decide the cause deserves support, I can look up the organization later and donate directly through its verified website. That approach removes the pressure and gives me time to make sure my money reaches the people I intended to help.

Kurt's key takeaways

Tap to pay remains one of my favorite ways to check out. I like the speed and I like the added security mobile wallets can provide. Still, technology cannot protect you from every number you personally approve. That's what makes this scam effective. Most of us have become so comfortable tapping that we barely think about the final transaction screen. I want that habit to change. Before you tap, look at the amount. If a stranger is asking for a donation, give yourself time to verify the organization first. And if anyone asks to take your unlocked phone during the process, my answer would be an immediate no. Your generosity should reach the cause you chose, rather than a scammer counting on a few distracted seconds.

Would you still tap your phone to donate to someone who approached you in public after seeing how easily a small gift can become a four-figure charge? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Female Little Leaguer is smashing records, CBS's new college football reporter & heartbreaking sports moments!
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Hump Day of August. Seriously. Weren't we just doing this in July? And now, we're six days away from September.

Lordy. Be careful. You blink, and it'll be Halloween. Blink again, and we'll be rocking around the Christmas tree. Summer goes by faster and faster each year, doesn't it?

As you get older, you really do understand what your grandparents meant when they said "it goes by faster each year." My grandma used to say that all the time. I rolled my eyes. Not anymore.

We're 72 hours away from kickoff in Dublin. Red Sox-Yanks this weekend in the Bronx for what is essentially a playoff series to decide who hosts who in October. I'll be in Daytona for the Firecracker 400.

Summer is certainly going out with a bang. Let's finish strong.

Welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where little leaguer Kinley Rasmus throws her hat in the ring for greatest LLWS player of all time.

LITTLE LEAGUE TEAM GETS ABSOLUTELY SCREWED ON FINAL PITCH OF NO-HITTER, FANS STUNNED BY CALL

Seriously. This girl is insane. Wait till you see her bloodline, too.

What else? I've got a beaten and battered Caitlin Clark, new CBS college football sideline reporter Jordan Giorgio reporting for duty ahead of Week 1, and this sports question is getting a lot of traction over on Elon's X today. Feels right in our wheelhouse. You'll see.

OK, grab you a drink, pour it out for Tim Curry, and then settle in for a Hump Day 'Cap!

Kinley Rasmus is an absolute machine on the diamond

Goodness, what a week. First Dolly, now Tim. Brutal. And how about the year for Home Alone II cast members?

We lost Catherine O'Hara in January. We lost Brenda Fricker — AKA the Pigeon Lady — last month. And now we lose Tim Curry.

Obviously, Tim is most well-known (I think?) for his work in "Rocky Horror Picture Show," but, for me, he's the hotel manager in Home Alone II. Other notable roles for Tim?

How about the original IT? Terrifying movie for us '90s kids to walk past in the horror section at Blockbuster Video. It gave me nightmares for WEEKS. And how about this for a real deep cut?

He was also the voice of Ben Ravencroft in the cult classic, "Scooby-Doo! and the Witch's Ghost." If you knew that, you get a gold star for today's class. Extra credit!

Anyway, we lost a good one in Tim. We lost a good one in Dolly. We're losing too many good ones right now. Not great.

OK, let's get this class started with Little League World Series star, Kinley Rasmus, who last night became the record-holder for most hits in the LLWS (5) for a girl, and also tied the all-time LLWS record for strikeouts by a girl (14), set by Mo’ne Davis.

What a phenom:

Caitlin Clark looks like she's having fun!

Amazing. I can't get enough of this story. I'm a sucker for a good LLWS story, and Kinley checks all the right boxes.

And how about this family tree:

Her dad is former MLB pitcher Cory Rasmus, who played for the Braves and Angels.

Her uncle is former MLB outfielder Colby Rasmus, who played for the Cardinals, Blue Jays, Astros, Rays, and Orioles.

Not a bad little family tree! Kinley, 12, is currently 5 for 8 in four LLWS games, and has 14 Ks in two starts.

There's a lot of talk right now about girls and guys (and ... others ...) playing in sports, and the fairness of it all. It's well documented. Sophie Cunningham. Ever heard of her?! Of course you have.

This is a nice way to veer off that path and cleanse the palette with something genuine. We all need it. Trust me.

I'm so tired of the WNBA stuff. It's why I led with Kinley today. She deserves it. Phenix City Little League (Alabama) plays again tonight at 7 p.m., for those looking to kill time before college football returns on Saturday.

OK, let's keep this class moving ... with the WNBA! Yes, that league.

I know it's exhausting, but when Caitlin Clark emerges from a game looking like she just got clawed to death, I have to report on it:

Worst sports moments ever & it's time to report for duty!

Lordy. Look at her! Just beaten and battered, and she still managed to put up 37 points.

Look, it's basketball. I get it. I'm not here trying to sound soft or whiny. Sports are violent. They're physical. I'd imagine the '80s and '90s Bulls and Pistons looked a lot like this after games. I assume a lot of players who went up against the Pistons back then did. I get it.

Now, replace the Bad Boy Pistons with the Mean Girls in the WNBA, and give them all fingernails and enough hate in their hearts to fill an ocean. That's what Caitlin is going up against every night.

They really do hate her. It's amazing.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big Hump Day night. First up? This sports question has gone mega-viral on Elon's X today, and it's perfect for this group:

"oh yeah you like sports? name five times your team has made you want to ...." You know the rest. I'm not going to finish the post here for legal reasons.

But you get the question.

It's a great topic because everyone has answers that immediately come to mind. For me?

Aaron Boone walk-off homer in Game 7 of the 2003 ALCS. I was 10 and cried for hours. Red Sox completing the September collapse on the final game of the 2011 season. I was in college this time, and also cried for hours. Dolphins losing to the Jets in the final game of the 2013 season to miss the playoffs. Chase Elliott running out of gas with two laps to go in the 2017 Daytona 500. Dolphins losing to the Bills in the final game of the 2023 season to lose the division. This was the beginning of the end for Tua.

It's a weird list, admittedly, but it's a solid one in terms of heartbreak. I'd also throw in Tim Tebow getting absolutely boat-raced by Alabama in his final SEC championship game in 2009. That one hurt, too.

OK, shoot me yours. I know we're all sickos here, so I'm expecting a full mailbox tomorrow morning.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

On the way out, here's new Big Ten on CBS sideline reporter Jordan Giorgio celebrating getting called up to the big leagues before Week 1. Congrats, Jordan!

See you tomorrow.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Top five heartbreaking moments in sports for you? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

World.title: Judge clears path for ICE agent accused in Minnesota shooting case to leave Texas jail
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal judge on Wednesday handed Minnesota a major setback in its fight to keep ICE agent Christian Castro behind bars in Texas, denying an emergency request that would have blocked his release Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. rejected Minnesota’s request for a temporary restraining order barring Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino from releasing Castro while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott decides whether to extradite the agent to face assault charges.

Castro’s 90-day detention period under Texas law expires Thursday. Trevino’s counsel told the court that without a court order or a rendition warrant signed by Abbott, Castro would be released from the Cameron County Jail.

Rodriguez wrote that Minnesota "fails to satisfy the requirements for the issuance of a temporary restraining order."

'POLITICAL STUNT' PROSECUTION OF ICE AGENT FOR 'ROAD RAGE' PROVOKES HEATED DHS RESPONSE

Minnesota had asked the court to force Abbott to immediately issue a rendition warrant and prevent Castro’s release in the meantime. The state warned Castro could flee to Mexico, pointing to jail calls with a woman described in court filings as his romantic partner who lives in Progreso, Mexico.

According to the order, Castro discussed buying property and moving to Mexico in the future. Minnesota argued that if he left the country, it could take months or years to secure his return and prosecute him.

But Rodriguez ruled that Minnesota’s lawsuit was premature because Abbott has not yet denied its extradition request.

"The record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro," the judge wrote.

Abbott instead directed the Texas secretary of state to investigate whether Castro should be surrendered, a step permitted under Texas’ Uniform Criminal Extradition Act. Rodriguez found that neither the Constitution nor state and federal extradition laws at issue impose a set deadline for Abbott to complete that review.

"The Court concludes that this matter does not present an issue ripe for adjudication," Rodriguez wrote.

Minnesota formally requested Castro’s extradition in early June, after he was arrested in Cameron County on the state’s warrant. The court noted Abbott has considered the matter for an "atypically-long duration," but said Minnesota identified no law requiring the governor to act within a particular time frame.

TIM WALZ PARDONS ILLEGAL ALIEN CONVICTED OF ARMED ROBBERY BEFORE ICE DEPORTATION TO LAOS

Castro was charged in May with four felony counts of second-degree assault and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime stemming from a January ICE operation in Minnesota.

According to the order, Castro fired one shot through the closed front door of a home, injuring a person in the leg.

The shooting sparked protests in north Minneapolis and has become part of a broader political and legal battle between Minnesota officials and the Trump administration over state prosecutions of ICE agents who took part in Operation Metro Surge.

15 ANTIFA RADICALS INDICTED, 12 ARRESTED IN SWEEPING FEDERAL PROBE INTO MINNEAPOLIS ANTI-ICE OPERATIONS

Minnesota prosecutors have separately charged ICE agent Gregory Morgan Jr. with two counts of second-degree assault after alleging he pointed a handgun at motorists during a traffic confrontation after an enforcement operation.

DHS has accused Minnesota "sanctuary politicians" of staging a "political stunt," while Minnesota officials have argued the agents’ alleged conduct fell outside their federal law-enforcement duties.

Abbott has raised questions about whether Castro can be considered a fugitive for extradition purposes because he returned to Texas on orders from federal immigration officials after the January incident.

Rodriguez, however, signaled skepticism of that reasoning in a footnote.

"The Court has doubts that caselaw supports the construction of ‘fugitive’ that Texas is considering," he wrote, noting that long-standing precedent appears to focus on whether an accused person left the state — not why.

Still, the judge said that question did not alter Wednesday’s decision.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The ruling leaves Castro’s immediate fate in Abbott’s hands. If no rendition warrant is issued and no court order intervenes, he is expected to be released Thursday.

Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Fox News' Patrick McGovern and Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

World.title: Judge allows Trump’s mail-in ballots plan to proceed, at least for now
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Wednesday allowed President Donald Trump, at least temporarily, to move forward with his effort to exert federal control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections.

The decision by Boston-based U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani to lift an injunction that applied nationwide follows a Supreme Court decision favoring Trump in a similar case on Monday.

But with litigation moving swiftly, there remains a strong chance that key aspects of Trump’s mail-in ballots executive order will be blocked at some stage, possibly as soon as later on Wednesday.

The executive order directs the U.S. Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters.

00:25 SCOTUS allows Trump’s mail-in ballot executive order 00:00 00:00

Multiple legal challenges to the proposal, which conflicts with the states’ traditional role in administering elections, are pending.

Trump has frequently criticized mail-in ballots even though they are widely used by Republicans and Democrats all across the country.

The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a nationwide injunction that had blocked the executive order in a case brought by California and 22 other states. That ruling left in place a second injunction in a separate case brought by various groups including the League of Women Voters, which Talwani lifted on Wednesday. She is overseeing both cases.

The Supreme Court, divided 6-3, concluded that Talwani had acted too hastily in ruling on the executive order, but did not weigh in on whether the underlying proposal or the Postal Service regulation to implement it is lawful.

The Trump administration argued that the injunction in the League of Women Voters case should be lifted in light of the Supreme Court ruling, as the same logic applies in both cases.

Talwani reluctantly agreed, while making it clear that the challengers have “substantial arguments that might persuade the Supreme Court to reach a different result” if the litigation ultimately returns to the justices.

Lawyers in the cases brought by the League of Women’s Voters and the states are both set to challenge the regulation.

Talwani, appointed by President Barack Obama, in a separate order issued on Tuesday said that the Trump administration violated her original injunction because it had moved forward with issuing the Postal Service regulation despite her instruction not to do so. But she elected not to impose any sanctions on the government, saying only that she was “identifying the violation.”

World.title: Sen. Darline Graham wins the Republican Senate primary runoff in South Carolina
World.content:
Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Republican primary runoff, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump, who recruited, endorsed and campaigned for her following her brother Lindsey Graham’s death six weeks ago.

With nearly all of the vote tallied, Graham was leading Norman roughly 52% to 48%.

At her election night party in Columbia, Graham paid tribute to her late brother and credited Trump for getting her across the finish line.

“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart. But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room,” she told her supporters.

“Mr. president, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country,” Graham continued. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”

An hour north in Rock Hill, Norman said he had not prepared a concession speech and lamented Trump’s involvement, though he said he accepted the results and planned to call Graham.

“I really hate it for the state. I don’t hate it for me. ... I hate it for the state. But the public of South Carolina made the decision,” Norman told his supporters. As for Trump’s involvement, Norman said, “He has that right. That’s his prerogative,” adding that “his policies are good.”

But Norman added, “I never understood why he got in this race. ... But it is, it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”

Trump had gone all in for Graham, who decided to run for a full six-year term after she was appointed to the seat by Gov. Henry McMaster. The president held an in-person rally for her Friday in Myrtle Beach and a tele-rally Monday evening, and his allied super PAC made a late $830,000 push to boost her.

During the Friday rally, Trump recounted how he asked her to run “because everyone loves her, everyone respects her.” He also said he’s supporting her to “honor Lindsey,” who had been one of his closest allies in Washington.

“She only knows how to put America first,” Trump told the crowd. “You vote for her, you’re going to be very proud of that vote.”

Sen. Darline Graham R-S.C., at a campaign event at Holt Bros BBQ in Florence on Aug. 19. Sean Rayford / Getty Images

Graham, 62, will now face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election, and is the heavy favorite in the deep-red state where her brother served in the Senate and House for more than 30 years.

To beat Norman, who’s spent nearly a decade in Congress, Graham had to overcome GOP attacks of nepotism and inexperience. She had never held or run for elected office before, though she did lead a 130-person state agency that helped blind people. In the initial primary earlier this month, Graham finished first with 33% of the vote, short of the 50% needed to avoid a runoff.

And the final week of the truncated, two-week runoff campaign was dominated by Graham’s blunder at a debate with Norman where she replied that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were important national security priorities.

“National security is not my thing,” she said.

It was a particularly notable moment given that her senator brother had served more than three decades in the Air Force and was one of the leading voices on national security on Capitol Hill.

Darline Graham said that she would be more focused as a senator on domestic policy issues, such as affordability.

“Her brother was very much about the world. … That’s good, that’s fine. But she’s more about affordability,” Trump said about the Graham siblings, who have both talked about their humble beginnings being raised in a single room next to their family’s bar and pool hall.

In the closing days of the campaign, she touted herself as someone who would continue her brother’s legacy and also be a reliable vote for Trump. In one ad, she noted she was the lead sponsor of a tough Russia sanctions bill that was renamed for her brother, and she highlighted her vote to confirm Todd Blanche, Trump’s nominee for attorney general.

Graham’s victory caps a tumultuous six-week stretch in South Carolina Republican politics. Fresh from a trip to Ukraine, Lindsey Graham died the night of July 11 from what doctors preliminarily said was a tear in the aorta due to the hardening of the arteries.

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., has clashed with President Donald Trump in the past. Meg Kinnard / AP

Three days later, Darline Graham was sworn in to serve out the rest of his term. Despite her appointment and Trump’s endorsement, the primary to replace her brother attracted a crowded field of candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry, former Gov. Mark Sanford and wealthy self-funding businessman Mark Lynch.

Norman first irritated Trump when he became the only House Republican to endorse former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary race.

Since then, he’s been a constant thorn in Trump’s side. Last year, Norman, a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, clashed with Trump and GOP leaders by initially opposing the president’s landmark tax-and-spending cuts package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” But he eventually voted yes after successfully negotiating to speed up work requirements for Medicaid recipients and the elimination of Biden-era wind and solar tax credits.

The runoff was a rare race that divided conservatives.

While Darline Graham had Trump, McMaster and Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., in her corner, Norman secured endorsements from former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, who now lives in the state; Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., his onetime rival for governor; former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, who had run in the special Senate primary race; and former Sen. Jim DeMint, R-S.C., who previously led the Heritage Foundation.

As expected, Norman performed well in the upstate areas in and around his congressional district. Graham, meanwhile, bested Norman in populous areas along the coast and around the capital city of Columbia.

Trump’s visit to South Carolina and Fry’s endorsement seem to have boosted her in Horry County, where the Myrtle Beach rally was held.

In the initial GOP primary two weeks ago, Fry won the county with nearly 14,000 votes. But in the Tuesday runoff, Graham crushed Norman there, winning more than 26,000 votes to his nearly 10,000.

World.title: Panda Express’ CEOs are on a ‘mission’ to help workers achieve the dream of home ownership
World.content:
Panda Express is famous for its orange chicken. But the founders of the iconic fast-casual Asian chain also want to be known for something else: helping their workers realize the American dream.

“I always believe that when you do well, you know, personally, then you can go out and take care of other people,” said Andrew Cherng, who is co-founder, co-chair and co-CEO of Panda Express along with his wife, Peggy Cherng.

“You want people to do well,” he said. “And you want to treat them well.”

Cherng measures progress in part by how many of his managers make $100,000 or more annually. He also tracks whether those managers can afford to buy homes, and he considers that a barometer of his own success.

Yet over the past decade, that American dream of homeownership has slipped out of reach for millions of middle-class families.

With low housing stock across the country, mortgage rates hovering at 6.8% and home prices in some cities at record levels, there is little relief in sight.

Panda Express co-CEO Peggy Cherng wants to help employees establish their careers and "mark that accomplishment by owning a home.” NBC News

Immigrant families are also less likely to own their homes than families headed by native-born U.S. residents, according to census data. Experts point to several factors that are likely to contribute to the disparity, including limited employment and income prospects, language barriers and inconsistent access to banks and financing.

Peggy Cherng said the couple recognize elements of their own journeys in those of their employees. “Most of our associates are first-generation immigrants,” she said.

Andrew was born in China and immigrated to the U.S. in 1966 after having grown up in Taiwan and Japan. Peggy was born in Myanmar and raised in Hong Kong.

The couple met at the University of Missouri and opened their first Panda Express in 1983 in Glendale, California. At the time, they envisioned it as a casual offshoot of Panda Inn, the full-service Chinese restaurant Andrew opened with his father in the early 1970s.

That immigrant experience remains central to how the couple run the business today, particularly a focus on investing in their employees, whom they consider their extended family.

Today, Panda Express is America’s largest Asian restaurant chain, with more than 2,500 locations across 49 states and restaurants in 12 countries. The privately held company employs around 55,000 people and generates around $7 billion in annual sales, according to data compiled by market research firm Technomic.

For Andrew, the foundation of that success is built from the ground up — starting with his employees.

“How do we help these people to have a better life? That’s our mission,” he said in an interview at the company’s headquarters outside Los Angeles, part of NBC News’ “Business in America” initiative.

Peggy said, “Our mission, our calling, is how we are able to help more associates realize their American dream, establish their business, their career, but most importantly, mark that accomplishment by owning a home.”

And despite the long list of obstacles to first-time homeownership, Andrew wants to help his Panda Express employees focus on what is possible rather than what stands in their way.

“We actually help everybody to think about owning a home very quickly,” he said.

Many of the managers he hires initially seem to view the position as just another job, he said, not a potential career path.

Managers “have to do a lot of things,” he said. “We teach them [those skills], but to have a good life, you turn that person from being sort of ‘task-based’ to ‘life-based.’”

That transformation, according to Andrew, often instills a deeper sense of purpose in his employees — one that extends to caring for others and their communities.

“We get people to see that quickly and see it clearly,” he said.

World.title: What to do if your CD account matures this September
World.content:
If time is running out on your current CD account, it makes sense to start planning your next moves now. Pla2na/Getty Images

With new unemployment, inflation and interest rate developments all looming this September, some savers may have forgotten that they also have another important date on the calendar. If they opened a certificate of deposit (CD) account in recent months or years, its maturity date could arrive in the month. And with many banks only offering a short grace period of approximately two weeks for savers to decide what they want to do with the funds before they rollover into a new account, it's critical to start contemplating your next moves now, while you still have plenty of time to shift your savings strategy.

Moving your maturing CD money into a traditional savings account, however, isn't really a viable option right now, no matter how advantageous that account may have once been. With an average rate of just 0.38%, according to an update released by the FDIC last week, leaving money there equates to a failure to outpace inflation. And with multiple, high-rate account types that can offer returns exponentially higher without restricting access the way the CD did, it's not necessary.

So, understanding that moving your maturing CD funds into a traditional savings account isn't viable or profitable, where should you instead move your money next? Below, we'll outline two credible options, both of which are positioned to earn more interest if the rate climate heats up again.

See how much interest you can be earning with a top savings account online now.

Where you should move your maturing CD account money this September

Don't let your maturing CD account money automatically rollover into a new account, especially as that can risk extending your loss of access and, potentially, lock you into an account with a lower interest rate than you're currently earning. Instead, prepare to shift your funds into one or both of the following account types once you regain access this September:

A high-yield savings account

With a top rate of 4.10% available now, a high-yield savings account could be your next best move. With this account you'll maintain access to your funds as you normally would with a traditional savings account, unlike the CD. And while the account does employ a variable rate that will rise or fall in response to market conditions, that's less of a concern now with interest rates holding steady and the possibility that they could rise later this year not insignificant.

That said, not every high-yield savings account will be created equally and online banks, in particular, will often offer more competitive rates than banks with in-person branch locations. So don't rush to open an account or transfer any money until you've found the right account with the right rate.
