Dulles Wang, director of Americas gas and LNG at the energy research firm Wood Mackenzie, says that last number is actually as low as five per cent, by his firm's estimates.

"It's relatively small," he told CBC News.

Natural gas pipelines sprawl across North America like a massive spider web, crossing the Canada-U.S. border in about two dozen locations. From heating homes, to generating electricity, and powering industries, the commodity plays a pivotal role in the daily lives of millions of people.

Enbridge, headquartered in Calgary, is North America's largest natural gas provider. In 2024, the company completed a $19 billion series of deals to acquire three U.S. utilities.

"Gas flows across the borders constantly, every day, every hour of the day. And we're not just talking about [a] one-direction flow in terms of trade," Wang said.

"The U.S. imports Canadian supplies, mostly for the western and the Midwest markets. At the same time, the U.S. also exports gas, and that's also going into the Canadian markets, mostly on the eastern side."

While Canadian shipments of natural gas to the U.S. may be small compared with America's domestic production, Wang notes it's where these deliveries take place that's important.

"You're not going to see any Canadian gas making its way down to Texas, because Texas actually produces more gas than it consumes," he said.

"In places like the Pacific Northwest, we're talking about Seattle, Oregon, and also Northern California … over 90 per cent of the gas is actually coming in from Canada."

The LNG Canada facility in Kitamat, B.C., started shipping liquefied natural gas to Asian markets just last year. The federal government has been trying to expand Canada's energy exports beyond the U.S. (LNG Canada)

Driven by rising use of artificial intelligence, these regions have seen a surge in data centre construction backed by American hyperscaler tech giants such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta. These energy-hungry facilities often use natural gas as a baseload power source to supplement clean energy.

"So not only will people freeze, but also your data centres won't be running either," Wang said.

Canada would be 'shooting itself in the foot'

Halting U.S.-bound natural gas shipments would be painful for the industry in Canada, according to Wang. He predicts a glut of supply trapped in Canada would see prices plunge as storage facilities max out capacity.

"We're talking about a quite severe economic impact to the downside if we were to stop exporting gas to the U.S.," Wang said. "Canada … would be shooting itself in the foot, so to speak, by eliminating their only customer, and crashing prices."

"There's no winner in this," he added.

Canada's federal government wants more non-U.S. buyers. Last year, the first shipments of liquefied natural gas left the LNG Canada facility in Kitamat, B.C., bound for Asian markets.

The government's Major Projects Office is backing the second phase of this project, as well as the floating Ksi Lisims LNG export facility that's awaiting approval for construction off on the B.C. coast.

"That level of commitment needs to be there to support these projects, otherwise we're probably just going to continue to be stranded, or dependent on the U.S. market," Wang said.

World.title: Sask. Premier Scott Moe announces retaliatory tariffs on U.S. booze
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe has announced counter-tariffs on U.S. alcohol products, matching the U.S. tariffs of 50 per cent.

At a news conference in Prince Albert Wednesday, Moe said the counter-tariffs will take effect Sept. 8.

On Tuesday, Ottawa announced counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion of U.S. goods. It also unveiled $7.5 billion in support for workers and businesses.

Moe said the province supports the federal government's "focused and targeted approach in its counter-tariffs on U.S. imports," after trade negotiations fell apart over the weekend.

He said the U.S. was "encroaching on international trade agreements," and called that unacceptable. Moe said Saskatchewan has been working to build trade relationships outside of North America, and that those efforts have been successful.

The premier said the new counter-tariffs cover about $1.5 billion, or 11.3 per cent, of Saskatchewan's annual imports from the U.S. He said the province is analyzing the counter-tariff list closely and is working with "affected industries to determine its potential impact on jobs and consumer prices."

Moe said the province is also reviewing the federal government’s support measures to ensure they work for businesses and workers.

"While this is the appropriate response to the latest round of U.S. tariffs, we can never lose sight of the fact that all tariffs hurt businesses, jobs, consumers and families on both sides of the border, and our ultimate goal must be to get back to a free and fair trade relationship with the U.S., as we have enjoyed for many years," Moe said.

World.title: More charges for former Manitoba MP Inky Mark after 445 guns, explosives found in home: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former member of Parliament Inky Mark, who was arrested on a dozen weapons offences last month, has been hit with 26 more charges, after police say they took a total of 445 firearms and 26.5 kilograms of explosives from his Manitoba home.

RCMP say the 78-year-old was rearrested on new charges on Aug. 12 after an ongoing investigation.

Mark was arrested during a July 7 search of his home near the western Manitoba city of Dauphin and was initially charged with 12 weapons-related offences , including firearms trafficking, possession of a firearm with a tampered serial number, three counts of unsafe firearms storage, two counts of careless use of a firearm and two counts of possession of a prohibited device.

Police said last month they took 439 guns from his home and seized other items, including an antique cannon and ammunition.

RCMP said in a Wednesday news release that after processing the evidence seized in July, they determined 445 firearms were taken from the home. Of those, 295 were unsafely stored, 10 were prohibited and 11 were restricted or prohibited firearms that were not registered to Mark, according to police.

A photo provided by Manitoba RCMP shows some of the weapons they say they found at Mark's home during a July 7 search. (Manitoba RCMP)

RCMP also now say they seized 26.5 kilograms of explosives — more than four times the amount licensed individuals are allowed to possess, according to police.

A number of the restricted or prohibited firearms were stored with readily available ammunition, and two firearms registered to Mark could not be located, the RCMP release said.

In total, 38 charges have now been laid against Mark.

The 26 new charges include w eapons trafficking, three more counts of possession of a prohibited weapon, nine counts of possession of a restricted firearm/prohibited weapon with ammunition, and nine counts of possession of a firearm when knowing it is unauthorized.

He's also been charged with another count of possession of a firearm with a tampered serial number, two counts of failing to report the loss of a firearm and having more than six kilograms of explosives.

A photo provided by RCMP shows more of the guns they say they seized from Mark's home in July. (Manitoba RCMP)

A few days after the initial charges were laid in July, Mark told CBC News that he broke the law by illegally transferring three guns, but denied he trafficked any.

Mark said at that point he's been legally collecting firearms since the early 1970s, but some of those weapons are now illegal to own due to gun law changes over the years.

During the initial search of Mark's home, RCMP also seized more than $300,000 in currency. Mark told CBC the cash was from property sales in Dauphin and denied it was connected with firearms trafficking.

RCMP also now allege that sometime between December 2024 and February 2025, Mark went unprompted to the home of a friend who had made a social media post about a coyote on their property, and handed that person a firearm and ammunition, according to Wednesday's news release.

The person did not use the weapon, which was later recovered by investigators.

Mark is a former MP who represented the Dauphin-Swan River-Neepawa riding. He was first elected to Parliament in 1997 and resigned his seat in 2010, after serving first with the Reform party, and later with the Canadian Alliance and finally as a Conservative.

He ran unsuccessfully for the seat again in 2015 as an independent.

Prior to his time as an MP, he was elected mayor of Dauphin in 1994. He ran unsuccessfully for that position again in 2010.

World.title: Video captures likely tornado in eastern P.E.I. amid 'wild day' of weather
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A mid-afternoon storm Wednesday on Prince Edward Island brought high winds, hail, rain, thunder and lightning.

The storm blew through Charlottetown at about 1:40 p.m. and knocked out power to thousands of Maritime Electric customers, mostly in Charlottetown.

CBC meteorologist Ryan Snodden called it a "wild day of weather" across central and eastern areas of the province.

"We've seen slow-moving thunderstorms producing very heavy rainfall, gusty winds and some localized hail," Snoddon said. "Rainfall rates of near 50 mm/h have been estimated on the radar."

He said it also appears a tornado very likely touched down near Souris in eastern P.E.I. A video submitted to CBC News shows trees being thrown high in the air and the funnel becoming visible once the tornado moves over the water.

In Little Harbour, near Souris, Brielle Campbell told CBC News about what she saw when looking at the storm from inside her house.

"It seemed like the clouds were spinning. It started just on the ground, in the field," Campbell said. "It spun things up. It was kind of crazy."

WATCH | RAW VIDEO: Possible tornado spotted in eastern P.E.I.: RAW VIDEO: Possible tornado spotted in eastern P.E.I. | Duration 1:09 Brielle Campbell told CBC News she saw what she believes was a tornado while watching the storm from her house in Little Harbour, near Souris.

Nearby, at Blair Chapman's house, the weather was also chaotic.

"That included some shrubs flying up in the air to the east of our property," Chapman said.

"We had two nice apple trees. They got toppled. Then we could see some trees at the treeline, they got uprooted. They were flying in the air like toothpicks.…

"It was like a scene from The Wizard of Oz."

Hail fell as part of the variety of weather a summer storm brought P.E.I. (Ken Linton/CBC)

The storm was unpredictable, too. People reported heavy rain, then sunshine, then a downpour again.

Charlottetown police warned of localized flooding in the city, and said drivers should be careful.

Some streets in the Sherwood and Parkdale areas were closed due to flooding. Some businesses closed as well, as did the sports centre at UPEI.

"The risk of severe thunderstorms will continue this afternoon and into early this evening, especially across the eastern half of the Island," Snoddon said.

World.title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, dead at 80
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tim Curry, the quirky British actor known for playing eccentric roles like the flamboyant, fishnet-wearing mad scientist Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at age 80.

His longtime manager and friend, Marcia Hurwitz, said Curry died at his Los Angeles home on Tuesday night, after originally saying he died Wednesday. No cause of death was immediately disclosed. Curry suffered a stroke in 2012 and had since used a wheelchair.

He surged into the spotlight in the 1970s as the star of the horror-comedy stage musical The Rocky Horror Show, and reprised his role for the 1975 screen adaptation The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

He became known for playing fiendish, loony villains, including the clown Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries adaptation of Stephen King's It. He also starred as another famous antagonist, Rooster Hannigan — brother of the bitter, gin-soaked Miss Hannigan, played by Carol Burnett — in the 1982 movie Annie.

Beyond being known for his mischevious humour and rubber face, Curry was beloved by many as a voice in many animated children's productions including The Rugrats Movie (1998), The Pebble and the Penguin (1995), Rugrats in Paris (2000) and The Wild Thornberrys Movie (2002).

His work on the stage earned three Tony nominations — for Spamalot, My Favourite Year and the title role in Amadeus — alongside an Emmy nod in 1994 for an appearance on horror anthology series Tales from the Crypt.

A genre-defying career

In an official statement released to CBC News, Curry's PR manager, Sean Katz, said the actor's strength was his ability to move fluidly between genres.

"Throughout his life, he refused to be boxed in or confined to others' expectations. Across five decades, he moved fluidly between comedy, horror, drama and music, delighting himself and his legion of fans with his countless dynamic personas."

He said Curry's greatest legacies were "his curious, expansive mind and generous, gentle heart, both of which remained open and filled with anticipation until his final breath."

In 1974, the Rocky Horror phenomenon made its American stage debut and began production as a feature-length film adaptation starring Tim Curry as the flamboyant Dr. Frank-N-Furter. (credit: FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)

Throughout his five-decade career, Curry would glide back and forth between genres — occasionally departing from comedy and horror to take on dramatic roles in features such as The Three Musketeers (1993) and The Hunt for Red October (1990).

He also played as the butler Wadsworth in the 1985 comedy cult classic Clue, the villainous Bill Sikes in the 1982 TV movie of Oliver Twist and corrupt music industry villain, Winston Newquay in the 1989 TV series Wiseguy.

His comedic roles included the suspiciously slick hotel concierge Mr. Hector in Home Alone 2 (1992), the eccentric, greedy philanthropist Herkermer Homolka in Congo (1995) and Long John Silver in Muppet Treasure Island (1996).

"I like playing the more curious corners of the human mind and human behaviour, partly because they're a tad more interesting," Curry told The Associated Press in 1993.

Tributes pour in

Following news of his death, tributes poured in from many of Curry's former colleagues and admirers.

Burnett, Curry's Annie co-star, honoured him on her Instagram, sharing a clip of the pair performing in the movie, calling him a dear friend and praising his talents. "Nobody could play lovable villains better than he could."

Actor and comedian Rob Schneider wrote on X that he was "gutted" by the death of his Home Alone 2 co-star. "A truly gifted performer of stage and screen, his one eyebrow could say more than most actors entire bodies. I am grateful to have the rare gift of watching him work, he made you better just standing near him."

The official Instagram page for The Rocky Horror show also posted a tribute. "Today, we mourn the loss of Tim Curry. A singular talent. A true original. And the man who first brought Dr. Frank-N-Furter to life."

The post continued, "He didn't simply play a character. He created an icon. Thank you Tim."

World.title: 24 Canadians among hundreds missing after flash floods kill at least 157 in Nepal, Tibet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Massive flash floods in a border area of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday killed at least 157 people, according to Nepali police, and left hundreds of tourists — including 24 Canadians — workers and others missing after sweeping through communities and bringing travel in some areas to a halt. The Prime Minister's Office in Nepal earlier reported at least 95 dead. China's state broadcaster CCTV said a mudslide in Tibet's Gyirong County near the border killed at least three and left 265 missing. The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, Nepali officials said. They issued warnings to residents in several of Nepal's districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. "We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts," said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government. Sunil Sharma, officiating director of the Nepal Tourism Board's public relation and publicity department, said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals were reported missing, including 24 Canadian citizens. Nepal's ambassador to Canada later confirmed the information about the Canadians. In an interview with CBC News, Bharat Raj Paudyal said while he cannot confirm the circumstances around the Canadians, he said the affected area is both popular with hikers and also a route often used by those on pilgrimage. Prime Minister Mark Carney called the flash flood "absolutely devastating." In a statement on social media, he asked all Canadians in the region to register with the ROCA (Registration of Canadians Abroad) system as soon as possible, and said Canada stands ready to provide support. "Canadians are thinking of all those in distress right now, those who have lost a loved one, and all those who are still waiting for answers," he added. The flash floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River are absolutely devastating.

Canadians are thinking of all those in distress right now, those who have lost a loved one, and all those who are still waiting for answers.

Our government is closely following the situation and… —MarkJCarney Security footage captured on the Chinese side of ⁠the Nepal-Tibet border showed many people fleeing before a wall of rock, mud and water destroyed buildings and ‌vehicles, with the people disappearing from view. Sharma said 133 of the missing are from India and on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing are 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia and 33 from Britain. South Korean and Malaysian government officials said separately from Sharma that several of their citizens were unaccounted for. At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking near the Gosaikunda lake in Rasuwa, coinciding with the upcoming local festival of Janai Purnima, Sharma added. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press that at least 28 police officials were missing. Nepal's steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors but precarious ones when disaster strikes. Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in the hard-hit Nuwakot district slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and stunned survivors were caked in mud. The U.S. Geological Survey reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake early Wednesday, about 100 kilometres north of Kathmandu, near the border with China's autonomous region of Tibet. The Trishuli river roughly parallels a highway north of the Kathmandu area that is used to reach one of Nepal's most popular treks in the Langtang area. WATCH | Warning: Some graphic footage: Hundreds of people, including tourists, missing after flood in Nepal | Duration 1:28 Rescue efforts are underway after an earthquake struck the mountainous Rasuwa district in Nepal. Officials say around 400 tourists and travellers — including from India, the U.K. and Malaysia — are missing as crews attempt to reach villages where homes are covered in mud. China, India prepared to help Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up the efforts for people missing after the mudslide, state news agency Xinhua reported. Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered help. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely co-ordinating on rescue and relief efforts," Modi said in a social media post. Dozens of multi-storey buildings, trucks, and vans were buried under vast quantities of mud in the district of Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected areas. Officials warned residents in several of Nepal's districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers. The same regions affected by Wednesday's disaster saw flash floods similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood. The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said. "The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream," said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group. "In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation," he added. The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries, including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Damaged houses and vehicles are seen in the aftermath of flash floods along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Wednesday. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press) Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region. Researchers at the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000, primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

World.title: Canada’s largest icebreaker makes 6th visit to the North Pole
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Coast Guard’s largest and most powerful icebreaker successfully visited the North Pole this month as part of an effort to resolve disputed claims in the Arctic.

The CCGS Louis S. St-Laurent, accompanied by the Swedish icebreaker Oden , reached the North Pole on August 16.

The polar mission is being carried out in order to map the floor of the Arctic Ocean with special sensors which researchers say will help better define Canada's claim on a portion also claimed by Russia and Denmark via its autonomous territory Greenland.

LISTEN | CBC's Front Burner from July 7, 2026: Front Burner 28:55 What does it take to defend Canada’s Arctic?

This marks the sixth trip the ship has made to the pole, an area which few humans have ever visited.

For Capt. Byron Briggs, this was his first time on the top of the world.

“It actually was even more of an adrenaline rush than I thought it was going to be after we successfully managed to get to the pole and play with the ship enough to actually get the GPS to tell us we were at 90 North ,” Briggs said, referring to the pole’s latitude.

“It was a pretty special moment for me, certainly. And based on the cheers from everybody else on the bridge with me, it was a pretty big moment for all of us.”

Briggs said they managed to rendezvous with Santa Claus when they reached the North Pole.

On the ice, crew members played a friendly game of hockey.

Crew dressed as Santa Claus and elves gathered for a photo at the North Pole (Submitted by the Canadian Coast Guard)

The ship has a crew of 77 in total, including 47 core crew, a doctor and nurse, a helicopter flight crew and a science team of 22.

In 2019 and 2022, Canada fulfilled its obligation under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and submitted data outlining the country's claims on the sea floor.

Kai Boggild, a scientist with the Geological Survey of Canada, is leading the research operation collecting that data.

"[This data] demonstrates where we believe these points are," Boggild said.

Information collected on this mission is intended to back those claims up, in particular around the Lomonosov Ridge, an underwater ridge which splits the Arctic Ocean into two basins.

Boggild noted that the importance of the trip goes beyond geopolitics and will provide critical scientific data.

“There are a lot of really fundamental questions about how we understand how the Arctic formed," Boggild said.

“So collecting these data for UNCLOS also allows us to learn a lot more about basically the natural history of the Arctic Ocean and, and how that's evolved over, over millions of years.”

Crew members of the mission to the North Pole took part in a hockey game on the Arctic sea ice. (Submitted by the Canadian Coast Guard)

In a statement issued by the Department of National Defence, David McGuinty, minister of defence, said the ship’s mission serves multiple purposes, including asserting Canadian sovereignty in the region.

“The arrival of CCGS Louis S. St-Laurent at the North Pole is an important milestone that reflects Canada’s enduring commitment to the Arctic,” McGuinty said. “This mission advances scientific knowledge, strengthens our presence in the North, and reinforces Canada’s sovereignty and security.”

The Louis S. St-Laurent’s crew left home port in St. John’s, Newfoundland, on July 8 and is expected to return in early November.

World.title: Testimony concludes in trial of U.S. mother accused of killing her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

Testimony concluded Wednesday in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a mother accused of strangling her three young children in a case that has drawn attention to postpartum mental health.

Closing arguments are expected to begin Thursday, before the jury begins deliberating.

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, with her lawyers arguing she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan Clancy at the family's home in coastal Duxbury, Mass., in January 2023.

The rare mental illness is linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.

FBI forensic psychiatrist testifies

Prosecutors say Clancy planned the killings and understood her actions were wrong.

Clancy did not testify during the trial, which is in its fifth week. The defence called 10 witnesses, including some of Clancy's friends and relatives, while prosecutors called more than 70 witnesses, including her then-husband.

Testifying as the final rebuttal witness for the prosecution, a forensic psychiatrist at the University of Virginia and a senior psychiatrist for the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit said Wednesday that he did not believe Clancy's account that a voice ordered her to kill the children.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague asked Dr. Gregory Saathoff a series of questions about Clancy's account: Did the voice tell her where to kill the children? How to kill them? What to use? In what order? Saathoff answered no each time.

"Having no instructions as to how to do it, but being able to execute those decisions … that is surprising that she's able to accomplish all of this without any other kind of direction or plan," he said.

Forensic psychiatrist Dr. Gregory Saathoff was one of the final individuals called to testify in the trial. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/The Associated Press)

All three children were strangled with exercise bands in the family's basement before Clancy tried to kill herself while her husband was getting takeout and at a pharmacy on Jan. 24, 2023. Saathoff said her ability to accomplish everything she did without direction indicated Clancy "had control, control of the sequence of what she was doing throughout."

"In the small amount of time that Miss Clancy had in the home without her husband, it was important, in order to carry this out, as well as her suicide, to do this quickly, methodically and alike," he said.

On Tuesday, Saathoff said he found it unusual that Clancy said the voice stopped once she was done strangling the children, that the voice was constant rather than intermittent and that she never previously reported hearing a voice to her medical providers. She also gave a different timeline to other evaluators about when she first heard the voice that day, he said.

"Committing the act is not curative of the voice," Saathoff said of the voice stopping abruptly. "I've not ever seen that."

WATCH | Focus on postpartum mental health: The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health | Duration 2:13 The trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy has put a spotlight on maternal mental health, which some medical experts say may be the only positive outcome in the tragic case. Her legal team argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for the murder of her three children because she was suffering from bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.

Psychiatrist's expertise in postpartum psychosis challenged

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington began his cross-examination of Saathoff on Wednesday by trying to cast doubt on Saathoff's expertise in postpartum psychosis and portray him as someone closely aligned with law enforcement, questioning him about his work with prisons, the Justice Department and the Virginia attorney general's office.

Saathoff testified that he treated women with postpartum psychosis while working at a state hospital in the 1980s and 1990s, while much of his more recent research has focused on such subjects as extremist violence, national security and political radicalization.

Reddington also asked Saathoff about Clancy's attempts to search online for information about postpartum depression, her visits to multiple maternal and mental health providers, disclosures to her mother and then-husband that she was suicidal and feared that she would harm her children, and calls to a suicide hotline — all attempts that Reddington contended establish Clancy realized something was seriously wrong and made a sincere effort over time to get help.

Reddington asked whether Saathoff believes that Clancy decided to kill her children because she "no longer liked the life she thought she wanted" and was making "a selfish choice" to "manipulate her providers, seek out a quick and easy fix when she was feeling depressed and anxious."

"I think that statement that you read really minimizes what she was going through," Saathoff responded.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
