A first national map of informal housing

The RAI report, detailed on 24 August, gives Guatemala its first nationwide baseline of informal urbanisation. The 924 Guatemala vulnerable settlements identified sit in nine of the country’s ten urban nodes, the metropolitan and regional hubs where unplanned growth is concentrated. Each settlement has been located, georeferenced and characterised, turning communities long absent from official statistics into identifiable units of public policy.

The practical purpose is targeting. With the registry, authorities can prioritise potable water, drainage, electricity and risk-mitigation works where vulnerability is highest, and municipalities can plan regularisation instead of reacting to emergencies. Housing officials describe the registry as an advancing national strategy rather than a finished census, with coverage still being extended to the remaining urban node.

Urban poverty is not a new theme in Guatemala, but the absence of reliable data has blunted every previous programme. The national map is meant to fix the information problem first, so that budget lines for housing and basic services can follow geography rather than politics.

Enade puts security back at the top

On 25 August, Fundesa presented Enade 2026, the twentieth edition of the National Business Encounter for Development, under the motto A Paso Seguro: integral security as the path to prosperity. It is the third time the summit has centred on security, after editions in 2007 on security and justice and in 2016 on justice and the rule of law.

The diagnosis Fundesa put on the table is progress stalled. Guatemala cut its homicide rate from 31 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2014 to about 16 today, but the indicator has stopped falling in recent years. The business foundation proposes halving it to 8 per 100,000 by 2036 through stronger institutions, better coordination among security and justice authorities, and sustained investment.

The economic framing is deliberate. Fundesa estimates the criminal economy costs Guatemala the equivalent of 7.7 per cent of GDP, a figure that turns security from a social issue into a balance-sheet one. Announced speakers include former Colombian president Iván Duque and Guy Nir, former intelligence chief of Israel’s police.

The summit programme goes beyond diagnosis. Fundesa wants the twentieth Enade to produce a cooperation agreement among security and justice authorities, the kind of institutional compact the business sector argues Guatemala has lacked since the homicide rate stopped falling. Whether the government of President Bernardo Arévalo signs on to the business-backed framework will be the first test of the A Paso Seguro agenda.

The choice of speakers signals the intended audience. Duque brings the experience of a Colombian government that negotiated security policy under fiscal pressure, and Nir brings an intelligence-led policing model that Fundesa has studied for years. Both are expected to address how middle-income countries can fund security without crowding out social spending, a trade-off at the centre of Guatemala’s budget debate.

Why the two agendas converge

The registry and the Enade agenda address the same underlying condition: state presence. The Guatemala vulnerable settlements mapped by the RAI are precisely the territories where public services, and often public security, are weakest, and where organised crime finds recruits and logistics. Fundesa’s proposal for a cooperation agreement among security and justice institutions would mean little without basic-services policy reaching those same neighbourhoods.

The economic backdrop adds urgency. Guatemala grew 4.4 per cent in the first half of 2026, among the fastest rates in Central America, but business leaders argue that insecurity caps investment and formal job creation. For the executives gathering at Enade, the Guatemala vulnerable settlements registry and the homicide target are two halves of one competitiveness argument: safer, better-served cities are cheaper to build businesses in.

What to watch next

For the registry, the test is execution: whether the 924 settlements translate into funded works in the 2027 budget, and whether the tenth urban node is incorporated to complete the national map. For Enade, the test is whether the homicide target survives contact with politics; the summit’s planned cooperation agreement among security and justice authorities would be the first proof.

Both tracks converge on credibility. Guatemala has announced ambitious targets before and missed them. What distinguishes this round, its backers say, is measurement: a georeferenced registry of Guatemala vulnerable settlements on one side, and a single number, 8 homicides per 100,000 by 2036, on the other.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the RAI and what did it find? The Registry of Informal Settlements is Guatemala’s national mapping of informal housing. Its latest report identifies 924 Guatemala vulnerable settlements located, georeferenced and characterised in nine of ten urban nodes, creating a baseline to target water, drainage, electricity and risk works. What is Enade 2026 proposing on security? Fundesa’s twentieth Enade summit, presented on 25 August under the motto A Paso Seguro, proposes halving the homicide rate from about 16 to 8 per 100,000 inhabitants by 2036 through stronger institutions and coordination. Fundesa estimates the criminal economy costs 7.7 per cent of GDP. How are the settlement map and the homicide target connected? Both target weak state presence. The settlements identified by the RAI are areas with the least access to services and often the highest insecurity, so Fundesa argues security policy and basic-services investment in Guatemala vulnerable settlements must advance together.

World.title: US Backs Honduras Energy Reform as Liberal Deputies Split on Bill
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Central America · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Diplomacy US chargée Colleen Hoey met Congress president Tomás Zambrano on 19 August to back the Honduras energy reform

— The bill reorganise state utility ENEE and open the door to private investment while keeping assets state-owned

— The split Liberal deputy Francis Cabrera says his bench will not back the current text; a counterproposal is due within days

— The hole ENEE ran a deficit of 11.2 billion lempiras (about US$417 million) in the first half of 2026, according to watchdog ASJ

— The stakes the utility loses roughly US$600 million a year, the biggest single drain on the national budget

Washington wants a modernised power sector; the Liberal bench wants a different bill. ENEE’s deficit is not waiting.

The United States has reaffirmed its support for the Honduras energy reform in a meeting between the US embassy’s chargée d’affaires, Colleen A. Hoey, and Congress president Tomás Zambrano in Tegucigalpa, even as the bill remains stuck in the legislature. The Liberal Party bench, whose votes the congressional board needs, has raised objections to the current text and plans to table a counterproposal, deepening a split that has stalled the overhaul of state electricity company ENEE since June.

A hydroelectric plant in Central America. Honduras’s stalled reform targets the restructuring of state utility ENEE. (illustrative)

Washington reaffirms its backing

The meeting between Hoey and Zambrano, reported by Tegucigalpa daily El Mundo, put energy-sector modernisation at the top of the bilateral agenda. During the encounter, the United States reaffirmed its commitment to keep working with Honduras towards a more efficient and reliable energy system capable of attracting investment, and stressed that a stronger sector would contribute to the prosperity of the country and the region.

Washington has publicly endorsed the Honduras energy reform since June, when the executive sent the bill to Congress and it cleared its first two debates. The diplomatic push comes as the government of President Nasry Asfura tries to deliver the overhaul before the end of the year, and as multilateral lenders, including the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, keep technical and financial support on the table.

The timing is not accidental. The legislature’s board hopes to bring the bill to its third and final debate in the coming weeks, and US encouragement is aimed at holding together a coalition that looks increasingly fragile.

Liberal deputies split over the text

That coalition now runs through the Liberal Party. The board of Congress is courting the Liberal bench to approve the decree, but the caucus has expressed reservations about the original document and remains unconvinced. Deputy Francis Cabrera has said his bloc will not accompany the Honduras energy reform in its current terms, and the Liberals are expected to present an improved counterproposal within days.

The counterproposal has been weeks in the making. La Prensa reported in late July that the Liberal bench would condition its support on acceptance of its own draft amendments, and El Mundo reported in early August that deputies were urging the party to table the document quickly. The legislature’s leadership says it expects the counterproposal as soon as possible, opening a new negotiation round over the future of the bill.

The split matters because the numbers in Congress are tight. Without the Liberals, the government lacks the votes to pass the Honduras energy reform in its current form, and further delay feeds uncertainty for investors who have watched the bill stall since mid-June.

What the overhaul would change at ENEE

The reform would reorganise the Empresa Nacional de Energía Eléctrica, separating generation, transmission and distribution into distinct units while keeping the company under state ownership. Regulator CREE has published a final draft incorporating input from unions, business groups COHEP and ANDI, engineers’ associations, renewable-energy group AHER and civil-society watchdog ASJ. On the most sensitive point, the sale or privatisation of assets, the final bill would raise protection to constitutional rank: any change to the public nature of ENEE’s assets, holdings or shares would require congressional approval.

The financial case is stark. According to ASJ, ENEE posted a deficit of 11.2 billion lempiras, about US$417 million, in the first half of 2026 alone, as energy-sales revenue covered only 65 per cent of its expenses. Annual losses run to roughly US$600 million, the largest single hole in the national budget.

Technical work is already moving. ENEE has awarded a five-month contract to Colombia’s Consorcio Oportunidad Estratégica-Diorama Group to prepare a financial and operational sustainability plan, part of a national transmission-support programme financed by the IDB. The consortium was one of 15 groups that expressed interest, according to BNamericas, which reported the award on 14 August.

What to watch next

The immediate variable is the Liberal counterproposal. If its text narrows the gap with the government draft, the third debate could be scheduled in September; if it hardens positions, the Honduras energy reform could drift towards year-end with ENEE’s deficit compounding.

Investors are pricing the outcome. The government argues the reform will cut losses, improve service quality and set clearer rules for private capital in generation and distribution. Washington’s public backing, restated in Tegucigalpa this month, raises the diplomatic cost of failure, but the votes that matter are still inside the Honduran Congress.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the United States say about the Honduras energy reform? Chargee d’affaires Colleen A. Hoey told Congress president Tomás Zambrano that the United States remains committed to helping Honduras build a more efficient, reliable energy system that attracts investment, reaffirming support expressed since June. Why are Liberal deputies blocking the bill? The Liberal bench objects to the current text and, in the words of deputy Francis Cabrera, will not accompany the reform as drafted. The caucus plans to present a counterproposal, which the congressional board expects within days. How bad are ENEE’s finances? Watchdog ASJ puts ENEE’s first-half 2026 deficit at 11.2 billion lempiras, about US$417 million, with energy sales covering just 65 per cent of expenses. Annual losses approach US$600 million, the biggest single drain on the budget.

World.title: IFX Data Centers Get US$400 Million AI Upgrade Across the Region
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Central America · BUSINESS

Key Facts — Investment more than US$400 million between 2026 and 2027 across Latin America

— Footprint 27 IFX data centers in 18 countries and over 150,000 km of dedicated fibre

— Country tranches US$169 million for Colombia, about US$19 million for Argentina, US$6 million for El Salvador

— Clients more than 6,000 corporate and government customers served by 3,000 employees

— Goal become the region’s reference digital-infrastructure operator for enterprise AI by 2030

The region’s largest independent data-centre operator wants Latin America’s artificial-intelligence workloads hosted on Latin American soil.

IFX, the Latin American digital-infrastructure operator, has unveiled a new corporate identity and an investment plan worth more than US$400 million for 2026-2027, aimed squarely at expanding IFX data centers for artificial-intelligence workloads. The announcement, made on 20 August 2026, pairs the company’s first major rebrand in 27 years with a build-out of computing capacity, fibre, cloud and cybersecurity operations from Mexico to Argentina.

Server racks inside a data center, the infrastructure at the heart of IFX’s US$400 million regional expansion.

A US$400 million bet on locally hosted AI

The company framed the plan as a wager that Latin America’s artificial-intelligence boom should run on infrastructure installed inside the region rather than imported from abroad. The investment will expand IFX data centers with specialized processors, greater energy capacity and connections designed for AI applications, while also strengthening the regional fibre-optic network and growing cloud and cybersecurity units.

The announcement coincided with the first significant brand renewal in the company’s 27-year history. Diego Cardoza, IFX’s country manager, said the change responds to surging demand for AI applications in strategic sectors. Chief executive Samuel Mezrahi was blunter: the investment, he said, is the company’s bet that the region will host that capacity on its own territory, and that IFX intends to be the operator on which much of the new economy relies.

Today, much of the infrastructure behind Latin American companies’ AI applications sits outside the region, in the hands of global operators. Hosting it locally lets sectors such as banking, government and health comply with local regulation, keep data within national borders and respond faster, the company argues. That sovereignty pitch is the commercial spine of the new cycle for IFX data centers.

Where the money is landing

Country-level tranches have emerged quickly. IFX will invest US$169 million in Colombia between 2026 and 2027 to boost data centres and AI infrastructure, Colombian business daily Portafolio reported. In Argentina the figure is close to US$19 million, according to local media, and in El Salvador the company announced on 25 August a tranche of nearly US$6 million for 2026-2027.

The group enters the cycle from a position of scale. It operates 27 proprietary data centres, the most recent being Orión in Guatemala, more than 150,000 kilometres of dedicated fibre from Mexico to Argentina, and serves over 6,000 corporate and government clients with a workforce of 3,000. Priority sectors for the new investments are banking, retail, government, health, education and critical industries.

The Colombian tranche illustrates the model. Portafolio reported that the US$169 million will go to data centres and AI infrastructure in a market where demand from banks and retailers already strains existing capacity. Argentina’s nearly US$19 million and El Salvador’s US$6 million are smaller, but they extend the same logic to markets where local AI-ready capacity barely exists.

For Central America, the plan reinforces a footprint that already includes the newest facility in the portfolio, Orión in Guatemala, and a fresh commitment in El Salvador. Regional executives see the isthmus as a connectivity bridge between North and South America, and IFX data centers in Guatemala and El Salvador position the company to capture nearshoring and digital-government demand.

Why the timing matters

The announcement lands as governments and banks across Latin America race to adopt AI tools while data-protection rules tighten. Hyperscale projects in Brazil and Mexico have dominated headlines, but mid-tier markets lack computing capacity close to users. IFX is betting that enterprises in those markets will pay for local, compliant capacity rather than routing workloads abroad.

Energy is the binding constraint for AI infrastructure worldwide, and the region is no exception. IFX says the new facilities will carry greater energy capacity and designs tailored to AI loads, a recognition that power availability now decides where data centres get built. The company’s fibre backbone, spanning more than 150,000 kilometres, gives it a distribution advantage that pure colocation rivals lack.

The 2030 horizon matters for investors reading the plan. IFX wants to consolidate as the reference digital-infrastructure operator for enterprise AI in Latin America, a goal that requires the current expansion of IFX data centers to be followed by sustained utilisation from banks, retailers and public agencies.

What to watch next

The near-term signposts are execution milestones: construction starts on the Colombian build-out, the ramp of the El Salvador tranche announced this week, and further country allocations from the US$400 million envelope. The company has yet to disclose how the remaining funds split across its 18 markets.

Customers and regulators will also watch whether the rebrand translates into contracts. The pitch, local capacity for local data, fits the regulatory mood in banking, health and government, but converting that mood into multi-year commitments will decide whether the bet on IFX data centers pays off on the 2030 timetable Mezrahi has set. Competitors are not standing still: hyperscalers and regional telecom groups are chasing the same enterprise AI budgets, and the window for a mid-tier operator to lock in anchor clients is short.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is IFX investing in AI infrastructure? More than US$400 million between 2026 and 2027, aimed at expanding IFX data centers with specialized AI processors, plus fibre, cloud and cybersecurity operations across Latin America. Which countries get the largest tranches? Colombia leads with US$169 million, followed by Argentina with close to US$19 million and El Salvador with nearly US$6 million. IFX operates in 18 countries, with 27 proprietary data centres including Orión in Guatemala. Why does IFX want AI workloads hosted in Latin America? The company argues that local infrastructure lets banking, government and health clients comply with data rules, keep information within national borders and cut latency, instead of depending on operators abroad.

World.title: Google Wins Auction for Spirit Airlines’ Massive Data Archive, Raising Privacy Alarms
World.content:
For all us fun that have flown Spirit to Costa Rica, it was announced that Spirit Airlines has agreed to sell a sprawling trove of internal company data to Google for $10 million, marking one of the more unusual chapters in the discount carrier’s bankruptcy liquidation. The budget airline ceased all flights in May 2026 and has spent the months since selling off aircraft, equipment and real estate through court proceedings. Now its digital records, accumulated over decades of operations, have become one of the sale’s most contested assets.

Google beat out competing bidder Mercor.io, an artificial intelligence data firm that offered $7.5 million, to win the auction in mid August. According to court filings, the winning package includes close to 100 million internal emails, roughly 500 million Microsoft Teams messages, and more than 175,000 employee records stretching back to 1986. It also contains 7.2 billion records tracking competitor flight activity and 7.5 billion passenger transaction records dating to 2008, along with material touching on revenue, aircraft operations, marketing campaigns, fraud investigations and pricing strategy.

Company officials have stressed that the deal excludes the airline’s core customer database. Court documents specify that about 97.5 million passenger profiles and 50.2 million records tied to the Free Spirit loyalty program are carved out of the sale entirely, along with credit card information. A court appointed third party is required to strip the remaining data of anything that could identify a specific individual before Google receives it, and the company says it will not attempt to reverse that process.

A Google spokesperson said the acquisition would help improve the company’s products and AI models and reiterated that no personal information would be received as part of the purchase. Spirit’s own statement echoed that position, saying the company takes data privacy seriously and is working with the appropriate parties to resolve any outstanding concerns.

Not everyone is convinced the safeguards go far enough. The Association of Flight Attendants CWA, which represents more than 5,500 of Spirit’s former cabin crew, filed a formal objection to the sale, arguing that scrubbing names and other obvious identifiers does not guarantee that individuals or small groups of employees cannot still be pieced back together from the underlying data. The union’s challenge was enough to delay the bankruptcy court hearing originally scheduled for August 19. It has since been pushed to September 9, when a judge is expected to weigh in on whether the transaction can proceed.

The sale is unusual by industry standards. Most airlines that collapse into bankruptcy are absorbed whole, data included, by a competitor. Spirit’s case instead treated its accumulated digital footprint as a standalone asset class, sold off separately from the physical business.

For all of us that ever booked a Spirit flight, worked for the airline or simply exchanged emails with someone who did, the episode is a reminder that corporate data can outlive the company that collected it, and that the line between anonymized information and identifiable information is not always as firm as buyers and sellers claim.

World.title: Scientists Name the Fault Behind Costa Rica’s Coronado Earthquakes
World.content:
Costa Rica’s seismologists now have a name for what shook the Central Valley awake yesterday, and it comes with a history. The National Seismological Network at the University of Costa Rica has linked yesterday’s earthquakes near Coronado to the Río Sucio fault system. The network calls the connection preliminary, but it rests on two pieces of evidence pointing the same way — the quakes and their aftershocks cluster tightly along where the fault runs, and the direction the ground moved matches how this fault is known to behave.

A fault is a fracture in the earth’s crust where two blocks of rock grind past one another. When they lock, strain builds. When they slip, the ground shakes. This one is not a surprise to scientists. Researchers at the university’s Central American School of Geology identified it back in the 1990s using satellite imagery, fieldwork and records of past quakes in the area. The system runs about 30 kilometers, roughly 19 miles, and the rock on either side slides sideways past itself rather than one block dropping below the other.

That sideways motion explains something thousands of people noticed. Security cameras across the valley captured buildings, lamps and hanging signs swaying side to side rather than jolting straight up. That is what this kind of fault does. The track record is the part worth paying attention to.

The network ties three earlier earthquakes to the same system. The most serious was the Patillos earthquake of December 30, 1952, a magnitude 5.9 that killed 21 people according to historical records. More recently there was Capellades on November 30, 2016, a magnitude 5.5. And in August 2023, a magnitude 4.4 struck with several smaller quakes just north of where Monday’s sequence unfolded.

Seismologist Lepolt Linkimer of the university network has said assessments of the fault put its potential at above magnitude 6. The National University’s Volcanological and Seismological Observatory is not ready to name a single culprit. Its position is that the area sits inside a broader zone containing several faults, and that more than one may have been involved.

“It is a series of faults, not just the seismic zone as such,” said observatory seismologist José María Sequeira. Work continues, he said, to establish which structure was directly involved, and whether one fault moved or several. Sequeira named Alto Grande, Río Patria, Lara, Río Sucio and La Hondura among the faults in that zone, most of them taking their names from the rivers running above them.

The zone stretches across the ground between the Turrialba and Barva volcanoes, passing Irazú, and belongs to a wider band of fractured crust reaching from the Limón lowlands to the Pacific side. Finding exactly where these faults run is harder than it sounds. Most are buried under soil with no visible crack at the surface, so geologists read the landscape for clues. The Río Sucio is one of the clearer cases — the river cuts an unusually straight line, and the small quakes cluster along it.

Mapping each aftershock sharpens that picture, showing where the movement concentrates both across the surface and at depth. The aftershocks kept coming all day. The National University’s observatory counted 80 between 1:39 a.m. and 6 p.m. Monday, an average of one roughly every 12 minutes. The university network logged 23 in a narrower window, counting only those at magnitude 2.2 or above — the same kind of methodological gap that produced the differing magnitude figures reported on Monday.

The university network recorded shaking intensity across the central region at levels five to six on a twelve-point scale, meaning it was felt clearly indoors, rattled objects and, at the upper end, moved furniture. Damage stayed limited to a garden wall in Coronado, a downed power pole in Moravia and rockfall that briefly closed Route 32.

No deaths or injuries were reported and both institutions expect the aftershocks to continue for hours and days yet, tapering off in frequency as sequences like this normally do. The university network says it will keep watching and update as new data arrives. None of this is unusual ground for Costa Rica as it sits where tectonic plates collide offshore and is threaded with active faults inland, which is why permanent monitoring exists at all. What changed this week is that one of those faults stopped being an abstraction on a map.

World.title: Beekeepers in Cayo receive training to expand Apiaries and boost Honey Production
World.content:
Beekeepers in Cayo receive training to expand Apiaries and boost Honey Production

By Zoila Palma: Fifteen beekeepers in the Cayo District participated in a training session on apiary expansion, bee colony rearing and good husbandry practices today.

The training was conducted by Extension Officers Noe Oliva and Moises Perez of the Cayo District Agriculture Office.

The theoretical sessions were held at the Agriculture Department’s Central Farm conference room, while participants took part in practical exercises at the demonstration apiary at Central Farm.

Key topics included monitoring beehives, hive divisions or splits, swarm prevention, swarm trapping and the importance of proper and consistent apiary management.

Participants also learned how to identify common signs and symptoms of pests in their apiaries at an early stage, allowing beekeepers to take timely action to protect their colonies.

During a hands-on exercise, the beekeepers observed and assisted in successfully carrying out a hive division using a nucleus.

The Ministry of Agriculture said the training is expected to strengthen beekeepers’ skills and improve apiary management, ultimately helping to increase honey production across the Cayo District.

World.title: Government of Belize and CARICOM Development Fund launch project to strengthen furniture, animal feed and turmeric industries
World.content:
Government of Belize and CARICOM Development Fund launch project to strengthen furniture, animal feed and turmeric industries

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, through the Directorate General for Foreign Trade (DGFT) and the CARICOM Development Fund (CDF), has launched a new initiative aimed at strengthening the competitiveness, climate resilience and inclusiveness of selected industries benefiting from Article 164 protection.

The 36-month project will run from September 2026 to August 2029 with support from a CDF grant.

Belize is serving as the pilot country for the regional initiative, which seeks to provide practical support to industries benefiting from Article 164, a provision that offers temporary protection to selected industries in CARICOM’s Less Developed Countries.

The project will focus on three priority sectors in Belize — furniture, animal feed and turmeric — identified through consultations with industry stakeholders and assessments of challenges and opportunities within the sectors.

The project will provide support in areas including industry research, policy development, business and technical capacity building, export readiness, climate resilience, sustainable practices and value chain development. The initiative was formally launched during a stakeholder and ministry kick-off session attended by representatives from Government ministries and agencies, technical institutions, industry stakeholders and other partners to discuss implementation, responsibilities and the expertise needed to support the project.

Through the partnership, the Government and CDF aim to help Belizean industries become more competitive, sustainable and resilient while generating lessons that can contribute to strengthening Article 164 industries across the wider CARICOM region.

World.title: Belize launches National Plan to protect critically endangered Hicatee
World.content:
Belize launches National Plan to protect critically endangered Hicatee

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has launched the Hicatee Conservation and Action Plan 2026–2031, establishing a national framework to protect and support the recovery of the critically endangered Central American River Turtle, known locally as the Hicatee or Tortuga Blanca.

The plan was officially launched on August 26 during the fourth day of Belize Climate Week by the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation and the Belize Fisheries Department.

The Hicatee (Dermatemys mawii) is classified as “Critically Endangered” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and is considered one of the world’s 25 most endangered turtle species.

The new plan was developed through collaboration between the Belize Fisheries Department, the Belize Foundation for Research and Environmental Education, the Turtle Survival Alliance, Zoo New England and other stakeholders.

The 2026–2031 plan outlines eight conservation goals and 58 actions focused on strengthening enforcement and regulations, protecting and restoring habitats, increasing research and population monitoring, improving public awareness, supporting captive management and reintroduction, and involving communities in conservation efforts.

Key threats to the Hicatee include illegal and unsustainable harvesting, habitat destruction, riparian deforestation, wetland drainage and pollution.

The Government has formally endorsed the plan and committed to supporting its implementation through coordination among agencies, policy development, technical assistance and the mobilization of national and international resources.

World.title: UDP expresses solidarity with Public Service Union and Belize Tax Service
World.content:
UDP expresses solidarity with Public Service Union and Belize Tax Service

By Zoila Palma: Today, the United Democratic Party (UDP) said that it stands firmly in solidarity with the Public Service Unions and the staff of the Belize Tax Service Department with their walkout today.

“Those who will be directly affected by the proposed Revenue Authority Bill, 2026 have a right to genuine, meaningful consultation not token engagement after critical decisions have already been made,” Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton said.

“The Government must immediately meet with the unions and employees in good faith, address their legitimate concerns sent to them in writing on August 10th, 2026 and ensure that their concerns are fully reflected before this legislation advances,” Panton added.

Panton said that consultation is a fundamental requirement of accountable governance, and the Government must respect it.

World.title: National Celebrations Commission contributes $20,000 to Queen of the Bay
World.content:
National Celebrations Commission contributes $20,000 to Queen of the Bay

By Zoila Palma: Today, the National Celebrations Commission made a contribution of $20,000 to the Queen of the Bay Committee as they prepare for the 81st Queen of the Bay Pageant.

Director Kim Vasquez presented the contribution on behalf of Francis Fonseca, Chairman of the NCC and the National Celebrations Commission.

The Queen of the Bay is Belize’s longest-running cultural pageant and historical tradition, first held in 1946 to symbolize national sovereignty and freedom.

World.title: Belize Electricity Limited says major outage due to loss of power from Mexico
World.content:
Belize Electricity Limited says major outage due to loss of power from Mexico

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) issued a statement updating the public on the major power outage that affected customers across the entire country last night.

At 7:28 p.m., BEL experienced an unplanned system collapse following a temporary loss of power from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), due to issues on the Mexican power system.

BEL says that at that time, available in-country generation stood at approximately 103 MW, with evening peak reaching 122MW, resulting in a shortage of approximately 19MW.

“The sudden loss of a significant portion of electricity supply activated BEL’s grid protection system to restore the system balance by shedding load in various parts of the national grid. This resulted in outages across several service areas countrywide until the supply from CFE was restored at 10:54 p.m,” BEL explained.

BEL noted that available in-country generation continues to be constrained by a combination of seasonal and maintenance-related factors. Certain renewable generation sources remain unavailable due to seasonal conditions, while some generating units are out of service for maintenance, and others are operating at reduced capacity. These factors continue to limit the overall availability of local generation sources.

The company says that their teams continue to closely monitor available generation and conditions on the national grid, while taking all available measures to minimize the impact on Customers.

World.title: BTL formally withdraws proposed acquisition of Speednet
World.content:
BTL formally withdraws proposed acquisition of Speednet

By Zoila Palma: Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) has formally withdrawn its submissions to the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) regarding its proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited.

he decision was communicated to the PUC in a letter dated August 24, 2026, signed by BTL Chief Financial Officer Ian Cleverly.

In the letter, BTL formally notified the PUC that it was withdrawing its previous submissions, which had been made in February 2026 as part of the proposed acquisition process.

BTL stated that it “no longer intends to proceed with the acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited” and said the PUC therefore no longer needs to consider the earlier submissions.

BTL said it had pursued the proposed acquisition in good faith, with the intention of strengthening Belize’s telecommunications sector and improving services for consumers.

According to the letter, the company sought to achieve “greater efficiencies, supporting continued investment and innovation, and delivering enhanced services and value to consumers.”

The company said it had engaged constructively with relevant stakeholders and authorities throughout the process but ultimately decided to abandon the transaction because of a “change in circumstances.”

World.title: Tax workers walk out over SARA as PM is out of country on personal leave
World.content:
Tax workers walk out over SARA as PM is out of country on personal leave

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Employees of the Belize Tax Service Department (BTSD) in Belmopan walked out of work on Wednesday morning in protest of the controversial Revenue Authority Bill, which seeks to transform the department into a Semi-Autonomous Revenue Authority, commonly referred to as SARA.

Channel 7 Belize reported the walkout on Wednesday morning as the long-running dispute between tax workers and the government moved into a new phase of industrial action.

The protest also comes while Prime Minister and Minister of Finance John Briceño is out of the country on personal leave. Channel 7 reported that Briceño departed Belize on Tuesday afternoon on a flight to Houston, shortly after returning from an official visit to Honduras, and is reportedly expected to remain away until early next week. As Minister of Finance, Briceño has been one of the principal government figures defending the SARA transition and the Revenue Authority Bill.

The action comes only days after the House of Representatives passed the Revenue Authority Bill despite strong objections from the Public Service Union (PSU), which represents affected public officers. Prior to the House vote, the union called on tax service employees to “stand ready” for possible action if the legislation continued to advance in its present form.

Government says SARA is intended to modernize tax administration by giving the authority greater flexibility to recruit specialized personnel, operate on a performance-based system and improve tax collection and compliance. Prime Minister John Briceño has argued that the present public-service structure limits the department’s ability to recruit and retain specialized employees. Government has also insisted that the legislation does not introduce new taxes.

However, the PSU has raised several objections. Among its most serious concerns is the governance structure proposed in the bill. PSU President Dean Flowers argues that the legislation leaves SARA’s seven-member board largely in an advisory role while giving the Minister of Finance significant authority over the appointment and removal of the authority’s chief executive. Flowers has warned that the arrangement does not provide sufficient institutional independence or checks and balances.

There are also long-running concerns about the effect of the transition on employees’ public-service status, pensions, gratuities, allowances and other accumulated benefits. Government maintains that there will be no job losses and says existing employees will have an opportunity to transition to SARA, while those who do not wish to do so can be redeployed elsewhere in the Public Service. Government has further said accrued benefits will be protected.

The PSU has also questioned the financial justification for establishing another authority. Flowers says millions of dollars have already been spent modernizing and amalgamating Belize’s tax administration and has challenged government to produce data demonstrating why another major restructuring is necessary and how the additional operating costs will be financed.

Another major source of friction has been the consultation process. The PSU says it submitted detailed recommendations and concerns but that a promised follow-up meeting never occurred and its submissions were not properly presented to the parliamentary committee considering the legislation. Briceño has disputed that account, arguing that the union failed to make its case at the appropriate stage of the parliamentary process.

The dispute over SARA stretches back to 2025, when the PSU formally declared a trade dispute over unanswered questions surrounding the proposed transition. Wednesday’s walkout represents one of the clearest signs yet that opposition among affected tax service workers is moving from negotiations and public statements to direct industrial action — and it comes at a time when the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance is away from the country.

World.title: Unhealthy trend: Student obesity surges to 15.3%
World.content:
The Global School-based Health Survey confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight. (Photo: Adobe stock)

MORE than three in every 10 students captured in a recent survey by the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) were overweight while 15.3 per cent of them were obese.

The Global School-based Health Survey (GSHS), which was conducted between January and March this year, had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools.

It confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight, while underweight remains a concern.

According to the survey, obesity moved from six per cent in 2010 to 15.3 per cent in 2026, while the number of overweight students jumped from 21.7 per cent in 2010 to 31.7 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, there was an uptick in underweight students, from 2.1 per cent in 2010 to 3.4 per cent in 2026.

The survey also found a dip in physical activity from 23.2 per cent in 2017 to 19.6 per cent in 2026, while 70.2 per cent reported less than eight hours of sleep, which can be attributed to the long hours students spend on the Internet as sedentary behaviour — sitting down for more than three hours per day increased from 56.4 per cent in 2017 to 68 per cent in 2026.

“Students [who are] less active, more sedentary, and many not getting enough sleep means that there is an increased risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems,” said the NCDA.

It called for more physical activity, greater promotion of recreation and sports, and encouragement for students to adopt healthy sleep habits.

The NCDA blamed unhealthy eating patterns for the rise in obesity among students, and recommended the promotion of healthy school food environment, expansion of nutrition education, and promotion of balanced diets.

But despite the increase in obesity and overweight, the survey found that in the 30 days before it was conducted there was a drop in consumption of one or more sodas per day by students.

In 2010 the NCDA found that 72.5 per cent on the respondents had consumed one or more sodas in the 30 days before the survey, while this year only 49.7 per cent of the respondents said they had done so in the past seven days.

The survey said underweight was highest among grade nine boys, 6.4 per cent, and grade 11 girls, 4.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the highest rate of obesity was among grade seven girls, 43.2 per cent, and grade seven boys, 40.5 per cent.

The Global School-based Health Survey, noted the NCDA, provides high-quality data to inform decision-making and action for school and youth health.

In his reaction to the survey findings, Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton urged parents and guardians to ensure their children eat healthy foods at home and school.

He said it is always a better choice to take a meal from home to school if the school does not have facilities for the preparation of hot meals.

Tufton also urged parents and guardians to encourage their children to participate in more physical activities if they want to ensure that they do not fall victim to diabetes, heart disease, and other non-communicable diseases.

“Parents and guardians must insist that their children become more health conscious. Fast food and sugary beverages are not healthy, and I want to remind you parents that, should these young ones get diagnosed with a non-communicable disease, it will follow them into adulthood and put more stress on your resources as well as the health system,” said Tufton.

The NCDA said the survey has shown that healthy eating, regular physical activities, and adequate sleep are essential for the well-being, learning, and long-term health of Jamaica’s children and adolescents.

It added that the lack of physical activity increases the risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID); and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: A different route for boys
World.content:
In this video grab Seargeant Kevin Wallace, dean of discipline and drill instructor at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Cadet Academy, inspects trainees during muster.Video: Jamaica Constabulary Force

As Jamaica continues to grapple with the persistent underperformance of boys in school, the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is offering an alternative path that combines academics, discipline, and mentorship to help young men find their footing.

The JCF Cadet Academy, established in September 2021, was born out of the police force’s experience working with young people through its Safe Schools Programme and other youth initiatives where cops observed particular challenges among boys, including truancy.

Speaking on the JCF’s Force4Good podcast, principal of the academy Deputy Superintendent of Police Tanecia Johnson said the force recognised the need for a setting where it could provide more focused support to young men.

“When those reports come in, it’s always about the boys outnumbering the girls in terms of truancy and so on, and so as a force… we decided that something must be done in terms of having a better structure to have these boys in an area where we can have that direct concentration,” she said.

The academy now combines traditional schooling with a highly structured boarding environment, with police, trained teachers, guidance counsellors, and other staff working closely with the students.

Johnson said the academy’s approach is based on more than discipline, with staff seeking to understand the circumstances affecting each student and build relationships that encourage them to open up.

“Oftentimes in the schools the students will tell us as the police, as their mentors, as their motivators, things that they will not tell a school principal, things that they will not tell their parents,” she revealed.

Those conversations, Johnson said, allow the academy to address issues such as anger, identity, purpose, attitude and a student’s plans for the future.

The approach is producing encouraging academic results.

This year’s Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) performance included a 100 per cent pass rate in information technology and physical education and sports, while human and social biology recorded 98 per cent, English A 92 per cent, and office administration 90 per cent. Mathematics recorded a 75 per cent pass rate.

At the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level, communication studies recorded an 88 per cent pass rate, information technology 93 per cent, law – unit one 84 per cent, and law – unit two 75 per cent. Johnson said the results represent the academy’s best academic performance since it was established.

For Johnson, however, the results are only part of what the academy is trying to achieve.

She recalled the experience of a 17-year-old student who arrived after struggling to gain CSEC passes. When staff spoke with him about his experience they discovered that his academic difficulties did not necessarily reflect his ability.

“Sometimes all it takes is a change of environment for these youngsters, and at the Cadet Academy we’re thriving because, first and foremost, we have educators, we have our teachers, but love is central to what we do,” she said.

Johnson said that philosophy extends to how students are treated when they make mistakes. Rather than focusing on punishment, staff speak of corrective measures and ensure students have immediate access to adults when problems arise.

According to Johnson, the academy normally takes about 80 students in an intake and has approximately 10 resident facilitators and 15 external teachers, in addition to administrators, guidance counsellors, and access to the JCF’s medical services. It currently offers seven CSEC and four CAPE subjects.

The academy also serves as a potential pathway into the JCF, although Johnson stressed that becoming a cop is not compulsory and admission to the academy does not guarantee recruitment.

Students who want to join the force must still meet the requirements, sit the JCF entrance examination, and undergo further background checks.

Of the 35 students who graduated on June 25 this year, 34 were awaiting the next intake to join the JCF, while one planned to attend university first.

Johnson said that, overall, 99.9 per cent of students who choose to pursue policing after completing the programme progress towards the JCF, with more than 175 former cadets now serving in the organisation.

But the academy’s purpose is not simply to produce police personnel.

Johnson said students are encouraged to pursue tertiary education or other careers if that is the path they choose, while the JCF hopes the education and personal development they receive will prepare them for life beyond the academy.

The academy’s model comes against a separate national conversation about the performance of boys in Jamaica’s education system, where they continue to face challenges in areas such as engagement, attendance, and academic achievement.

That wider concern provides an important backdrop to the academy’s results, but Johnson said the programme itself grew from the JCF’s direct experience with young people and its decision to create a more concentrated intervention.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid’s Rebel Music gets new life
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid .

Fifteen years can change a lot in music. Trends come and go, audiences shift, and artistes inevitably evolve. But for Kabaka Pyramid, the years since his breakthrough Rebel Music EP have not meant abandoning the foundation on which his career was built. Instead, the Grammy Award-winning reggae artiste is returning to it.

On August 28, Kabaka will release Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape, a 10-track project marking the 15th anniversary of the EP that helped introduce him to a wider audience and establish his reputation as one of Jamaica’s more lyrically conscious voices.

But the project is less about recreating 2011 and more about examining what has endured since then. Since his breakout year in music, he has moved from emerging artiste to international stages and even Grammy success with The Kalling.

Through it all, his ability to move between reggae, dancehall, and hip hop while maintaining an unmistakably Jamaican perspective has remained a defining feature of his music.

That musical identity is again at the centre of Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape. Three songs already released from the project — Rotation, From Weh Day and We Dem Wah — offer a glimpse into the different influences that have shaped the artiste.

“There is so much going on in the world, and I really believe if we played more reggae we would be better off,” Kabaka Pyramid said. “Reggae has a healing nature. The music has always been able to uplift people, bring people together and give us something positive to hold on to.”

With that said, he is encouraging DJs, selectors, and veteran artistes to invest in younger talent, a plight that makes the anniversary project about more than Kabaka’s own journey.

Fifteen years after Rebel Music helped him find his audience, he is using that milestone to question whether emerging reggae acts are being given similar opportunities to find theirs.

Across its 10 tracks, the project moves through cultural commentary, reflection, reggae consciousness, dancehall energy, and lyrical competition. In doing so it connects the artiste he was becoming 15 years ago with the one he is today.

For an artiste, longevity is not simply measured by how long one manages to remain visible. Sometimes it is also measured by whether the things that mattered at the beginning still matter after the success arrives. Fifteen years later, Kabaka Pyramid appears to be making his answer clear: The music may evolve, but the foundation remains.

Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape will be available on all major digital streaming platforms.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: HARD ROCK CLEARS CABINET HURDLE
World.content:
Hard Rock International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, but separate regulatory approval is required before casino gaming can begin..

HARD ROCK International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, clearing a key government hurdle for a planned hotel and casino within a wider three-phase development, with projected investment of US$756.9 million.

The approval was disclosed to the Jamaica Observer last Monday by a person familiar with the process who asked not to be identified because the decision had not yet been publicly announced.

Hard Rock subsequently confirmed the approval in written responses to Business Observer queries.

“Hard Rock International is pleased to confirm that we have been granted a provisional casino licence for an integrated resort in Montego Bay,” the company said on Friday.

“We are honoured by this opportunity and look forward to bringing our distinctive blend of world-class hospitality, entertainment, and exceptional guest experiences to Jamaica.”

Hard Rock did not identify the government authority that issued the approval, the legal entity that received it, or any conditions attached.

The approval moves the project forward but it does not by itself permit Hard Rock or an affiliated company to operate a casino in Jamaica.

Casino Gaming Commission Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen, responding to questions from the Business Observer, said Jamaica’s regulatory framework requires separate approvals for an integrated resort development and the operation of a casino.

At the first stage, a developer must secure approval from the minister responsible for finance through an Approved Integrated Resort Development (AIRD) Order under Section 9 of the Casino Gaming Act.

“The making of an AIRD Order does not, by itself, authorise casino gaming,” Allen said. “Rather, it establishes the developer’s eligibility to proceed to the second stage by applying to the Casino Gaming Commission for a casino gaming licence.”

Allen did not say whether an AIRD Order has been formally issued for the Hard Rock development or whether Hard Rock or an affiliated Jamaican company has applied to the commission for a casino gaming licence.

Jamaica allows casinos only as part of larger tourism developments offering hotel accommodation, entertainment, sporting facilities, and other visitor services.

Government filings place the proposed Hard Rock hotel and casino within a three-phase development on the same property in Montego Bay.

A table prepared by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), and included in the Government of Jamaica’s annual report for the 2025/26 financial year, identifies UNICO Resort as the first phase of the Hard Rock Hotel development.

The 451-room UNICO is under construction. Work began in October 2023 and completion is expected by the end of 2026, according to the report. Jampro placed the projected capital expenditure at US$250.2 million and estimated that the development would generate 1,000 temporary and 1,000 permanent jobs.

The second phase, identified as Hard Rock Hotel – Phase 2 – RCD Hotel Group, is projected to have 1,100 rooms and require US$373.3 million in capital expenditure.

Jampro said land clearing and preliminary groundwork had started on that phase, which will be built on the same Montego Bay property adjacent to UNICO. It projected 1,300 temporary jobs during development and 1,200 permanent positions.

DOMA Residences, the third phase, is planned as a 250-room development valued at US$133.4 million. The government report said construction was estimated to begin in 2026 on the same property, beside UNICO and the Hard Rock hotel.

Together, the three phases account for a projected 1,801 rooms, US$756.9 million in capital expenditure, 3,300 temporary jobs and 3,200 permanent positions, based on the figures supplied to Jampro.

The government filing does not specify whether Cabinet’s integrated resort approval covers all three phases or only the proposed hotel and casino component.

Hard Rock International is owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, which acquired the brand in 2007. The company says its network comprises more than 300 hotels, casinos, cafes, entertainment venues and retail locations across more than 80 countries.

The process followed by Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover, illustrates the distinction between approval of an integrated resort and the licensing of its casino.

Allen said an AIRD Order for the Princess Integrated Resort Development was issued in August 2023. The resort opened in December 2024, and an application for a casino gaming licence was submitted in August 2025.

The commission approved the application in July 2026 after completing its assessment and due diligence. It was the first casino operator’s licence granted under Jamaica’s regulatory framework.

The licence was issued to Adamas Grand Casino Limited, which will operate the proposed casino at Princess Grand under a management agreement with Grupo Orenes, a Spanish gaming and hospitality company.

The licence does not allow the casino to open immediately. Adamas must first meet the commission’s pre-operational requirements and receive clearance to begin operating.

World.title: ‘RAIN DELAY’ FOR JCA AGM
World.content:
A view of Sabina Park, headquarters of the Jamaica Cricket Association, during a rain delay in a West Indies versus Sri Lanka One-Day International game in June.garfield Robinson

JAMAICA Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the voting annual general meeting (AGM) is likely to be held in October, after it was previously postponed.

The JCA annual meeting and election were to have been held in May but were pushed back pending ratification of proposed governance changes to its constitution.

Bennett told the Jamaica Observer that the board will get the opportunity to ratify the changes in just over two weeks.

“We will have a special meeting in September to deal with matters that we have had hanging around for years. Immediately after that September 10 meeting we will set a date for the AGM. I imagine that we will have the voting AGM in October,” he said.

Bennett, who had previously served as JCA vice-president, swept to power in April 2024 when he defeated the incumbent President Wilford “Billy” Heaven.

He admitted that, ideally, he had wanted the elections to be held months ago, but those plans had to be put aside.

“I would have preferred to have had the AGM exactly after two years — which would have been about March/April — but it didn’t happen.

“The AGM is not constitutionally due until December but… we don’t want to take it down to the last,” he said.

Though choosing to not outline granular details, Bennett insisted the constitutional changes are important for the greater good of cricket in Jamaica.

“It’s a matter of our constitution and [about] what we have and what we need to have,” he said, noting there are current glaring governance loopholes in how the JCA can regulate clubs and parish associations.

The JCA president said he is eager to be given a fresh mandate in his bid to improve the struggling sport in the country, and by extension the region.

“I get the impression there are some positive movements in the game, so I’m just hoping we can accelerate that process because we really want to get back to the top as soon as possible. It’s very important for West Indies cricket that Jamaica does well. Jamaica has the largest economy and the largest population so it stands to reason that if Jamaica does well then West indies cricket will do well,” he argued.

While Bennett is likely to return to the top post unopposed, there is intrigue surrounding the first vice-president job. Both the incumbent Fritz Harris, the Clarendon Cricket Association president, and Nehemiah Perry, former West Indies off spinner and current head of Kingston Cricket Club, were previously nominated.

However, Bennett confirmed that the nomination process will be redone ahead of the rescheduled elections.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: Atlantic Hardware turns to e-commerce as profit triples
World.content:
For both its three-month an half-year results, Atlantic posted record revenues and profits.

ATLANTIC Hardware & Plumbing Company Limited is preparing to introduce e-commerce and expand its product portfolio after revenue jumped 69 per cent and profit more than tripled during the first half of 2026.

Managing Director Deanall Barnes told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that the hardware distributor had begun discussions on establishing an e-commerce platform as part of a wider effort to strengthen its digital footprint and use technology to improve its operations.

“On the technology front, we have commenced discussions on introducing an e-commerce platform, alongside broader consideration of how technology can be used to enhance the business — from inventory management to customer service — ultimately with a view of continuing to improve our bottom line,” he said to the Business Observer.

The digital push follows a sharp increase in sales at the company, which listed on the Junior Market of the Jamaica Stock Exchange in April 2025.

For the three months ended June 30, Atlantic reported record revenue of $776.4 million, up 92 per cent from $404.8 million in the corresponding quarter last year. Net profit rose 140 per cent to $42 million from $17.5 million.

Revenue for the six-month period increased 69 per cent year-on-year to $1.46 billion, while net profit more than tripled to $116.3 million from $33.9 million.

The company’s balance sheet also strengthened, as shareholders’ equity rose to $596.3 million and cash and cash equivalents more than doubled year-on-year to $255 million. Total assets on the other hand stood at $1.6 billion at the end of June.

Atlantic, which has operated since 1994 and distributes more than 2,400 hardware and building products from leading global brands, including Stanley, DeWalt, Black & Decker, Bosch and WD-40.

For its 2025 financial year, the company recorded revenue of $1.8 billion and net profit of $68.9 million.

Barnes said Atlantic’s new agricultural distribution division had become a significant contributor to revenue and was expected to support further growth as the company added products.

Launched earlier this year, the division has distribution rights for brands, including Bonanza seeds, Nutramix feed, and Bellota machetes. It generated approximately $300 million in revenue during the first half of 2026.

“We continue to expand within that category and will shortly be introducing a wider variety of seeds and pesticides — these products have already been tested by our suppliers, orders have been placed, and we anticipate arrival by mid-third quarter,” Barnes said.

He said Atlantic also sees opportunities to expand the division into fertilisers, veterinary products, and home and garden lines while assessing other categories that complement its existing distribution infrastructure and broad customer base.

As the company adjusts its procurement strategy in response to disruptions to global shipping, Barnes said it continues to deepen relationships with local and regional suppliers to reduce the risk of stock-outs as it manages its expanded portfolio.

The strategy has become increasingly important as Atlantic continues to widen its product offerings while seeking to maintain reliable supplies for customers.

Despite potentially subdued macroeconomic conditions, Barnes said management remains cautiously optimistic about the company’s prospects for the remainder of the financial year.

As the company plans to continue growing market share by widening its range of traditional hardware and building products alongside increasing its participation in government projects, the managing director said it will also tighten partnerships with suppliers to target major hotel developments.

“Disciplined capital allocation and continued balance sheet strength remain central to funding this growth,” Barnes said.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”

World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) conducted January to March 2026 — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while it noticed an emergence in the use of ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: Merz unites EU budget-cutters as Costa gropes for deal
World.content:
With the bloc racing to strike a deal on its budget before elections next year in France, Spain and Italy that risk turning the chance of agreement from difficult to nye-on impossible, the next four months are critical for the EU’s stability, Costa’s legacy and whether leaders like Merz and Stocker can prove to their voters that Brussels isn’t wasting their money.



The leaders meeting in Berlin don’t just want the size of the budget to shrink by hundreds of billions of euros, they also want shift the way it is spent away from areas such as agriculture toward defense and security. And they want to impose conditions to stop governments getting cash if they breach democratic standards.

The discussion is unlikely to result in the publication of any precise numbers but instead produce a united front for the negotiations to come, three people familiar with the preparations said. Ireland, which is shepherding the budget process as part of its role at the helm of the six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, is to put forward fresh compromise numbers in October ahead of a summit of EU leaders later in the month.

“The general priorities of the [budget] proposal are worthy of support and in line with Finland’s objectives,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement. “However, the overall level of the proposed framework is too high.”

Some countries, such as Spain, believe the Commission shouldn’t reduce the size of the proposed budget and are resisting moves to direct expenditure away from agriculture.

Getting closer?

Costa, who has already visited Bratislava, Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius, believes governments aren’t as far apart as their public statements suggest, according to a senior EU official familiar with the negotiations, who like others mentioned in this article were granted anonymity because the talks are at such a sensitive stage.

While leaders are defending domestic red lines they do all seem to be committed to reaching a deal by the end of the year, the official said.

World.title: Andy Burnham to host Emmanuel Macron in London as part of diplomatic push
World.content:
A U.K. government official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record, said Burnham is looking forward to welcoming Macron to Downing Street.

The Elysée declined to confirm the trip.

It follows Burnham’s recent trip to Kyiv to mark Ukraine’s independence day, which saw him meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and pledge closer support to equip Ukraine with blueprints for Storm Shadow long-range missiles, allowing Ukraine to manufacture components for the weapon domestically.

Britain’s new prime minister has focused heavily on domestic issues such as the cost of living and a shortage of prison spaces in the weeks since he took office, but his recent diplomatic blitz shows he is determined to signal continued solidarity with the U.K.’s key allies.

In one of his first calls to international counterparts, Burnham told Macron he was “looking forward to building” on “the strong U.K.-France relationship to deliver for people on both sides of the Channel.”

Continuing work on the “reset” of relations between London and Brussels begun under Keir Starmer is likely to be high on their agenda, together with tackling illegal migration.

World.title: France is not ready to face cheap drones yet, warns top general
World.content:
The French defense industry is not producing low-cost weapons at scale yet, said Gen. Fabien Mandon.

PARIS — France is not yet ready to face cheap, mass-produced threats like drones, the country's chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, warned Wednesday.

Defending in a financially sustainable manner against low-cost weapons manufactured in bulk, including Iranian-made Shahed drones, has been one of the main challenges for Western armed forces since the war in Ukraine started.

"We have enemies who have developed a large number of low-cost solutions that will wear down our models," Mandon said at an event organized by France's main business lobby Medef. "We’re not there yet. It’s nothing catastrophic, we’re still at peace. But we need to make this move."
