World.title: Romania’s First Lady, UNICEF reaffirm commitment to children's rights and participation
World.content:
The First Lady of Romania, Mirabela Grădinaru, met on Tuesday, August 25, with a UNICEF delegation led by Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, to discuss promoting children's rights and strengthening the participation of children and young people in decisions that affect their lives.

The discussions highlighted the progress made by Romania in promoting the views of children and young people in the public decision-making process, including through legislation adopted in 2024, which strengthens children's opportunities to contribute to the development of policies and legislation that concern them.

“I know how important it is for every child to have access to care, protection, education and opportunities to develop. We must never forget that they are our number one priority. The way we care for children today will shape tomorrow's society. I welcome the continuation of cooperation between Romania and UNICEF to support children and families, to ensure that the voices of young people are heard and to make sure that every child can reach their full potential, regardless of where they live or the circumstances in which they were born,” said Mirabela Grădinaru.

In turn, Edouard Beigbeder said that Romania has taken important steps to strengthen children's participation and integrate it into the decision-making process, and its experience can offer valuable lessons both to countries in Europe and to those outside the region.

The meeting addressed Romania's experience in implementing the integrated community services model, as well as the implementation of the European Child Guarantee. Opportunities to promote internationally the lessons learned and good practices developed in Romania were also discussed.

The discussions also focused on continuing cooperation in areas such as children's participation, education, combating climate change, online safety and preventing violence against children.

Earlier this summer, Romania’s First Lady presented the "Romania in Light" project during a panel within the NATO Summit in Ankara. The project focuses on protecting children in the context of technological development and educating them in an environment where the virtual world supports learning and development.

World.title: Social Monitor: Romania exceeds EU average for household internet access but ranks last in digital skills
World.content:
Romania has moved above the European Union average for household internet connectivity, with 95.47% of homes having access in 2025. However, the country ranks last in the EU for the share of people with at least basic digital skills, according to Eurostat data analyzed by the Social Monitor, a Friedrich Ebert Foundation project.

The share of Romanian households with internet access increased by almost 10 percentage points from 86.24% in 2020. Romania now ranks 12th among the EU’s 27 member states and exceeds the bloc’s average of 94.76%.

The Netherlands recorded the highest household connectivity rate at 99.28%, followed by Luxembourg at 99%, and Malta at 97.77%. Croatia ranked last with 87.91%, behind Greece at 88.73%, and Lithuania at 89.35%.

Internet use among Romania’s general population also rose significantly, reaching 93.15% in 2025 compared with 78.46% in 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ireland had the EU’s highest internet usage rate at 99.78%, followed by Denmark and the Netherlands, both at 99.71%. The lowest rates were recorded in Croatia at 85.9%, Bulgaria at 86.85%, and Greece at 89.15%.

“The data also show that the share of Romanians who have never used the internet fell sharply to just 4.91%, compared with 14.05% in 2020. However, Romania continues to perform below the EU average on this indicator,” reads the Social Monitor report.

The highest proportions of people who had never gone online were recorded in Croatia at 10.33%, Portugal at 9.56%, and Greece at 9.14%, while Ireland, the Netherlands, and Sweden had the lowest rates.

According to the same source, despite the improvement in access and usage, only 31.84% of Romania’s population has basic or above-basic digital skills, placing the country last in the EU and well below the bloc’s average of 60.4%.

Bulgaria followed with 38.26%, while Slovenia and Latvia recorded 46.5% and 48.43%, respectively. The Netherlands led the ranking at 83.61%, followed by Ireland at 82.82%, and Denmark at 81.45%.

Digital skills are assessed based on activities performed online or with software by people aged 16 to 74. The evaluation covers information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem-solving.

World.title: L’Étape Romania by Tour de France brings traffic restrictions to Bucharest this weekend
World.content:
The fifth edition of L’Étape Romania by Tour de France will take place in Bucharest on Sunday, August 30, with almost 2,000 cyclists expected to participate. As such, traffic will be restricted on several major streets and boulevards in the city between 7 a.m. and 2 p.m.

The restrictions will affect Unirii Boulevard, Mircea Vodă Boulevard, Splaiul Unirii in the direction of Bucharest, Decebal Boulevard, Basarabia Boulevard, Calea Victoriei, Regina Elisabeta Boulevard, Schitu Măgureanu Boulevard, Știrbei Vodă and Ion Câmpineanu streets, Kiseleff Road, Buzești, Berzei, Vasile Pârvan and Bogdan Petriceicu Hașdeu streets, and Libertății Boulevard.

The organizers said they were working with the Traffic Police to establish alternative routes.

Constituției Square will serve as the starting and finishing point for all three races.

The 14 km City Adventure route, open to participants aged 7 and over, will begin at 7:30 a.m. The 42 km Ride will start at 8:30 a.m. and is open to cyclists aged at least 15, while the 85 km Race will begin at 10 a.m. and has the same minimum age requirement.

The race routes are scheduled to close fully at 1 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony at 1:30 p.m.

Almost 2,000 cyclists from 17 countries and more than 170 cities and towns have registered. International participants include cyclists from Bulgaria, Greece, the United Kingdom, Serbia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany, Cyprus, France, Belgium, and Austria.

The 42 km route is expected to attract the largest field, with approximately 1,200 cyclists at the start. More than 250 children and teenagers under the age of 18 have also registered.

“To make sure race day is exactly what every participant has been looking forward to, my advice is simple: have your bike checked - brakes, tires and gears - and don’t leave this until the last minute. Also, avoid overtraining during this final week: your fitness has already been built, and now it’s all about rest, hydration and sleep. Don’t try anything new on race day, whether it’s equipment or nutrition, and come to the Race Village on Saturday to collect your race kit, so you can enjoy every kilometer on Sunday morning without a worry,” said Răzvan Jugănaru, MTB Academy, event organizer.

Registration is open until the end of August 26 or until all available places are filled. Participants must collect their race kits on August 29, between 10 a.m. and 7 p.m., from the Race Village in Constituției Square.

World.title: Drone fragment discovered on beach in Romanian seaside resort Olimp
World.content:
Video

A drone fragment was found on Wednesday, August 26, on a beach in the Romanian Black Sea resort of Olimp. The fragment was brought onto the beach by waves and was noticed by several people who notified the authorities.

Authorities restricted access to the area, and specialists went to the scene to analyze the object. Around 10:30 AM, they decided to detonate a part of the fragments that contained explosives. A separate drone fragment is still on the beach and does not contain explosives, according to Digi24.

Another drone fragment was discovered on Tuesday, August 24, near the Casino in Constanţa. The object was noticed near the seafront by people walking in the area. They notified the authorities, who recovered the object, which most likely did not have an explosive payload.

Drones on the Black Sea coast

The discoveries in Olimp and Constanța are part of a series of similar incidents reported in recent weeks on the Romanian coast. Fragments or devices that authorities determined came from drones have been found in several coastal areas, including Costinești and Saturn.

Earlier this month, the Romanian Army also recovered drone fragments from other Black Sea resort towns like Port Tomis, Eforie Sud, Eforie Nord, Costinești, and Năvodari. Around the same time, other drone parts were spotted near a Constanţa beach. In all cases, specialized crews intervened to remove the fragments.

According to the Ministry of Defense, Romania has seen 59 attacks near its borders with Ukraine since the start of the year, and 25 unauthorized entrys in its airspace. Four drones were also brought down by Romanian or allied fighter jets after infringing the national airspace.

Increased defense measures

Romania's Senate Defense Committee met yesterday to discuss an incident from the beginning of June, in the Port of Constanţa, when a Ukrainian drone self-detonated after it was lost from control. General Dragoş Iacob, deputy chief of the Defense Staff, said that following the incident, the security of maritime ports had been strengthened, and the warning system was working better than three months ago. Representatives of the Naval Forces, as well as of the Ministry of Defense, SRI and STS, were present at the meeting.

“There are several questions that institutions need to answer in the chain of response. Who detects the drone, who identifies what type it is, who coordinates, who tracks, and who destroys the drone,” said liberal Nicoleta Pauliuc, chairwoman of the Senate Defense Committee, cited by Radio Romania Actualitati.

World.title: Romania Passes Controversial Law on Officials’ Integrity to Access EU Funds
World.content:
A plenary session of the parliament in Bucharest, Romania, 05 May 2026. Photo: EPA/Robert Ghement.

Romania’s parliament on Wednesday overwhelmingly approved a new integrity law intended to strengthen sanctions for abuses by public officials, in order to allow the country access to a 770-million-euro EU-funded National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The legislation was also supported by the centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL), which is part of the interim government led by Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, alongside two smaller centrist parties.

“Although we initially opposed the law in its current form, we decided to vote in favour because the country’s interest in meeting the PNRR milestones takes precedence over any other debate,” Bolojan said. He added that the PNL would seek to amend the law in the near future.

The law revises Romania’s rules on public officials’ asset and interest declarations, and strengthens the penalties if discrepancies or conflict of interest are determined. It also replaces detailed public wealth declarations with financial-interest forms that disclose less information about officials’ assets and holdings.

But it has sparked controversy after the Social Democratic Party (PSD), with support from the far-right Alliance for Unity of Romanians (AUR), introduced a provision stipulating that officials who have been found responsible in conflict-of-interest cases and whose three-year sanction period barring them from public office temporarily has not yet expired, would have their mandates terminated within 30 days of the law entering into force.

The amendment has been criticised as being specifically aimed at Dominic Fritz, the mayor of the western city of Timisoara and president of the centrist Save Romania Union (USR), part of the interim government.

Fritz, a German national who was first elected mayor in 2020, was found to have been involved in an administrative conflict of interest related to an urban planning document he approved that year.

Critics, including USR and PNL members as well as civil society representatives, have argued that the amendment could violate the principle of non-retroactivity and amount to the use of the law against political opponents.

The criticism has also been echoed at European level. The centre-right European People’s Party and liberal Renew Europe in the European Parliament groups on Monday asked European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to withhold the 770 million euros from Romania, citing concerns over the rule of law.

The integrity law is part of a broader package of reforms Romania has committed to adopt by the end of August in order to unlock further EU funding under PNRR. European funds are vital to Romania’s strained budget, supporting healthcare, education and infrastructure projects. EU funding is equivalent to around a third of the country’s GDP.

The present political crisis stems from Romania’s prolonged political instability. Last June, a coalition comprising the PSD, PNL and two smaller centre-right parties took office, with a primary mandate to stabilise the economy.

However, a series of unpopular austerity measures introduced by Ilie Bolojan to curb the deficit placed increasing strain on the coalition. Tensions came to a head in May , when the PSD withdrew its support, deepening the political turmoil.

The PSD subsequently allied with the far-right AUR to oust the government. Since then, Bolojan has been in a caretaker position, after two nominations for premier made by President Nicusor Dan were rejected by the main political parties.

World.title: Kosovo’s Ruling Party Optimistic About Resolving Deadlock Over New President
World.content:
Photos of Kosovo’s presidents to date on the wall at the presidency office. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja.

Vetevendosje deputy leader Glauk Konjufca expressed optimism on Wednesday that an agreement can be reached with the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, to give the country a new president when the leaders of two parties, Albin Kurti and Lumir Abdixhiku respectively, hold their next talks on the troubled issue.

Kurti and Abdixhiku are expected to meet this week to discuss concrete names following two previous meetings in recent weeks in which they both said they have been focused more on “principles” of a deal which would avoid new potential snap elections, the fourth within less than two years

“I consider that there is a great probability of having a [new] president, an agreement on a president,” Konjufca said.

“Vetevendosje is ready, Prime Minister [Albin] Kurti is ready. We have [proposals for] names but, I am sorry, I will not share them with you because then the negotiation process would lose its meaning,” he added.

Konjufca’s comments came amid political deadlock, with the parliament derived from the June 7 polls yet to be inaugurated.

MPs have failed for three weeks to elect a new parliament leadership, creating a fresh institutional logjam as the provisional parliament speaker, Avni Dehari from Vetevendosje, refuses to resume the inaugural session which started on August 6. Vetevendosje is refusing to submit a name for the speaker, as it first demands an agreement with other parties on the election of a new president.

Parliament’s rules require him to invite the MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker.

But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was on August 8, and that session lasted only a few minutes after Vetevendosje leader and incumbent Prime Minister Kurti asked for “more time” for negotiations with other parties about a new president.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting them well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats and has insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti is likely to obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved. The parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new assembly, otherwise a new election will be triggered.

With two other opposition parties, Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and the Alliance, AAK, snubbing Kurti’s calls for further meetings while holding daily makeshift sessions in the parliamentary chamber, the LDK is the only party who could strike a deal over the presidency.

“As far as I am aware of, there is still no exact date for the new meeting [between Kurti and Abdixhiku],” Konjufca said. But he added: “They will meet to propose concrete names and I believe that new President of Kosovo will derive from those names.”

World.title: North Macedonia Sees Drop in New School Pupils amid Demographic Woes
World.content:
A child near North Macedonia’s capital, Skopje, going to school. Photo: Robert Atanasovski.

In the latest indication of the country’s demographic problems, Education Minister Vesna Janevska said on Tuesday that enrolment for the 2026-27 school year, while still not final, is already sharply below last year’s 17,921 first-graders.

“We expect this trend to continue next year, which is disappointing,” Janevska told media.

The decline is even more striking over a longer period. In the 2016-17 school year, 23,266 children entered first grade (f, data from the State Statistical Office shows. The number fell to 21,656 the following year and, despite occasional slight increases, continued a broadly downward trend.

By 2025-26, it had dropped to 17,921. The current preliminary figure of 14,500 means the country has lost about 8,800 first-graders, or nearly 38 per cent, in just a decade.

The shrinking cohorts are already forcing changes to the school network. Janevska said that around 200 fewer classes will operate in primary education this year, while secondary education will have around 100 fewer classes.

The government also expects 26 rural schools to close during the school year because they have either too few or no newly-enrolled first-graders.

Some have only five to eight pupils in total, Janevska explained, arguing that keeping very small schools open can leave children in combined classes with pupils from several grades, limiting both the quality of teaching and opportunities for socialisation.

She said that pupils would generally be transferred to larger schools, but that combined classes in smaller schools would still remain where necessary, particularly where they are at a significant distance from more populated areas.

Demographer Donco Gerasimovski, a former director of the State Statistical Office, told Meta.mk news website that low birth rates and the emigration of young families are driving the decline.

Gerasimovski noted that many children also disappear from school rolls during a school year as families leave the country.

“According to my calculations, we ‘lose’ between 1,500 and 2,000 pupils in just one school year because of emigration,” he told Meta.mk.

The shrinking number of first-graders is only the clearest visible signs of a demographic decline that has been building for years.

Over the past three-and-a-half decades, the small landlocked country has failed to produce tangible economic and democratic uptick that could have kept people from leaving, or join the EU, in large part due to the former Greek blockade over its name and the current Bulgarian impasse that centres around contested identity issues.

The results of the last national headcount carried out in 2021, showed the country’s population has shrunk by 9.2 per cent over two decades since the previous census, from roughly 2.1 million to just over 1.8 million.

World.title: Plea Deals Reveal Logistics of Smuggling Macedonian Marijuana into Serbia
World.content:
Shortly after midnight on January 15 this year, a truck crossed from North Macedonia into Serbia. Several hours later, having crossed the length of the country, it caught fire near Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad.

According to paperwork, the truck was carrying textiles for export to Britain. In reality, it was stuffed with tonnes of marijuana; the smugglers set it on fire to cover their tracks.

Two weeks later, police seized five tonnes of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, near the central Serbian town of Krusevac.

According to plea bargains reached last week between prosecutors in North Macedonia and two of the smugglers, the January shipment was just one of five carried out between mid-2025 and early 2026.

More people are under investigation. Sources close to the probe say prosecutors in North Macedonia are also looking into the finances of three companies tied to Skopje-based Alfapharm Group, which allegedly served as a front for the drugs production.

The case is the latest to raise questions about North Macedonia’s legal medicinal marijuana industry, legalised in 2016, and whether it is fuelling the smuggling. In recent years, 14 firms have lost their permits to grow medicinal marijuana for failing to comply with the law, the Health Ministry said.

World.title: Riots, Teargas and ‘Gruesome Photos’ Behind Serbian Photographer’s Success
World.content:
An Orthodox priest talks to a young man during street protests in Belgrade. A police cordon faces the crowd in Serbia’s capital, holding plastic shields. A wounded demonstrator lies prone as riot police run past him.

These images date back to March 2011, when protesters packed the streets after the arrest of Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic. They were the first photos that Andrej Cukic sent to EPA Images (European Pressphoto Agency). Now he is set to lead the organization, as editor-in-chief.

“I was in the right place at the right time,” he tells BIRN. “I had some gruesome photos. Somebody thought that they were very good, and they ran them, and the photos were kind of published everywhere.”

The photos led to Cukic gaining regular work from Belgrade for EPA Images, an international news photo agency based in Frankfurt. BIRN has a contract with EPA and regularly uses its images.

World.title: Greek Neo-Nazi Casts Himself as Political Martyr Ahead of Prison Release
World.content:
On the Greek capital’s bustling Omonia Square, a group of young men held Greek flags and chanted: “Ilias, stay strong on the road to freedom” and “Remember Ilias, we are with you”.

It was July 20 and Ilias Kasidiaris - on day release from prison - was inaugurating the offices of a new party he had announced the previous month.

Convicted in 2020 of directing a criminal organisation, Kasidiaris has no legal grounds to lead a political party, but media reports this month suggest a relative of his has submitted a request to do so before the Supreme Court.

Addressing his supporters, Kasidiaris called on them to gather outside Domokos prison come mid-September, when he is due to be released.

Together, he said, they would “send a message of resistance to all those who are selling out Greece”, and vowed to run in the next parliamentary election, expected in the spring of next year.

World.title: Bulgaria Violated Rights of Roma Families by Demolishing Settlement, Court Rules
World.content:
Bulgaria breached the human rights of dozens of Roma families in Sofia by demolishing their homes without giving them a chance to contest the decision, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday.

The government must pay 10,000 euro in damages to each party to the case and reform its demolition procedures.

The demolition took place in Sofia’s Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in August 2023, despite residents insisting that the authorities had not consulted them over the plans. Some of the families said they had lived in their homes since the 1950s.

The authorities insisted that they had carried out a formal process for issuing demolition orders. This was denied by the residents, who said the authorities deliberately concealed their intentions, gave evasive answers to repeated requests for information and refused to engage directly with the community.

The court ruled that Bulgaria had violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects family life and homes. It found that residents had no effective procedure to challenge the plans for demolition based on their personal circumstances, including length of residence, vulnerability and the availability of alternative housing.

The court also ruled, however, that the residents held no property rights in the demolished houses that would be recognized under Bulgarian law.

The ruling is not yet final and Bulgaria has three months to request that the case be referred for further review. The residents may make a similar application.

The flattening of Roma settlements in Bulgaria has become a repeated problem and a source of tension between the ethnic minority and local authorities. Demolitions also took place in the Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in 2017.

The ECHR has now heard four cases involving Roma settlement demolitions since 2012. In 2025, BIRN covered two similar cases: in April 2025, despite an ECHR ruling warning the municipality not to “proceed with the demolition of the homes of the applicants until further notice”, authorities still flattened houses in the enclave which had been there for decades.

A similar operation followed in the town of Stara Zagora in August the same year.

World.title: Serbia Again Requests “Humanitarian” Release of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic has once again called for the release of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic. On Tuesday, he asked the UN war crimes court in The Hague to consider a new request by the family of the former Bosnian Serb military leader.

Vujic made the plea in a letter to Graciela Gatti Santana, the president of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, IRMCT. It follows last week’s decision by the IRMCT to reject a request by Mladic’s defence for conditional early release and transfer to Serbia on health grounds.

Vujic noted a report by the medical officer at the detention unit in The Hague stating that Mladic had entered the final phase of his life, after a rapid decline in his health. The minister argued that, under these circumstances, Mladic should be allowed to spend his final days in Serbia. The government has offered to transfer him to Belgrade’s Military Medical Academy and accept restrictions and monitoring imposed by the court.

In last week’s decision rejecting an early release, the IRMCT ruled that Mladic was receiving comprehensive medical care and assistance, as well as an exceptional visitation regime allowing meaningful contact with his family. It said that his condition alone did not justify humanitarian early release, given the gravity of his genocide conviction and life sentence. The court stressed that it would continue to protect Mladic’s fundamental rights and dignity.

This is not the first time that Mladic’s defence has sought his release on humanitarian grounds. During his time in custody in the Netherlands, Mladic has had several serious medical problems and has suffered two strokes and a heart attack.

In June 2025, Mladic’s lawyers made an urgent request to the IRMCT for his release after he was transferred to palliative care, saying he had only has months to live. His defence again sought his immediate release in May this year after a serious medical episode, arguing that he was approaching the end of his life.

Mladic has been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011. He is serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The court confirmed his conviction and sentence after an appeal in 2021.

World.title: Billionaires Gather on 200 Million Euro Yacht Near Mljet
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Multiple billionaires have come together on a 200 million euro yacht near the southern Croatian island of Mljet. Jeff Bezos, and Jan Koum are among them.

Poslovni reports that this impressive vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros. Mljet is set to be hosting a meeting of two of the world’s biggest technology billionaires, Jan Koum and Jeff Bezos, over the next few days. They met on Koum’s yacht worth nearly 200 million dollars.

Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp whose wealth is estimated at 17 billion dollars, anchored his superyacht Moonrise near Mljet, and the same day Jeff Bezos, owner of Amazon, arrived in the company of American media mogul Barry Diller. Koum arrived on the Moonrise by helicopter on Monday, and Bezos visited him in the late afternoon hours. The three billionaires, Koum, Bezos and Diller, thus found themselves on the same vessel in the middle of the Adriatic Sea.

Koum is no stranger to the Croatian coast; he has holidayed in our beautiful country before. His superyacht Moonrise was photographed between the islands of Lopud and Šipan back in 2021 and 2024, and it was recorded that on one occasion he arrived for a summer holiday in Croatia with as many as three vessels: in addition to Moonrise he was accompanied by the 74-metre yacht Mogambo and the 55-metre Power Play, which served him as a helipad. The Amazon owner regularly summers on the Mediterranean on his superyacht Koru, where he cruised the Adriatic in the summers of 2023 and 2025, with recorded stays on Hvar, Mljet, Korčula, and a visit to the Šibenik archipelago.

The yacht Moonrise isn’t just an ordinary vessel. It’s a 100-metre superyacht from the Dutch shipyard Feadship, built in 2020. The sophisticated exterior design is by De Voogt, while the interior is the work of French designer Rémi Tessier. The vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros.

World.title: Pula Receives 12 Electric Buses Worth 6.8 Million Euros
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Pula has received 12 electric buses worth a total of 6.8 million euros with an aim of increasing passenger comfort and being more environmentally friendly.

Pulapromet has put another six new electric buses into service, thereby completing the project of acquiring a total of 12 electric vehicles for Pula’s public transport. Index reports that the project was fully financed with funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, and the total value of the purchased buses amounts to 6,763,900 euros. For the project, Pulapromet had been allocated 6,994,998 euros, but after the public procurement procedure the total value was somewhat lower.

Specifically speaking, Pulapromet acquired six MAN and six Iveco electric buses. Director Tomislav Josipović said that this is an important step in modernising the vehicle fleet and raising the quality of public transport.

“By putting these new six electric buses into service today, we are completing the project through which Pulapromet has received a total of 12 new electric vehicles,” said Josipović, adding that almost 6.8 million euros of investment has been directed into the development of public transport without any financial burden on Pulapromet. The new buses should reduce emissions of harmful gases and noise while increasing energy efficiency and passenger comfort.

an increase in public transport use in pula

Pula Mayor Peđa Grbin said that the project does not stop at the acquisition of buses. He announced the installation of solar panels on the canopy at the depot (Remiza), for which the City is waiting for the opening of appropriate co-financing tenders. “The goal is for these electric buses to run on electricity that will be produced here, in Pula, from the most ecological possible source, which is solar energy,” said Grbin. He added that since the beginning of the year the use of public city transport has increased by almost 10 percent. According to him, this has also been contributed to by the City of Pula’s decisions on free transport for pupils, students and pensioners.

Istria County Prefect Boris Miletić thanked the City of Pula, Pulapromet, the surrounding municipalities and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure for implementing the project. He emphasised that electric buses, especially if powered by energy from solar sources, can contribute to reducing the impact of traffic on the environment. Miletić also said that Pulapromet first secured the infrastructure and charging stations, and then acquired the vehicles. He assessed that higher-quality public transport could further increase the number of passengers.

World.title: Istria Showcased in Front of Millions of German Viewers
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Gorgeous Istria has been showcased in front of millions of German viewers, shining the spotlight on Croatia’s largest peninsula.

Morski reports that one of the most successful German travel programmes, “Wunderschön”, devoted a full 90 minutes of airtime to Istria, presenting the diversity of the peninsula to a million-strong audience in the German-speaking world – from Kamenjak, Pula and the Brijuni Islands, via Učka, Buzet and Pazin, to Poreč and Rovinj.

The project was realised in cooperation between the Tourist Board of Istria County and its long-standing PR partner ART Redaktionsteam from Salzburg. Viewers are guided through Istria by well-known German television presenter Stephanie Müller-Spirra, under the direction of award-winning journalist and author Stephan Heise. Alongside numerous local protagonists, the programme also features Marko Purišić – Baby Lasagna, Rade Šerbedžija and extreme alpinist Ines Papert. Istria is presented to the audience through a blend of natural and cultural attractions, active holidays, local stories and top-class food and local wine.

The first broadcast of the report reaches around two million viewers, while through further screenings in Germany, Austria and Switzerland the total viewership is expected to exceed five million, making the project one of the most significant television promotions of Istria on its most important outbound market.

World.title: Belišće – The Croatian Town Around Which an Industrial Empire Grew
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Belišće isn’t a name you’ll likely have ever heard if you’re not from Croatia, but this Croatian town had an industrial empire grow out of it.

It’s also unusual because of the fact that it is one of the few Croatian towns whose beginning can be fixed almost like a date of birth. Putni kofer turns the hands of the clock back to the year 1884, and we find ourselves in a place with a pasture-and-arable clearing called Belistje. It sits just beside the banks of the Drava, and the reason a large sawmill that the Gutmann family builds there. Soon after, a railway, workers’ houses, a school, a post office, an electricity network and a water supply all arrive. In just a few decades, the industrial plant thus created an entire settlement around itself, and from it grew today’s town.

the family company that built an entire town

In 1884, two companies belonging to the Gutmann family from Velika Kanjiža bought from the Valpovo landowner the right to a ten-year use of a huge expanse of oak forests. They erected the sawmill on the Belistje clearing, after which the settlement later took its name. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon notes that the Gutmanns further expanded their business by purchasing forests from the Prandau family of Valpovo and that at the beginning of the 20th century they controlled massive swathes of of forest and land. From the very start Belišće was therefore tied to one of the most valuable resources of the area, Slavonian oak.

the biggest and most modern sawmill in europe

According to data from Belišće, the sawmill was one of the most modern of its time and probably the largest in Europe for cutting oak timber. Large-scale production also needed a good transport link, so already in 1884 the first kilometres of the forest-industrial railway were laid. Over time the network grew to 335 kilometres and developed into the Slavonia-Podravina Railway with public transport, a station, a locomotive shed and a workshop in Belišće. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon emphasises that this railway also carried passengers and thus compensated for the lack of state railways in this part of Slavonia.

Alongside the sawmill and the railway an industrial colony grew. Official sources state that the first residential houses were soon built and a fire brigade founded; in 1886 a school classroom and a post office were opened, and in 1890 a primary school was constructed. By 1892 the place already had an electricity network and a water supply with sewerage, which was still rare in the surrounding villages at that time. Development was also visible in the architecture. Next to the workers’ houses arose a house for the owners and offices, the officials’ social centre Casino, and in 1905 the Gutmann Palace, known in Belišće as Palej. Up to the First World War the workers’ settlement continued to expand, and some of its parts remained known by the names Five Stars, Green Houses, Mitrovica and Pekmez Street.

workers arrived from across the world

Industry drew workers from the Valpovo and Miholjac areas and from Lika, while specialists arrived from other parts of Austria-Hungary. Among them were many Germans, Hungarians and Czechs. With the newcomers cultural life also developed. The Rosenberg family arrived in 1888, and their son Sigmund spent part of his childhood precisely in Belišće. Later, in the United States under the name Sigmund Romberg, he became a well-known composer of operettas and musicals and dedicated the Belišće March to the place of his childhood.

By the time 1918 rolled around, the company moved its headquarters from Budapest to Belišće, and in 1927 the place became an independent municipality. After 1945 followed the period of the Kombinat, and a new major industrial phase began in 1960 with the opening of factories for semi-cellulose, paper and packaging. The old production lines and the narrow-gauge railways gradually closed down, but their traces still determine the appearance of the town today. The Gutmann Palace has been restored as an interpretation centre of industrial heritage; nearby is a gate from the first sawmill, installed in 1889; the complex of workers’ houses is protected as a monument ensemble; and a train with a locomotive from 1913 has also been preserved. Belišće has thus turned its industrial past, from which it literally arose, into the most recognisable part of its own heritage.

World.title: August 25th 1991 – The Battle of Vukovar Begins
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – On August the 25th, 1991, the battle of Vukovar began, marking the start of one of the most devastating chapters of the Croatian War of Independence.

The most harrowing episode of the Homeland War began on this day in the eastern Croatian city of Vukovar when members of the JNA from the barracks in Vukovar joined Serbian paramilitary units. After doing so, they jointly launched an attack on both Borovo and Vukovar. Index writes that the siege lasted 87 days and transformed Vukovar into a symbol of Croatian resistance and heroism during the Homeland War.

the initial conflicts begin

Slobodan Milošević – NATO

After Croatia declared independence on the 25th of June 1991, local conflicts in eastern Slavonia had already begun. For centuries Vukovar had been a city where Croats, Serbs and Hungarians lived in peace, but the situation changed at the end of the 1980s with the rise of nationalism and the policies of Slobodan Milošević, who wanted to consolidate power in Belgrade.

On the 25th of August, the JNA left the barracks with six tanks that blocked the road towards Bogdanovci. The very next day a new attack on Borovo began that lasted the entire day. The firing briefly stopped, and already during the following night another offensive started. By the 30th of August, the clashes continued one after another, after which a short ceasefire occurred during which weapons were delivered to the Croats in Vukovar from Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci and Zagreb. At that time Mile Dedaković arrived in Vukovar and organised the army and defensive positions in the city.

the serbs wanted to go all the way to zagreb

The JNA commander in Vukovar was Života Panić, who wanted to capture Vukovar as quickly as possible in order to prevent further mobilisation of the Croatian army. The original JNA plan was to take Vukovar and Osijek, then occupy all of Slavonia so that the road towards Varaždin and Zagreb would be open. However, problems already appeared when fewer than two thousand Croatian soldiers withstood numerous JNA attacks in Vukovar.

The plan was not helped by the fact that only 13% of those fit for military service responded to the call-up. After news arrived of the large number of casualties in Vukovar, many soldiers deserted, and by the end of 1991 there were six thousand open court proceedings against deserters. The failure of mobilisation meant the cancellation of the grandiose conquest of the whole of continental Croatia, culminating with Zagreb.

the fall of vukovar and horrific crimes against humanity

Vukovar endured a three-month siege in which seven thousand projectiles fell daily. On the 18th of November the city fell, although only 10–15% of the buildings actually remained. The rest were entirely destroyed. The army entered the city and the expulsion of the non-Serb population and horrific war crimes and crimes against humanity began. Neighbours accused other neighbours of being a defender, informed on where families were located, and just a few days later more than 250 civilians were brutally killed at Ovčara in one single night.

The sight of the murder of hundreds of innocent civilians – Perun

The total number of victims is measured in the thousands of people, and there are probably other undiscovered mass graves containing those who disappeared during the war. The Serbian government under Aleksandar Vučić refuses to cooperate so that the remaining mysteries from the war can finally be resolved.

The city was returned to Croatia only in 1998 through peaceful reintegration, and the 18th of November is marked in Croatia as the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Homeland War. Vukovar has still not recovered from the war: today it has just over 25,000 inhabitants, while in the years before the war it was home to 45,000 people. As the largest Croatian port on the Danube, Vukovar was a busy centre of trade and transport.

Today. it is only a shadow of what it once was, and Croatian authorities from the 1990s until today have not invested enough in it. It was the fifth-largest city in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, then larger even than Zadar, while today it is not ranked among the ten largest Croatian cities.

World.title: Croatia is Full of Tourists, But “Coolcations” Are Increasingly Popular
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia remains full of tourists, but with horrifically hot temperatures now the norm, “coolcations” pose a serious threat to hotter countries as they become increasingly popular.

The director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, Kristjan Staničić, said that there are still more than a million tourists per day in Croatia and that August is so far at the level of last year’s results. Index reports that when speaking on HRT’s Dnevnik, Staničić said that Croatia is still at the peak of the tourist season, but he did not want to forecast what August would be like until the end. “For now I can say that August is at the level of last year’s figures,” he said.

“coolcations” are becoming more and more popular as people tire of overwhelming heat

Staničić also commented on a new tourist trend, the so-called “coolcation”, or the growing interest in cooler destinations in northern Europe. As he explained, because of ever higher summer temperatures and repeated heatwave cycles, many people are looking for places where July and August are more pleasant than on the Mediterranean and in southern Europe. He believes this trend will continue in the coming years and that the tourism sector must be prepared for it. He recalled that climate change has been affecting travellers’ decisions for a longer time, but considers that Croatia, thanks to its diverse offer, can respond to such changes as well.

As an example he mentioned Gorski kotar and Lika, where lower temperatures, quality accommodation, good gastronomy and contents linked to nature and active holidays can be found even during the summer.

inspectors clamp down on illegal rentals and s

Staničić also commented on the intensified work of the tourist inspection this season. Because of illegal operation, eight campsites, 23 holiday homes, 56 apartments, one smaller hotel and one hostel have been closed. He thanked the staff of the State Inspectorate and everyone involved in combating the black market. “Unfortunately, this is a phenomenon that is present and to which a response is needed,” he said. He added that cooperation of all institutions, tourist boards and competent services in the field is important, especially when there is knowledge of unregistered guests or facilities that provide services without being registered for it.

croatian tourism requires proper order

Staničić also spoke about the amendments to the Hospitality Activity Act, against which the Association “Save Small Family Renters” has submitted an objection to the European Commission. They object, among other things, to re-categorisation every decade, the need for co-owners’ consent in multi-apartment buildings, and the conditions for obtaining host status. Staničić expects the law primarily to help in combating the black market.

As one of the most important novelties he singled out the introduction of a registration number that every accommodation service provider will have to have if they want to advertise on global platforms. According to him, such a system should enable more effective control of both accommodation facilities and the online platforms on which they are advertised.

“Everyone has the right to turn to the European Commission,” Staničić said, adding that Croatia has taken over the European acquis which includes the introduction of a registration number. He assessed that this measure should be one of the key tools for combating the black market and “introducing order into Croatian tourism”.

World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Basketball star Henri Drell to be 'man in the mask' in Hungary qualifier
World.content:
National team basketball forward Henri Drell is having to don a mask during this week's FIBA World Cup qualifier away to Hungary, following an injury.

Estonia's basketball team arrived in Miskolc, Hungary, on Tuesday ahead of tomorrow's game.

Drell (Neptūnas Klaipėda) had an excellent game in a recent friendly against Lithuania, but then took a blow to the nose against Italy. He will be able to play, but will have to wear a mask. "Nothing else directly restricts him, his breathing is unobstructed and he can play. After the window, the relevant specialists can deal with it further," team doctor Kaido Stroom said. "It will certainly cause some discomfort, but Henri is very professional in that regard. It doesn't directly limit his playing minutes; that's up to [team coach] Heiko [Rannula] to decide."

Guard Martin Paasoja will however miss the game, as he is recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection, Stroom said.

Kasper Suurorg, another guard, fell awkwardly during training and knocked his elbow on his non-shooting hand, so will miss the Hungary game.

Beyond that, the team will take the traveling to and fro between Estonia and Hungary in their stride, Stroom added.

The national team reached the second phase of the qualifying campaign with a record of 3:3, the same as other group L teams Slovenia, Hungary and Sweden. After playing Hungary, Estonia faces Finland at the Unibet Arena on Sunday.

Both the Hungary and Finland games can be watched live via ERR's Sport portal.

World.title: Difficult to believe Putin would meet CIA chief, says Ex-ISS director
World.content:
Former Internal Security Service Director General Arnold Sinisalu said the head of the U.S.' Central Intelligence Agency's visit to Russia this week does not necessarily mean a secret agreement is being made and it is worth remaining calm.

On Tuesday, it was reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had unexpectedly flown to Moscow via Latvia. U.S. media wrote that he held talks with Russian officials, but the subject of the discussions is unknown.

The last time the head of the U.S. intelligence agency visited Moscow was a few months before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The Americans wanted to make it clear to the Russians that their plans were known and to advise them to stop.

Sinisalu, now a visiting professor at the University of Tartu's Johan Skytte Institute, told Vikerraadio's "Uudis+" program on Wednesday that communication between the services of two major powers is normal and could cover many topics, not only Ukraine.

"We should not think that the only issue between Russia and America is the war in Ukraine," he said. Sinisalu said the military conflict between Iran and America may be the top priority, as it also affects U.S. domestic politics.

Sinisalu said if the U.S. had wanted to keep the visit completely secret, it could have done so. "They could have changed planes several times," he explained.

Additionally, the ex-general director said there is no reason to fear that the two countries are making secret agreements with each other, because the level of trust between them is low.

However, the large aircraft on which Ratcliffe flew to Russia should be looked at separately. He explained that both the FBI and CIA chiefs generally use smaller aircraft to travel. Sinisalu concluded that there must be something on board the aircraft or that it is a matter of security.

Prisoner exchange?

"There has been speculation about many different things here, including whether this is a prisoner exchange," he said. Sinisalu noted that this would seem the most logical explanation. At the same time, prisoner exchanges have been carried out much more quickly and have sometimes even been shown live. "We should take this calmly and proceed from the assumption that it is probably something with much simpler content," he said.

Sinisalu added that the CIA director has generally not traveled to Russia in person for prisoner exchanges, but said there could be something accompanying it. "For example, last-minute bargaining over someone that can only be decided at the very highest level, excluding the presidents," he explained.

The former director general said the question is rather how broad a spectrum of issues the major powers discussed. "U.S. intelligence certainly has various pieces of information that are being used in attempts to start Ukraine-Russia negotiations or resolve the situation with Iran," he said.

Sinisalu noted that there has recently been a great deal of speculation about whether Russia is planning some kind of operation against the Baltics or NATO. He said that Russia currently does not have the strength to carry out a frontal attack in the sense of conventional warfare. "That would also be foolish, because it would give the Ukrainians an excellent opportunity to launch a counterattack, since Russia simply does not have the manpower or weaponry," Sinisalu said.

Developments in space should not be forgotten either. "There has been talk of certain satellites monitoring European and American satellites," Sinisalu noted.

Remain calm

The U.S. newspaper The Wall Street Journal reported that Ratcliffe may also have met with President Vladimir Putin to deliver some kind of warning to him. The U.S. has gathered intelligence indicating that Russia is making preparations for a possible mobilization and also plans to test NATO's resolve.

Sinisalu said that Putin generally does not meet with officials of this kind. "Some kind of message may be relayed there, but I find it difficult to believe that he would physically meet with him," he noted.

Sinisalu said talk of testing NATO is psychological pressure aimed at keeping people in Europe anxious and creating domestic political turbulence.

"Some small special forces provocation is possible, but a large-scale war would be seen coming, and NATO's land, sea and airspace along the borders is monitored very closely," he said, adding it is worth remaining calm.

Sinisalu noted that since the meeting did not take place covertly, it cannot be called a secret meeting.

World.title: Expert: Center Party leader can't stop his MPs voting in presidential election
World.content:
Kõlvart, who is not a Riigikogu member, said earlier in the week that his party would not be voting in the Riigikogu ballots next Wednesday and Thursday, as there is no alternative candidate to Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise.

"A party chairman cannot forbid any member of the Riigikogu from taking part in a presidential election. At this point, I would recommend that Mihhail Kõlvart read the Constitution," political expert Annika Arras told ERR's "Otse uudistemajast" on Wednesday.

The fact that there is only one candidate registered to run – Madise, who was signed off on by 75 MPs where only 21 are needed – along with the process generally over the summer, has raised questions again about the way in which Estonia elects its president.

The head of state is not directly elected by the people, but by the Riigikogu in the first instance, passing to a regional electoral college if this draws a blank. This system was put in place to avoid undue outside interference in the election of the head of state.

Arras said direct presidential elections would certainly be much more exciting than the current vote at the Riigikogu. "In that case, candidates would have a reason to travel around Estonia, present themselves and talk to the people. There would be considerably more opinion polls than there are today," she said.

Also, the issue of outside interference applies to Riigikogu and local elections too, Arras noted, though these enfranchise all Estonian citizens – plus all EU citizens in the case of local elections. "In reality, there is no really watertight argument as to why [the president] could not be directly elected, but it is a matter for discussion and a question of choices. I would be fine with either option," she went on.

The transparency or culture of the presidential elections is ultimately up to the politicians and their actions, she noted; amending the electoral system would not change that on its own. At the same time, Arras noted, another criticism of the process this time around and at past presidential elections is how last-minute the formal nomination of candidates is, or even their public presentation.

"If we altered it so that candidates got nominated earlier, we asked them questions, held debates right here at the public broadcaster and at other media outlets, then politicians would make their choice and people would have a much better idea of whom parliament is electing," she went on.

As for why Isamaa swung the balance further by getting behind Madise last week, Arras said most likely Madise impressed at her meeting with the party's Riigikogu faction – potential candidate Tiit Land had also met with the party before that – and this convinced Isamaa she would be a good head of state.

Also, it might have been difficult to stem a flood of support for Madise from individual Isamaa MPs and others – as Kõlvart has been trying to do with his party.

"This in turn demonstrates that presidential elections in Estonia are so important to every member of the Riigikogu personally that the classic party discipline often used with different parliamentary votes is not easy to maintain," Arras added.

Annika Arras appearing on 'Otse uudistemajast'. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

The Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) simply cracks down on dissenters by expelling them, but this rigid discipline is likely behind their ongoing marginalization, Arras went on, noting that recovery can and does happen too. EKRE put forward party founder Mart Helme as presidential candidate, but lacked enough seats at the Riigikogu to register him on their own.

One further consideration is the March 2027 Riigikogu elections. Arras said the parties that backed Madise will score political points if she does get elected president, particularly the Social Democrats (SDE), who were the first to publicly endorse Madise.

"But I believe that, overall, all those who have now rallied behind Ülle Madise will benefit in any case," she added, noting that the office of president continues to carry a high degree of public trust.

With four of the six Riigikogu parties backing Madise, the presidential elections are unlikely to prove decisive come March, Arras went on. "There are still five or six months to go until the parliamentary election, which means that anything can still happen. The election results have not been decided today."

Recent opinion polls put Madise's rating with the public as high as 43 percent.

Kõlvart: Party still deciding how to act at presidential election

Kõlvart on Wednesday denied that members of the Center Party faction are prohibited from participating in the Riigikogu vote on Madise September 2-3, adding the party has not yet decided how exactly it will vote on that day.

He reiterated that there had been no debate on Land as an alternative candidate.

"We proceed based on the principle that a party should have a consistent and comprehensible policy and position. From the very outset, we have expressed the view that there should be a broader debate, and to do that you need more than one candidate. We have also expressed our support for Tiit Land. There has been no debate; we have only one candidate," Kõlvart told ERR.

This means the party still sees the situation as less than ideal, he went on. "The Riigikogu group will still decide how we express our position. But in our view, the process we are seeing now is not right, and we also do not believe it is right to take part in it."

The true issues cannot be revealed if a candidate runs unopposed, the Center chair continued. "A debate would show that. It is not possible to say on the basis of one meeting. That is why, in our view, there should have been genuine competition and a debate lasting longer than one day, so that not only the Center Party but society as a whole would have a broader understanding of what the vision of one candidate or another actually means."

The current Riigikogu composition does not reflect public support, he added, reiterating his party's support for direct presidential elections. Madise's election as head of state would remain "an appointment" and not an election, he added, noting that Madise's meeting with the Center Party did not prove sufficient to determine her suitability; a proper debate over a longer period would have been needed, he said.

Overall, the past two months has been little more than a "performance," with spectators looking on to see if Madise would run, or not.

At the last presidential election in 2021, Alar Karis ran unopposed and was voted in after the second ballot. Karis announced in mid-summer he would not be seeking re-election, even though he is eligible for a second term.

World.title: Up to 400 children without school places, says education minister
World.content:
Minister of Education Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) believes between 300 and 400 children will be missing from the school system by mid-September as Estonia introduces compulsory education until the age of 18.

From this academic year, Estonia has raised the age of compulsory education to 18 years old, meaning all children must attend high school. However, discussions have arisen in recent weeks about the lack of school places.

When a student is marked missing from the school system, it means the state or local government cannot contact them and does not know where they are.

The minister told ETV's morning program "Terevisioon" on Tuesday that many students have not submitted high school applications. This is partly due to students returning to Ukraine for the summer, but some Estonian children have also disappeared from the system.

However, students who have submitted applications have also not received places.

Kallas said holding students back a year to repeat 9th grade is not an option in many cases, especially if they have not received sufficient support throughout their school years.

"These students need a different learning environment, teachers and approach, and preparatory studies are intended precisely for children who have such significant learning gaps or health problems that they need completely different support from what they have received at school so far," she explained.

Kallas also disagreed with teachers that preparatory studies will actually help solve the problem.

Critical situation in Tallinn

Kallas said that the situation is currently most critical in Tallinn. "A child with grades slightly below average can no longer get into any school," she said.

The number of children from outside the capital applying to study in Tallinn has also been higher than average. This has taken places away from local students, she said.

Kallas said that all Tallinn upper secondary schools are currently full, but admissions are still ongoing at almost all of them. This means that students are constantly moving from one school to another.

"Places are turned down again, places become available again. You have to constantly be on the lookout for where places become available," the minister explained. She said this is very stressful and the system should be reviewed.

Karl Erik Kirss, chairman of the board of the Estonian School Student Councils' Union, said it is important that students without a place get clarity on the situation and should be allocated a point of contact from the state or local government.

Kirss explained that many students, particularly non-Estonian-speaking students, are currently uncertain about how their studies will continue on September 1.

"On Tuesday, we instructed our state schools in Tallinn that if a student comes in who appears unlikely to cope even in vocational education because, for example, they do not speak Estonian at all, they should be officially registered as a candidate for preparatory studies," Kallas said.

She explained that this would allow the ministry to know how many additional preparatory study places the state needs to commission.

Vocational schools a viable alternative

Kallas said that new curricula have been launched in vocational education over the past two years.

Significantly more young people are entering vocational education this year than in previous years. "It has become significantly more attractive," she added.

The minister noted that over time, vocational education will become a fully viable alternative after basic school.

Kirss said that the new curricula in vocational education help change students' perception that vocational school is somehow a worse choice than upper secondary school.

"Of course, the current situation, where upper secondary school places are full and all students without a school place are being directed to vocational schools, probably reinforces the perception that vocational school is still a second choice," he added.

The minister said Tallinn College of Technology has more than 400 vacant study places. "If you are interested in the field of technology, then you should definitely contact that school in Tallinn," she added.

If it turns out that there is no suitable study path there after all, the information will be forwarded to the Education Ministry and the ministry can deal with the child individually. "If upper secondary school places are needed, then in Tallinn they are predominantly provided by the city, and in that case the Education Department should be contacted," Kallas said.

World.title: Painting conservator: Soviet‑era artists had to paint with whatever materials they could get
World.content:
Polina Richter, a painting conservator at Kumu art museum who is researching Soviet‑era oil‑painting materials for her master's thesis, says that the scarcity of supplies in that period forced artists to invent creative solutions.

Richter is studying in the master's program in heritage protection and conservation at the Estonian Academy of Arts and is currently writing her thesis. Her research focuses on the materials used in Soviet‑era oil paintings — specifically the peculiarities of material use at the time and how artists obtained what they needed.

Richter said artists working during the Soviet period mainly got their materials from the Artists' Union shop. Quantities were limited, and artists were often allocated a fixed amount of specific paints. "Many came up with quite interesting solutions because of the lack of materials," she said.

She has not heard of artists making their own pigments when supplies ran out. "But certainly someone may have gone that far," she added.

Dentist tools in the conservator's toolbox

Richter's work at Kumu centers on preparing paintings for exhibitions. Many works have already been conserved, but some were restored decades ago and need to be reassessed before being shown again.

"Unfortunately, time does its work, so they need a bit of touching up again for the exhibition," she said.

Richter compares painting conservation to treating a patient. First, the conservator must determine the artwork's history and current problems, then choose the appropriate methods to address them.

Kumu's painting department has four staff members. The museum also has departments for paper, sculpture and frames. Workload varies throughout the year — autumn and spring are busier because more exhibitions are prepared then.

Before an exhibition, conservators assess which works need preparation and whether there is enough time to restore them all. The job also involves working closely with curators, storage staff and other museum employees.

Removing old varnish not always a necessity

A conservator's toolbox includes chemicals, primers and paints. "One of the most interesting things conservators use are actually dentist tools — something you wouldn't expect, but they're great for picking and doing fine detail work," she said.

Every intervention must be carefully considered. For example, removing old varnish is a decision conservators discuss thoroughly.

"Varnish is generally part of the painting. Since varnish yellows over time and undergoes various changes, you have to look very carefully at whether it should be removed at all," Richter explained.

If the materials of a work are not well known, tests are done before starting. Samples may be examined under a microscope or sent to a lab if needed.

Unexpected situations can arise during conservation. "These are usually accidental and human. They don't happen often, but the team tries to find solutions. And since we're conservators, we have to fix them ourselves," she said.
