The National Bank must examine the investor’s financial position, ownership structure and the source of the funds. It will make a decision after completing the review.

The sale of the Biltmore hotel is also subject to the completion of the relevant legal procedures.

What exactly is Arins Group buying?

Terabank has operated in Georgia since 1999. It has used several names over the years and adopted the name Terabank in 2016.

The bank ranks sixth in Georgia by assets. In July 2026, its assets stood at 2.27 billion lari ($835 million).

Sheikh Nahayyan Mubarak Al Nahyan of the United Arab Emirates owns 80% of the bank. Another 15% belongs to Sheikh Mohamed Butti Al Hamed. The remaining 5% is owned by Russian company Investment Trading Group LLC.

Sheikh Nahayyan’s investments also financed the construction of The Biltmore Tbilisi hotel. According to opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze, the construction and fitting-out of the hotel cost $140 million.

By selling both assets, UAE-based Dabi Group is leaving the Georgian market. Roman Gotsiridze attributes the decision to Georgia’s investment climate. However, the company itself has not publicly explained why it decided to leave.

Terabank sale and possible Russian link

World.title: Lawyers call prison ban on Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer act of censorship
World.content:
The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) says the refusal to allow writer Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer into a prison violates freedom of expression and amounts to censorship.

According to GYLA, the arguments put forward by the Special Penitentiary Service to justify the ban run counter to international human rights standards, including case law established by the European Court of Human Rights.

In early August, reports emerged that the Rustavi prison administration had refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel The Observer to be delivered to Nana Sander, a prisoner convicted of taking part in a 4 October 2025 protest.

The Special Penitentiary Service’s response to a request from lawyer Giorgi Chkheidze, dated 24 August, later circulated in the media and on social networks. The agency explained why it had refused to allow the book into the prison.

The service referred to an annex to Justice Minister’s Order No. 1166 of 21 January 2026. Under the rules, prisoners and detainees may receive parcels containing books, but publications that could pose a threat to their safety or the normal operation of a prison are excluded.

According to the Penitentiary Service, the title The Observer creates uncertainty about the novel’s content and does not allow it to be interpreted unambiguously. The authorities therefore deemed it inappropriate to allow the book into the prison.

GYLA says this justification amounts to an arbitrary restriction of prisoners’ right to receive information.

GYLA argues that freedom to receive information forms part of freedom of expression. It covers not only receiving information itself, but also accessing it in different forms, including through literature. Imprisonment does not in itself mean that a person loses their rights, although certain restrictions may apply because of the conditions of detention.

However, GYLA says such restrictions can only be justified if they serve a lawful, legitimate and necessary purpose.

Under European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) case law, when authorities refuse to deliver publications to prisoners, they must provide sufficient and specific reasons. These may include incitement to or justification of violence, threats to prison security and order, or facilitating communication between members of criminal organisations.

Under ECHR standards, however, the grounds for a ban must be directly linked to the publication’s content. Authorities must identify the relevant passages and demonstrate a connection between the specific text and the threat that the restriction seeks to prevent.

GYLA says the argument that the book has a “vague” title clearly fails to meet these requirements. In the case of fiction, the organisation says, such a factor cannot provide sufficient grounds for a ban.

The Observer is a dystopian novel depicting almost half a century of rule by a despot in Georgia. In March 2026, the book, along with other publications, was targeted in an act of vandalism at a bookshop.

GYLA says the Penitentiary Service’s decision is particularly concerning in this context, as it suggests that the book was censored because of its anti-repressive and political content.

About Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer

World.title: ‘We pray together’: Georgian and Russian Orthodox churches to exchange hundreds of icons
World.content:
The Georgian diaspora in Russia has announced the launch of the “We Pray Together” project, which will involve creating hundreds of icons and exchanging them between the Orthodox churches of Georgia and Russia.

The icons created as part of the project will depict Saint Gabriel and Saint Seraphim of Sarov. The organisers say the icons will share the title “Friendship of the Peoples of Russia and Georgia”.

According to the Federal Georgian National-Cultural Autonomy in Russia (FGNCA), the first batch of icons has already been painted in Georgia and is ready to be handed over to the Russian Orthodox Church.

In a statement, the FGNCA said the project would “serve as a major civilisational response to the challenges of our time” and bring the peoples of Russia and Georgia closer through their shared faith and centuries-old traditions.

The head of the Georgian diaspora in Russia, David Tsetskhladze, described the project as “one of the largest Orthodox initiatives” in the history of Russian-Georgian relations.

“We are not simply exchanging gifts. We are bringing together the patron saints of our peoples to show that spiritual kinship is stronger than any political circumstances. The exchange of hundreds of Orthodox icons will create a historic precedent,” Tsetskhladze said.

The idea of creating the icons came from a group of volunteers led by journalist and filmmaker Konstantin Tsertsvadze.

The statement also says that the initiative received the blessing of the late Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia Ilia II in 2018.

Georgia-Russia icon exchange

World.title: Tourism support package: Can Azerbaijan reach its target of 3.8 million visitors?
World.content:
State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

A new state programme, approved by a decree from President Ilham Aliyev, sets out plans to develop the tourism sector in the coming years, attract more foreign visitors and expand tourism beyond Baku.

The programme comes into force as the tourism sector faces declining figures. In the first half of 2026, 1.09 million foreigners and stateless people arrived in Azerbaijan. This was 10.3% fewer than in the same period last year. Arrivals from the Gulf countries fell by 31.4%, while hotel stays declined by 8.3% and hotel revenues by 3.8%.

Target for 2030: 3.8 million tourists

Under the State Programme, the value added generated by industries directly linked to tourism — in other words, the sector’s actual contribution to the economy — should rise from 6.96 billion manats (about $4.1 billion) in 2025 to 8.51 billion manats in 2027 and 12.17 billion manats (about $7.2 billion) in 2030.

The programme targets real growth of around 40% in the tourism sector by 2030. “Real growth” means an actual increase in the volume of production and services, rather than a nominal rise caused by higher prices.

The government plans to increase the number of foreign arrivals from 2.57 million in 2025 to 3.8 million by 2030.

The target for 2026 is 2.42 million arrivals. Given the 10.3% decline recorded in the first half of the year, the figures will need to improve significantly in the second half to meet this target.

Competition is also intensifying. Azerbaijan ranks 56th among 119 countries in the World Economic Forum’s 2024 Travel and Tourism Development Index. Georgia ranks 45th, Kazakhstan 52nd and Uzbekistan 78th.

In 2025, Georgia reported 5.5 million tourist trips, Uzbekistan 11.7 million foreign tourists and Kazakhstan 15.7 million foreign visitors. The countries use different methods to count tourists and visitors, so these figures cannot be compared directly. Nevertheless, they show that Azerbaijan’s tourism sector faces strong regional competition.

Subsidies, new flights and easier visa rules

The programme provides for extensive government support. Authorities plan to offer subsidies to local tour operators that bring tourists to Azerbaijan, as well as to micro and small businesses operating in the tourism sector.

The measures also include partial compensation for charter flight costs, incentives to open additional scheduled flights to Azerbaijan from priority markets, and financial support for concerts and other entertainment events.

Another area concerns easier entry into the country. The programme provides for expanding visa-free access to citizens of 34 target markets, widening access to e-visas and introducing a “digital nomad” visa in 2027-2028. It will target people who work remotely and want to live in another country for an extended period.

The plan also calls for the development of regional tourism zones, walking routes, health tourism and gastronomic tourism. These measures could help reduce Azerbaijan’s tourism sector’s dependence on Baku, expensive hotels and major international events.

A 2026 World Bank analysis also highlights shortcomings in transport links, accommodation infrastructure, local tour operators and the quality of services in the regions.

At least on paper, therefore, the programme correctly identifies many of the sector’s existing problems.

The problem is not just a lack of subsidies

The key question is whether government support alone can make Azerbaijan a more affordable and competitive tourist destination.

The State Programme itself also highlights the high concentration of the air travel market, meaning that a relatively small number of companies provide most of the services. It also points to limited hotel supply, high prices, and problems with hygiene and service quality.

At the same time, budget airlines have expanded their presence in Baku compared with previous years. In July, Heydar Aliyev International Airport said that around 20 low-cost and hybrid airlines operated flights from Baku to more than 20 international destinations.

The problem can therefore no longer be reduced to the claim that “Azerbaijan has no budget airlines”. Other questions have become more important: how frequently do these airlines operate, which cities do they serve, and does competition between airlines actually affect ticket prices?

The position of major business groups in the tourism and hotel markets also matters in this context.

According to publicly available information from PAŞA Holding, whose shareholders include the president’s father-in-law and daughters, its wholly owned subsidiary Absheron Hotel Group operates hotels including Four Seasons Baku, JW Marriott Absheron and Ritz-Carlton Baku. Another group company, PAŞA Travel, brings tourists to the country, books hotels and provides transport services.

This means that companies belonging to the same business group operate at different stages of the tourism chain. Economists call this model “vertical integration”.

Vertical integration is not in itself illegal or necessarily harmful. However, even without complete public data on market shares, an important question remains: what rules will govern the distribution of subsidies among companies of different sizes?

The main question is this: will government support help new and small companies enter the market, or will it mainly benefit companies that already have significant resources?

Who will receive the money, and for what?

Under the presidential decree, the Cabinet of Ministers must develop rules for awarding subsidies within three months. So although the programme has already been approved, one key question remains unanswered: which companies will receive public funds, according to what criteria and in return for what results?

The Centre for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communication has been tasked with monitoring and evaluating the programme.

However, effective oversight will depend not only on which institution is responsible for it. It will also depend on how accessible information is to the public about the companies receiving subsidies, the amounts they receive and the results they achieve.

Previous audits of other government support programmes by the Chamber of Accounts have identified problems such as insufficient justification for spending on individual projects and a lack of data needed to assess their results. These findings do not directly concern the tourism programme, but they highlight the importance of building the new subsidy mechanism around clear and measurable criteria from the outset.х.

A tourist’s decision is not based on price alone

Entry requirements also directly affect the competitiveness of the tourism sector.

At present, travellers can enter Azerbaijan by air, while crossing the land border remains largely restricted and subject to special rules. Since 25 May, exceptions have applied to rail travel with Georgia for Azerbaijani citizens and some foreign nationals who can enter the country without a visa.

The country’s overall reputation also affects tourists’ choices. The UK Foreign Office generally considers crime levels in Baku to be low, but notes that there are occasional reports of foreign nationals being asked for unofficial payments.

In Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Azerbaijan ranks 171st out of 180 countries. In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, it ranks 130th out of 182 countries.

These rankings do not directly determine whether tourists will visit Azerbaijan. However, they form part of the broader picture that shapes international perceptions of the country, assessments of the predictability of its legal and business environment, and investors’ perceptions of risk.

State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

World.title: Azerbaijan confiscates cryptocurrency in favour of state for first time
World.content:
Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

The Yasamal District Court in Baku has sentenced two people arrested by the State Security Service, B.H.R. and I.R.F., and ordered the confiscation by the state of virtual assets identified as the proceeds or subject of the crime.

Details of the case

The defendants were found guilty under Article 206-1.3 of the Criminal Code. The article provides for criminal liability for organising the illegal covert transfer of particularly large sums of money out of Azerbaijan or into the country using set-offs and other forms of settlement.

According to the court’s ruling:

B.H.R. received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of 3,623,568 manats (about $2.13 million);

received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of (about $2.13 million); I.R.F. received a three-year restriction of liberty and a fine of 31,399,709 manats (about $18.47 million).

The court also ordered the state to confiscate 830 units of cryptocurrency held in an account on the international virtual-asset platform Binance. Investigators had frozen the assets during the preliminary investigation.

Official reports do not specify which cryptocurrency was involved, whether Bitcoin, Ethereum or another asset.

Legal basis

Under Article 99-1 of the Criminal Code, special confiscation involves the compulsory and free transfer to the state of tools and means used to commit a crime, as well as property obtained through criminal activity.

The Law on Combating the Legalisation of Property Obtained through Crime and the Financing of Terrorism also classifies virtual assets as property obtained through criminal activity.

The court has therefore applied the same legal regime to digital assets as it does to physical property for the first time in practice.

Context and significance

In 2025, the State Security Service had already secured a court order to freeze cryptocurrency in a similar criminal case. At the time, Baku’s Sabail District Court ordered the assets to be frozen. On 24 August, the process moved to the next stage: the authorities confiscated the assets.

Azerbaijan does not yet have a separate law governing virtual assets. The Central Bank previously said it expected the relevant draft law to be adopted by the end of 2026. Against this backdrop, the court ruling shows how authorities are addressing the existing legal gap in practice and could set a precedent for future regulation.

Experts note that international exchanges generally comply with court orders promptly. However, the authorities have not yet disclosed what will happen to the confiscated assets, including whether they could be sold at auction, transferred to state reserves or used in another way.

The case marks a new stage in Azerbaijan’s fight against digital crime and expands law enforcement agencies’ ability to track and confiscate virtual assets. At the same time, it highlights the real risks faced by people operating in the unregulated cryptocurrency market.

Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

World.title: Is Georgia expecting a new wave of migrants from Russia?
World.content:
Upper Lars checkpoint, 2022. Photo: Mediazona

While rumours of a possible mobilisation circulate in Russia, Georgia is bracing for a new wave of Russian migrants. However, current data from the Upper Lars checkpoint on the Russian-Georgian border do not yet indicate a mass exodus from Russia.

In mid-August, Russia’s Customs Service said that Upper Lars had seen a “record flow” of travellers. The agency said more than 20,000 people crossed the border in passenger cars on 18 August.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry disputed the Russian figures. According to its data, 7,880 citizens of various countries entered Georgia from Russia between 8 and 19 August, while 8,406 people left Georgia for Russia. In total, 16,286 people crossed the border in both directions.

Russia’s customs authorities later clarified their figures, also saying that more than 16,000 people had crossed the border in both directions. This time, however, they did not describe the figure as “record-breaking”. They noted that more people were travelling towards Russia as the tourist season came to an end.

The figures nevertheless caused concern in Georgia. Many people remembered September 2022, when tens of thousands of Russians entered Georgia after Moscow announced a partial mobilisation.

That large influx drove up property prices significantly. Many people in Georgia now fear that the situation could happen again.

Why are people expecting a new wave of migrants?

Reports of a new mobilisation in Russia remain unconfirmed, but they are spreading widely. The reports claim that mobilisation could be announced after September’s State Duma elections. The Russian authorities have made no official statements to that effect.

Nikoloz Urushadze, managing partner at the consulting company G. Miller International Georgia, says that even these rumours could prompt some Russian citizens to leave the country.

“Even if Russia ultimately does not announce mobilisation, the expectation of it still affects people. They are afraid, and fear is often a powerful factor driving people to move,” he told BusinessPressNews.

Urushadze believes Georgia remains one of the most accessible destinations for Russian citizens and could face a new influx of migrants if Russia announces mobilisation.

The experience of 2022

In September 2022, immediately after Russia announced its partial mobilisation, the queue at the Upper Lars checkpoint stretched for 20-30 kilometres on the Russian side. Around 5,500 cars were waiting at the border. Authorities even set up a mobile military recruitment office in North Ossetia, where the checkpoint is located.

According to Georgia’s then-interior minister, Vakhtang Gomelauri, around 10,000 people crossed the border each day. Before the mobilisation announcement, the figure stood at about 6,000.

As a result of the influx, around 100,000 Russian citizens lived in Georgia for a period. Some local residents called on the authorities to introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens.

How could a new influx affect property prices in Georgia?

According to Nikoloz Urushadze, a new wave of Russian migrants would primarily affect the property market. Increased demand would push up rental prices again. Georgia experienced this in 2022-2023, when the arrival of large numbers of Russian citizens sharply increased rental costs in Tbilisi and Batumi.

Russian citizens, along with Ukrainians and Belarusians, are also actively buying property in Georgia. In the first half of 2026, they accounted for 18% of all buyers. A year earlier, their share stood at 13%. During the same period, the share of Georgian citizens among apartment buyers in the resort city of Batumi fell from 43% to 33%.

Urushadze points to another problem. In his view, some Russian citizens do not integrate into local society and the economy. Instead, they create their own closed infrastructure.

“Georgia is a country where 300,000 Russians could come and create a little Russia here, with their own schools and universities. They would not need the Georgian language or anything else at all,” he says.

At this stage, the situation on the Russian-Georgian border does not resemble the mass exodus of 2022. The queues in August were mainly linked to the tourist season and a temporary border closure due to bad weather. Many people were leaving Georgia rather than entering it, returning to Russia.

The real scale of any new influx will become clearer later. The decisive factor will be whether the Russian leadership officially announces mobilisation.

Russian migrants in Georgia

World.title: ‘Ice cream’ and cold showers: Keeping cool on hot days at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
As summer temperatures rise, Tbilisi Zoo switches to a special routine. The keepers’ main task is to help the animals cope with the heat and protect them from overheating.

A range of measures is used, from cooling the enclosures to providing special diets. The first and most important rule is to ensure that all the animals have a constant supply of clean, cool drinking water.

The water is refreshed several times a day, while keepers provide additional ways for the animals to cool down in their enclosures when needed. One method is to spray the enclosures with water. Zoo staff regularly hose down the floors and surrounding areas to maintain humidity and lower the temperature.

Large animals require particular attention. For elephants, for example, water treatments are a real treat. Keepers hose them down all over their bodies, helping them cool off quickly.

The zoo also creates mud wallows specifically for the elephants and the rhinoceros. As the mud dries on the animals’ skin, it forms a protective layer against strong sunlight, possible sunburn and insects. The layer also helps keep their bodies cool.

Summer heat also affects the animals’ daily care. Keepers adjust feeding methods so that the animals receive both physical and mental stimulation. Seasonal juicy fruits are added to their diets, providing another way to help them cool down.

For primates and herbivores, keepers freeze fruit and vegetables. For the animals, this is a kind of “ice cream”, but it serves more than just a cooling purpose. The animals have to make an effort to get to the frozen food, providing both physical and mental stimulation. It also allows them to display natural behaviour.

The same principle applies to predators, for which keepers freeze meat. “Meat ice cream” helps lions and tigers cool down while also providing sensory enrichment.

It is also important that the doors to indoor enclosures, where temperatures are lower and it is cooler, remain open at all times. This allows the animals to choose where they want to stay.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

The heat at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Sabah FC expresses its gratitude to President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. The “Sabah” football club expressed its gratitude to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, for his congratulations on the team’s historic qualification for the group stage of the UEFA Champions League.

The Baku club issued a statement addressed to the head of state following its victory over the Israeli club Hapoel Be'er Sheva in the tournament's playoff round.

"Dear Mr. President!

We would like to express our deep gratitude for the close attention you have given to Sabah Football Club’s historic qualification for the UEFA Champions League for the first time. Your congratulations have made this victory even more enjoyable for our team.

Your constant attention and support for Azerbaijani sports, including the development of soccer, as well as the opportunities you have created for the growth of sports clubs, serve as a great incentive for achieving such historic successes and reinforce our sense of responsibility.

We will continue to fight selflessly to represent our country with dignity in Europe’s most prestigious soccer tournament and to further elevate the prestige of Azerbaijani soccer.

Ultimately, it is from you that we learn the determination to fight to the end and believe in victory. As the source of the Azerbaijani people’s great victories, we draw strength and inspiration from you.

On behalf of the “Sabah” Football Club, we once again express our deep gratitude to you for the high regard you have shown us,” the statement reads.

Meanwhile, in the first match, “Sabah” lost to “Hapoel” 1–2, but in the return match in Baku, they won 5–2, advancing to the group stage of the UEFA Champions League for the first time in their history.

World.title: Reduced fertiliser use linked to cleaner water flowing to Great Barrier Reef
World.content:
Two separate studies claim to show a connection between improved water quality in Great Barrier Reef catchments and farmers changing the way they fertilise their crops.

Researchers also believe healthier water flowing to the reef could improve its ability to recover from the growing impacts of climate change, including coral bleaching.

In collaboration with scientists from CSIRO and James Cook University (JCU), two research papers have been produced using data that spans decades.

One study found water quality had improved across multiple river catchments, while the other documented significant reductions in the use of synthetic fertiliser, particularly in sugarcane-growing areas.

Sediment from agricultural runoff has had a detrimental impact on parts of the Great Barrier Reef. (Supplied: TropWATER JCU)

Aaron Davis from TropWATER JCU said there was a clear link between the two studies.

"We've been able to document those substantial fertiliser reductions that they've undertaken over the last 30-odd years," he said.

" We're also now able to tie that into improvements in water quality with real data and significant downward declines in dissolved inorganic nitrogen concentrations at the end of catchment with real data. "

Aaron Davis has been working with farmers to reduce their synthetic fertiliser use without losing productivity. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Studies explained

Stephen Lewis from TropWATER JCU said the fertiliser study drew upon 100 years of data.

"The fertiliser records we compiled [show] the amount of synthetic nitrogen and phosphorus fertiliser application for all river catchments across the entire Great Barrier Reef catchment area," he said.

"What that showed was there was a marked reduction by up to 25 to 50 per cent reductions in nitrogen and phosphorus fertiliser application across the vast majority of basins for the Great Barrier Reef catchment area, and this occurred over the past one to two decades."

CSIRO researcher Rebecca Bartley, who worked on the water-quality study, said it was the largest and most comprehensive analysis of its kind undertaken across Great Barrier Reef catchments.

For that study, nearly 40 years of water-quality data was analysed.

Stephen Lewis and Rebecca Bartley say the study has shown improvements in water quality. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"We evaluated water quality at nine sites. That doesn't sound like a lot, but it actually represents an area the same size as New Zealand, so a really big catchment area," Dr Bartley said.

"At those nine sites, 75 per cent of them showed improvements in water quality over about a 40-year record."

She said the sites that did not show improvements were generally in smaller catchments.

She said the results were positive, with landholders playing a significant role in water-quality outcomes, which would ultimately aid the reef.

The sugar cane industry says it tries to mitigate its impact on the Great Barrier Reef. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

"It's well established that climate change and repeat coral-bleaching events are the biggest threat to the Great Barrier Reef at the moment," Dr Bartley said.

"But it's really, really important that we have good water quality getting out to the reef during those events as it's been shown that corals will recover more quickly from bleaching and coral disease and the seagrasses will recover if water quality is in good condition.

"That's why this news is so encouraging."

Improved water quality should help the reef recover faster during climate change events. (Supplied: Zohar Ouzana)

The Great Barrier Reef Park Marine Authority (GBPRMPA) was not involved in the study, but its Marine Monitoring Program was one of the key data sources analysed.

GBRMPA chief scientist Roger Beeden welcomed the study's findings, which he said highlighted the importance of long-term monitoring.

"The challenge with anything to do with conservation is it takes a long time to get really clear outcomes and these are complex systems," Dr Beeden said.

"One of things [the study] did was disentangle the long-term trends from what happens with episodic events like floods.

"That's really useful to be able to see through the noise and it also indicated that you get these periods of recovery."

The findings come as Australia prepares to report to UNESCO in 2028 on progress under its Reef 2050 water-quality plan, with trends in nutrient pollution forming part of the assessment.

Of the monitored catchments, 75 per cent showed an improvement in water quality. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Practices in sugarcane farming

Sugarcane farmers have been changing when and how they apply fertiliser to reduce the amount of nutrients washing into waterways.

Cane farmer Neil Maitland, from near Cairns, said timing was critical, particularly ahead of the region's heavy summer rain.

"We found … that you need to put the fertiliser on as early as you can after about the middle of September to try to miss that first flush," he said.

Neil Maitland is reducing the amount of synthetic fertiliser he uses on his crops. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Mr Maitland has also been using sunn hemp and other cover crops to naturally add nitrogen back into the soil, reducing his reliance on synthetic fertiliser.

He said reducing fertiliser use had environmental benefits while also cutting farm-input costs without decreasing yields.

"With these high nitrogen and high fertiliser prices, the saving is unbelievable, and still not losing any productivity," he said.

Neil Maitland is using cover crops to add naturally add nitrogen back into his soil. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Nearby canegrower John Ferrando has adopted similar practices and said protecting the condition of the land was central to the future of farming.

"Farmers have always invested in their soils," he said.

"We wouldn't be fourth-generation farmers if we were [ruining] the soil. So, [our] legacy is to leave the farm in a better condition, pass it on to the next generation."

World.title: Tasmania Police cancels $6m KPMG contract — but can't say why
World.content:
Tasmania Police terminated a digital contract with KPMG after spending more than $6 million on incomplete projects that had faced extensive delays, quality concerns and questions about cost increases.

The project is now under review, while the settlement deed between the state government and the accounting firm includes a non-disparagement clause and a confidentiality clause.

The deed — a portion of which was tabled in Tasmanian Parliament — also makes reference to a "dispute" between the parties.

It centres on upgrades to an intelligence management system, known as Atlas, which Tasmania Police purchased off-the-shelf in 2019 for $13 million.

Tasmania Police Commissioner Donna Adams says the upgrades are now being reviewed. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Atlas was billed by the government as improving police criminal intelligence capabilities, but has since been described as "clunky" by Commissioner Donna Adams, with it taking officers up to 30 minutes to file intelligence.

In 2024, Tasmania Police awarded a $14.8 million contract to KPMG to integrate Atlas and manage the project as part of its broad Project Unify upgrades.

Tasmania Police paid the firm $1.3 million at the signing of the contract, and a further $654,000 to begin the project.

The contract was intended to run until April this year, but was terminated in January, with KPMG having received $5.4 million for the work; the ABC understands there were project management issues.

There was no termination payment, according to Tasmania Police.

The contract termination included clauses that prevented the public from knowing why it had been cancelled.

"Each party will not make or cause to be made any statement or comment which disparages the other party or any related entity in relation to … a project or the dispute," the deed reads.

Commissioner Adams told parliament in June that the project has since been paused while an independent review is carried out, with police looking to add a new interface to the existing Atlas program.

"I'm not going to apologise for the fact that we've paused the project to make sure that our decision-making moving forward is going to set us up," she said.

Crime reporting portal not up to standard

Police officer in alleged relationship with criminal 'lied' about her whereabouts A man of "dubious character" who was under active criminal investigation was in an alleged relationship with a Tasmanian police officer who disclosed police information to him, an investigation has found.

During the contract period, Tasmania Police agreed to add more work for KPMG, which included developing a public online crime reporting portal known as Project Link.

This was added as an "agreed variation"; it's unclear if this went out to open tender.

KPMG received $637,000 for this project, but the ABC understands Project Link faced delays due to significant functionality issues.

It was due to go live in November 2024, then April 2025, before it was paused several months later.

"The system was not going to be up to what the community would expect in terms of submitting a minor crime report," Commissioner Adams told parliament.

After KPMG left the project in January, it took Tasmania Police a further seven months to complete it, and it went live this month.

Deputy Commissioner Jonathan Higgins told parliament that Project Link's original funding allocation was $1.75 million.

Do you know more? Contact Adam Holmes at holmes.adam@abc.net.au.

A later answer on notice showed it was originally $500,000, and that the remaining funding had been transferred from a firearms register program that was no longer required.

An independent review into the projects is ongoing.

A Tasmania Police spokesperson said this would guide the next steps.

"As part of that process, work completed to date, including the design and build of additional modules, is being assessed," they said.

"It would be premature to comment further while the review is underway."

The spokesperson said it could not provide further details regarding the KPMG contract.

Funding questions remains

The projects were part of an overall $46 million suite of ICT upgrades for Tasmania Police, starting in 2020.

In its answers tabled in parliament, Tasmania Police listed seven projects to reach this figure.

It did not include a $4.1 million infringement notice system upgrade or a $5.47 million interface for Atlas.

The interface project is going through a "proof-of-concept" phase and is intended to be rolled out later this year.

Tasmania Police officers have had to manage with outdated filing systems. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Independent upper house MLC Meg Webb, who questioned police about the KPMG contract, said there are "serious probity oversight and accountability concerns" with the project.

She said the settlement deed could prevent the public from knowing why the contract failed.

"This begs the question: how was this was allowed to continue for so long and at such a cost," Ms Webb said.

"And also, why was it considered necessary or appropriate for these non-disparagement and confidentiality clauses in the state's settlement agreement when parting ways with the contracted consultancy KPMG?"

Commissioner Adams told parliament that ICT projects have "many curves and hurdles".

"What has happened for us within this three-year period is the complete transformation of technology, the emergence of AI," she said.

Departments face digital upgrade issues

Tasmania Police is among a range of government departments to face scrutiny over its ICT contract procurement practices.

The Health Department spent $61 million on 742 labour hire contracts which were worth less than $99,999 each as part of its Bluegum digital transformation project.

Contracts of this value can be awarded directly without a tender process.

Auditor-general Martin Thompson assessed the department's practices, finding 80 contracts that started before the award date; in one instance, a contract started four months before it was awarded.

In response, the state government described the pace of delivery and the need for specialist skills as reasons for the contracting system.

The auditor-general was also critical of a human resource information system program, which he described as not being effective or economical.

World.title: Most people don't survive brain cancer. Researchers hope to change that
World.content:
Simran Singh was just 12 years old when excruciating headaches led to her first brain tumour diagnosis.

"I had a brain surgery and experienced six months of remission," she said.

She was also diagnosed with vertigo and epilepsy and began having yearly MRI scans to monitor the tumour.

But at age 17 while in year 12, the tumour had returned and spread.

Doctors discovered a brain tumour called a neurocytoma, a rare type of brain tumour.

"It was right in the middle of my brain," she said.

"There were different tumours sitting on different parts of my brain."

Simran Singh was diagnosed with a brain tumour at age 12. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Australian doctors suggested proton beam therapy, but it was not available in the country and Ms Singh had to travel to Florida, United States, for treatment.

She described the experience as an incredibly difficult time for her and her family.

"I had to repeat year 12," she said.

Today, the science undergraduate is observing the work of an Adelaide-based research team investigating a treatment she once endured.

Simran Singh undergoing proton beam therapy in Florida. (Supplied)

Researchers want to make radiation better at killing cancer cells, while protecting healthy tissue.

Their project will also look at how radiation affects the immune system.

The Adelaide researchers received $240,000 — the first team to be allocated funding under a new national initiative from the Mark Hughes Foundation Centre for Brain Cancer Research to fast track new approaches to brain cancer and brain tumour treatment.

Improving brain cancer survival rates

Adelaide University biophysics professor Ivan Kempson said survival rates for brain cancer have shifted slowly in the past few decades.

"For families affected by brain cancer, advances are urgently needed," Professor Kempson said.

"The outcomes are very poor, and survival rates have changed little in the past 35 years, with only two in 10 patients surviving beyond five years.

" It kills more children than any other disease and more people under 40 than any other cancer. "

Professor Kempson said the research would largely look at how radiation interacts at a microscopic level with cancer cells and normal cells.

"What we want to achieve is that patients can get better outcomes in terms of better survival rate … and also improve the quality of life beyond treatment," he said.

Professor Ivan Kempson is pioneering new approaches to brain cancer radiotherapy. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

While radiotherapy has advanced significantly over the decades, Professor Kempson said that brain cancer has unfortunately not responded as well as other malignancies.

"We haven't seen the improvement in brain cancer treatment," he said.

"With looking at the molecular microscopic view, we think we can start to piece together the fundamental information that we need to lead to the next breakthroughs in how brain cancer is treated."

Specialised tools are being used in the project to allow researchers to measure radiation damage to DNA with a level of precision that has not previously been possible, according to Adelaide University.

World.title: 'Bohemian' Melbourne schoolteacher Faye Berryman suspended
World.content:
The Victorian teaching watchdog has suspended Fitzroy Community School (FCS) co-founder Faye Berryman's teaching registration on an interim basis.

Ms Berryman and the alternative primary school she established with her husband Philip O'Carroll in their family home 50 years ago have been the subject of multiple complaints by parents and former students to the Victorian Institute of Teaching (VIT).

Faye Berryman, 82, taught classes at the Brunswick Street campus of FCS until recently. (Supplied)

A VIT spokesperson confirmed to the ABC that the regulator had suspended the registration of 82-year-old Ms Berryman, who is registered as a teacher under her married name Faye O'Carroll, "on an interim basis while it conducts its investigations".

The VIT said Ms Berryman was "unable to teach in any school while suspended".

Ms Berryman, the FCS and its board were contacted for comment but did not respond to questions.

Do you know more? Contact Josie Taylor using josiegtaylor@protonmail.com or Coco Veldkamp using cocoveldkamp@proton.me

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Sons also under investigation

Ms Berryman's son and former FCS teacher, Nick Berryman, is also suspended from teaching and the ABC understands he is due to face a formal VIT hearing at a date to be set to determine whether he is stripped of his teaching registration.

Nick Berryman still features on the FCS website, despite being suspended, and soon to face a formal VIT hearing. (Supplied)

His brother, former FCS principal Tim Berryman, is also under investigation by the VIT and was found "unfit" to hold a senior position at any Victorian school, along with Ms Berryman and his sister, Catherine O'Carroll.

In 2020, Ms Berryman was awarded a Medal of the Order of Australia for "significant" services to education.

Faye Berryman has taught children at the Brunswick Street campus of Fitzroy Community School since 1976 in what was originally her family home. (Supplied)

The Office of the Official Secretary to the Governor-General declined to comment on whether Ms Berryman's award would be re-examined in light of these developments.

"All terminations and cancellations of appointments and awards in the Order of Australia are announced in the Government Gazette," the spokesperson said.

FCS emails to parents, seen by the ABC, show the school has considered closing its Brunswick Street campus at the end of the school term.

In 2020, Faye Berryman was awarded a Medal of the Order of Australia for "significant" services to education. (Supplied)

The ABC understands two staff, in addition to Ms Berryman and her two sons, have been stood down by the school while police and regulatory investigations continue.

As well as founding their school, Ms Berryman and her husband established the phonics book series, the Fitzroy Readers.

Two local councils have recently removed the Fitzroy Readers books from library shelves.

"These books are no longer kept at Bargoonga Nganjin, due to its proximity to the school, as a courtesy to families in the neighbourhood who might genuinely find their presence on the shelves distressing," a City of Yarra spokesperson said.

Merri-Bek Shire Council said it had removed Fitzroy Readers from its five libraries until investigations had finished.

Parents contacting police

Victoria Police declined to comment on whether it would allocate a specialised taskforce to investigate multiple sexual abuse allegations made at the school, but said the issue was under "ongoing review".

"Victoria Police continually assess the nature, scale, and complexity of investigations and will allocate resources as required," a spokesperson said.

"Victoria Police encourage anyone with information relating to criminal offending to come forward, regardless of how long ago the alleged conduct occurred."

A group of former FCS parents has written to Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush asking him to ensure all former students are "proactively" contacted by officers.

Faye Berryman has been a teacher for 50 years. (Supplied)

FCS has hired former Australian Federal Police detective Simon Davies to conduct an independent investigation into allegations.

Mr Davies, director of Safeguarding Services, said he would investigate if allegations happened on the "balance of probabilities" and would make his findings to the head of the school.

FCS has appointed Simon Davies to conduct an independent investigation into allegations against the school. (Supplied)

"They [the school] then report the findings back to the [Victorian] State Services Regulator," he said.

"The days of old are sort of gone where things could be brushed under the carpet. You've got a regulator monitoring my process, the school's process."

However, Mr Davies said he could not begin his investigation without clearance from Victoria Police.

"There's a number of criminal allegations that have been made so we have to be guided by Victoria Police," Mr Davies said.

"We are in discussions with Victoria Police as to what they may or may not let us do."

He urged victim-survivors to have the confidence to contact him.

"We're keen to get to the truth, whatever that looks like," he said.

VIT asked anyone with information or concerns about the conduct of teachers associated with FCS to get in contact.

World.title: Live: Hundreds missing, including Australians, in deadly Himalayan flash floods
World.content:
There are conflicting reports as to what was likely the primary cause of the flash flooding, but a picture is beginning to emerge.

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal initially told the country's parliament an earthquake had triggered an avalanche, which caused the sudden flooding of the Bhote Koshi river in Nepal's Rasuwa district.

The German Research Centre for Geosciences said there was a magnitude-4.4 quake just minutes before the water struck border communities.

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, however, said a collapsing glacier on the Nepali side of the border was likely the primary cause, blocking the river then releasing a sudden surge downstream.

The same region also saw flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures.

Nepal's disaster authority is now saying satellite data indicates a "snow-rock landslide" on the border triggered the flood, which would be consistent with both glacier melt and an earthquake as a triggering event.

Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate due to climate change, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000.

Reporting with Reuters, AP

World.title: How a national screening program aims to improve treatment of Australia's deadliest cancer
World.content:
Suzi Scott was a child when her mother died of lung cancer, aged just 49.

Almost half a century later, the 57-year-old was herself diagnosed with Australia's deadliest cancer last year.

But unlike her mother, the cancer was picked up early, before she had any symptoms.

Ms Scott is one of more than 117,000 people who have been scanned since Australia's National Lung Cancer Screening Program began in July last year.

Recalling the trauma of losing her mum June to lung cancer as a nine-year-old, she talked to her general practitioner about joining the free program and "made it happen".

More Australians die from lung cancer than any other type of cancer. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Ms Scott is convinced that decision saved her life.

She had a bulk-billed low dose CT scan as part of the new screening program, which detected a 1.6cm tumour in her right lung.

About four weeks later, the cancer was removed at The Prince Charles Hospital, in Brisbane's north. She spent four days in hospital, was off work for six weeks, but has not required any further treatment.

Ms Scott has also quit nicotine.

The silent killer

By the time her mum was diagnosed in the 1970s, the cancer had already spread beyond her lungs.

"I remember a big lump had appeared on mum's neck," Ms Scott said.

"That was the reason why she got checked."

Suzi Scott was one of almost 100,000 people screened in the first year of Australia’s lung cancer screening program. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

To be eligible for the lung cancer screening program, Australians must be aged between 50 and 70 and have a significant history of smoking, equivalent to a pack of cigarettes a day for 30 years.

They must also have no signs or symptoms that suggest lung cancer, which kills about 9,000 Australians a year.

The program aims to detect lung cancer at an early, more treatable stage.

Ms Scott said she had no indication that she had lung cancer before the tumour was found.

"I never was coughing, I didn't bring up blood," she said.

"I didn't have chest pain. I was running. I was physically fit. I was doing my job.

"Lung cancer is a silent killer. So many people don't need to be dying from lung cancer. They need to go and get the screening. Don't be scared."

You're eligible for the screening program if you: are aged between 50 and 70 years old

show no symptoms of lung cancer and

have a history of cigarette smoking equivalent to smoking a pack of cigarettes a day for 30 years

are currently still smoking or have quit in the past 10 years

Ms Scott, who works in security, is among almost 400 people who have had lung cancers detected under the program, Australia's first new national cancer screening program in two decades. It joins similar screening programs for bowel, breast and cervical cancers targeted at early detection and prevention.

While more than 900,000 Australians are estimated to be eligible for screening under the program, it was significantly under-subscribed in the first year.

Lung Foundation Australia CEO Mark Brooke said although the foundation was "absolutely delighted" with the first-year uptake, there was "always room for improvement".

He's called for increased investment to support general practitioners in referring patients for screening.

Mark Brooke, CEO of Lung Foundation Australia. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Mr Brooke also suggested there may be value in extending the age range for screening and to include people with a family history of lung cancer and those in high-risk occupations, such as stone masons, miners, construction workers, firefighters, and agricultural workers.

"We don't want to unnecessarily screen people and expose them to radiation where there's not a need to do that," he said.

"Targeted programs deliver the best health outcome but also the best economic outcome.

"We know that people who currently smoke or have previously smoked are at highest risk of lung cancer. That's about six or seven out of 10 people go on to be diagnosed with a lung cancer."

Australia 'winning' at cancer screening

Mr Brooke said Australia was being hailed as the global leader in lung cancer screening, with one expert telling a recent conference "Australia has not only won the Ashes, but they're winning the lung cancer screening race as well".

"I think lots of people around the world are sitting up and taking notice of how Australia has implemented this program," he said.

Curtin University respiratory specialist Fraser Brims said while more could be done to raise awareness about the program and to get eligible people through the door for testing, the rollout should be considered "a great success".

Curtin University respiratory specialist Professor Fraser Brims. (ABC News)

But he said receiving care after a lung cancer diagnosis was still a challenge in some regions.

"We know the Australian health system for lung cancer has some excellent care, [however] it is uneven in places," Professor Brims said.

"When there's challenges of getting to experts at the right time, that can worsen outcomes for some Australians.

Australia's lung cancer screening program has started Lung cancer is the number one cause of cancer deaths in Australia, but it's not just a smokers' disease.

"There is a need … for a national clinical quality program to monitor health services and their outcomes and for the system to become a learning system and to become accountable."

Professor Brims also argued for better integration of smoking cessation support within the screening program.

"We know from studies that are going on within Australia and also internationally, that the benefit of smoking cessation at the time of screening is magnified," he said.

"You've got the effect of screening, and then the effect of stopping smoking successfully, which is not only about lung health, not only about the 15 other cancers that tobacco can cause, but also heart health and stroke."

People who currently smoke or have previously smoked are at highest risk of lung cancer. (Unsplash: Robina Weermeijer)

Professor Brims joined Mr Brooke in calling for more specialist lung cancer nurses.

"We know around the time of a diagnosis and starting treatment, this is an incredibly difficult time for patients and families," he said.

"Up to 80 per cent of patients report quite significant effects on their mental health.

"The presence of a specialist nurse during that time improves the quality of life, it improves the timeliness and the efficiency of treatment and even the uptake of treatment."

'If you leave it, it will get you'

Suzi Scott considers herself "lucky" her cancer was "found early" and it could be successfully removed.

Other patients she was in hospital with were not as fortunate.

The mum and grandmother started smoking as a 14-year-old in the 1980s.

Suzi Scott says she had no symptoms of lung cancer before a 1.6cm tumour was found in her right lung. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"I was out having parties, and I was having fun and I smoked. Smoking was everywhere. It was a social activity," she recalled.

"I lost my mum to lung cancer, but I was nine years old.

"I didn't even realise how I could get lung cancer from smoking until it was too late, really."

After almost 40 years of smoking, she quit five years ago but then started vaping nicotine. She stopped vaping after the lung cancer was removed.

Ms Scott said the lung cancer screening program was "aimed at people who grew up in that era and smoked because the culture was different".

She's hoping her story will encourage others of her generation to get screened.

"If you leave it, it will come and get you," Ms Scott said.

World.title: Beneath the Bondi royal commission's calm surface lies a deep tension
World.content:
The antisemitism royal commission has been about as far from a Judge Judy-style reality show as you could possibly imagine.

There has been very little grandstanding.

No-one was playing to the crowd, nor to the dwindling number of reporters in the press gallery.

Much of the testimony has gone unchallenged.

Commissioner Virginia Bell SC has occasionally intervened, often cutting through with a razor-sharp observation, but otherwise the retired High Court justice has assumed the role of kindly matriarch, appearing most animated when announcing the morning tea break.

The questioning, led in sonorous tones by senior counsel assisting Richard Lancaster SC, has been low-key, at times languid, but the proceedings have been anything but a sleepy affair.

The public sessions have vividly exposed the raw pain, fear and anger of Jewish Australians, and the deep and bitter divides in Australian society about what constitutes antisemitism and what to do about it.

There have been nine blocks of hearings. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Don't mention the war

The war in Gaza has been the little-mentioned backdrop to the commission's work.

Many witnesses have given harrowing accounts of the racist abuse they have been subjected to since the October 7 terrorist attacks on Israel.

What happened in the aftermath of the Hamas terrorists' rampage has not generally been spelled out.

It took until the seventh hearing block for the Gaza war to really come to the fore in the form of the testy cross-examination of a prominent Jewish witness, David Ossip.

Ossip, president of the New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, was being pressed by Dominic Toomey SC, representing the Palestine Action Group (PAG), on the context of an October 9, 2023 protest that ended at the Sydney Opera House.

Flares and fireworks were lit in the crowd and thrown onto the forecourt steps of the Sydney Opera House. (AAP: Dean Lewis)

Multiple Jewish witnesses have testified about their disgust and fear surrounding the rally, at which, the commission heard, some protesters chanted, "Where's the Jews?" and "F*** the Jews".

The cross-examination centred on a point of fact about when military action on Gaza began in response to the October 7 attack.

Ossip said it was "unfathomable" that the PAG protest was called when "while women were still being raped, while children were being kidnapped, whilst families were being burnt alive".

Toomey put it to Ossip that by the time the protest was called the Israel Defense Forces had begun conducting air strikes on the Palestinian territory in response to the October 7 attacks, and that it was intended as "a rally for a free Palestine and no war on Gaza".

Ossip questioned the relevance of being asked about the "minutiae of the timeline of a foreign military operation", but Bell quickly shut down his protestations.

Outside the commission, it has been a different matter.

Alex Ryvchin was one of many witnesses who fronted the royal commission. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The appearance of Toomey and Ragni Mathur SC, a lawyer for the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN), was condemned, among others, by Executive Council of Australian Jewry's Alex Ryvchin, New South Wales Premier Chris Minns and federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.

Bell hit back, refuting claims that the lawyers had "hijacked" proceedings.

A difficult demarcation line

As the evidence before the commission has laid bare, the line between legitimate discourse about Zionism and Israel's conduct, and antisemitism, is deeply contested.

Hearing block three's evidence on the public broadcasters ABC and SBS shone a light on the complexity of the issue and the circular nature of some of the arguments being put forward.

Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism Jillian Segal, who appeared before the commission a total of three times, accused the ABC and SBS of overemphasising the Gaza war "relative to other global conflicts", and "disproportionately giving voice to anti-Israel perspectives".

The line between legitimate discourse about Zionism and Israel's conduct, and antisemitism is deeply contested. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

The Special Envoy argued this exacerbated "the prevalence of antisemitism in Australia and the conflation of Jewish identity with the State of Israel".

Segal said there was "a very strongly held perception" among the Jewish community that the coverage had "created an impression of great negativity about Israel".

She argued that ABC reporters and management did not understand how this led to the conflation of the actions of Israel with Jewish identity and thus to a rise in antisemitism.

Yet, her proposed remedy was less about tackling any conflation head on, and more about achieving "balance" in coverage with more favourable stories about Israel.

"They could run positive stories about other things Israel is doing, amazing start‑up nation — things like that. They very rarely do that. There's no attempt at that part of the agenda."

Jillian Segal said the public broadcasters disproportionately gave voice to anti-Israel perspectives. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The testimony of the president of the Australian National Imams Council (ANIC), Sheikh Shadi Alsuleiman, was also illustrative of stark differences of opinion on what is legitimate discourse.

Alsuleiman agreed that comments made on October 8, 2023, at a rally in Lakemba in south-west Sydney by Sheikh Ibrahim Dadoun, in which he described October 7 as a "day of pride" and a "day of victory", were "inappropriate".

Alsuleiman said Dadoun had been spoken to and pointed to Dadoun's subsequent Facebook post on the matter.

But neither that post, nor a statement co-signed by ANIC on October 12 and raised in cross-examination by Nicholas Bender SC, acting for several Jewish organisations, included anything resembling an apology for the comments.

Instead, the media was blamed for taking his remarks out of context, with the statement saying the sheikh had not been celebrating the loss of innocent lives, but the fact that Palestinians had broken free of "the Israeli blockade that has imprisoned them for over 16 years".

Alsuleiman spoke at the royal commission in August. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

A tight deadline

As the sickening accounts of witnesses have demonstrated, antisemitism has pervaded daily life — leaving Jewish Australians feeling they need to conceal outward signs of their faith, kids afraid to be out in public, and one witness facing a request to use a less obviously Jewish name in order not to potentially upset a client.

As an exercise in highlighting the breadth and depth of the issue and in listening to witnesses, the hearings have been powerful.

Now the harder work begins.

Jewish Australians are grappling with a rise in antisemitism. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

In a few short months the commission must make recommendations on defining what constitutes antisemitism and how to respond to it.

Calls, led by federal MP Julian Leeser and backed by Taylor, for an extension to the reporting deadline did not gain traction, with Ryvchin telling the ABC it would be "lamentable" if the commission had to push back the report.

But on Wednesday, Bell said she had asked for a short extension to the December 14 reporting deadline, moving it to December 18. She said the four-day change was not a "meaningful" extension.

She said she had listened to the concerns of the Jewish community that publishing the report on the first anniversary of the attack would be a distraction from solemn memorials.

An extension, in any case, seems unlikely to make a tall order any more achievable.

World.title: Proposed cuts to SRL not counted towards total cost
World.content:
"Bells and whistles" cut from the Suburban Rail Loop never counted towards the cost of the $34.5 billion mega project, the responsible authority has revealed, calling into question Premier Ben Carroll's claim that he can cut the price tag.

Mr Carroll on Tuesday said he had identified $1 billion worth of savings from the first leg of the mega project, SRL East, slashing the cost from $34.5 billion to $33.3 billion. Two underground station interchanges and a multi-level car park would no longer go ahead, he said.

But the estimated total cost of the project never included the interchanges, a report by the Victorian Auditor-General's Office (VAGO) revealed on Wednesday. And not enough had been budgeted for the parking at Glen Waverley, the audit said in a warning of possible cost blowouts.

The Suburban Rail Loop Authority (SRLA) explained the items had not been counted towards the total cost because the government never agreed to building them.

"These items represent potential future scope options, not approved project costs," the SRLA told VAGO.

"It is standard practice on major infrastructure projects for optional or additional scope elements to be identified, assessed and considered separately from the approved scope until a final decision is made regarding their inclusion.

"Accordingly, no cost liability exists until government determines whether these items will proceed."

A government spokesman insisted the decision to avoid "unnecessary scope" would reduce the total estimated investment to $33.3 billion.

The government was hoping the cuts would slash the cost from $34.5 billion to $33.3 billion. (Supplied: Victoria's Big Build)

Government insists adequate contingencies in place

The report confirmed authorities had been preparing to abandon the possibility of building station interchanges at Glen Waverley and Box Hill for months, challenging Mr Carroll's claim the savings amounted to a "new direction" under his leadership.

Box Hill was not projected to be awash with extra commuters for decades, the SRLA told VAGO, and adding an interchange at Glen Waverley may not be value for money "given the advanced age and significant upgrade costs needed for the existing Metro station".

VAGO said the interchanges at Cheltenham, Glen Waverley and Box Hill stations would cost a total of $1.7 billion but that just $104 million had been included in the total estimated cost of the project. The Glen Waverley and Box Hill interchanges are not proceeding.

Latest estimates found the multi-level car park was likely to cost $137 million, but only $84 million had been included in the total estimated cost of the Suburban Rail Loop. Contracts for $7.5 million in design work had already been signed.

A map of the proposed suburban rail loop for the outer suburbs of Melbourne. (Supplied: Infrastructure Victoria)

Despite the announcement it will not proceed, VAGO said the car park was necessary to get approval through the environmental effects statement process.

Asked by the opposition about the supposed savings in question time on Wednesday, Public Transport Minister Vicki Ward said the government had used scrutiny to identify the savings.

Further details of cuts were commercial in confidence, Mr Carroll said on Tuesday. But the government hopes to find another $1 billion saving following a technical review.

The government has rejected VAGO's finding that the SRL East, which will connect Cheltenham to Box Hill, is unlikely to be delivered on time and on budget.

But the watchdog found the SRLA, which will be abolished under Mr Carroll's announcement this week, has already burned through a "significant portion" of the $9.5 billion set aside to deal with unforeseen risks. The government insists there are adequate contingencies.

Loading...

The Department of Treasury and Finance and Department of Premier and Cabinet have consistently warned the government that the state budget cannot fully fund the project "without limiting spending in other areas and missing fiscal targets", the audit said.

The report further revealed the state had added a secret tax onto public transport fares from January 2025 to help fund SRL East. The government disputes this, claiming the 1 per cent levy went towards all public transport, which is currently half price.

The levy will raise about $8 billion over 37 years to 2062. By 2062, a daily full fare of travel within zones 1 and 2 would be $12.10 more expensive as a result. It amounts to $1.60 extra a day by 2035.

The increase was hidden in annual fare hikes to account for inflation.

Daniel Bowen from the Public Transport Users Association said the government needed to be clear about the levy and why they have imposed it.

"To have this levy imposed on public transport fares for decades to come, but not telling people about it, I think that's not a great look," Mr Bowen told the ABC.

Treasurer Colin Brooks conceded on Wednesday that the government should have been more transparent.

Mr Carroll, who was in Sydney for national cabinet on Wednesday, said his government "levels with Victorians".

"When costs change, we'll tell you. When we find savings, we'll bank them," he said in a statement.

"I'm a premier taking the state in a new direction, and Victorians deserve to know what their money is buying. Under my leadership, they will."

The SRLA and Victorian government were contacted.

World.title: Nepal floods live updates: Dozens of Australians missing, at least 160 dead as devastating floods hit Rasuwa, Nuwakot regions
World.content:
The Australian embassy in Nepal said it was “deeply saddened” by the devastating flash flooding in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions of the country, where 34 Australians remain missing and 157 people are confirmed dead.

The embassy released a statement with the embassies of the United Kingdom, France, Finland, Norway and Switzerland.

A resident after the flash floods hit Devighat in Nepal. AFP

“Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time,” they said.

“We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”

World.content:
One Nation Senator Malcolm Roberts has given yet another interpretation of the party’s migration policy in an interview with an influencer associated with white supremacists, whose apparent membership of One Nation has prompted the Coalition to weaponise Pauline Hanson’s links to extremists.

Roberts also defended the right of the nation’s main neo-Nazi group, White Australia, to exist on free speech grounds. The remarks were made during an interview with Andre Mamet, who uses the online moniker “Ausmaxx”, posted to X on Tuesday.

One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts pictured with party colleagues Pauline Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and David Farley. Alex Ellinghausen

Mamet is a right-wing influencer who came to attention when he interviewed Hanson at a conservative conference in London in July – during the same week she met controversial far-right activist Tommy Robinson. The 19-year-old has 14,000 followers on Instagram, and 2300 on X.

This masthead subsequently reported that Mamet is closely associated with figures who attended Nazi training camps. He also enjoys sponsorship from a bookstore selling Adolf Hitler texts and was a paid-up member of One Nation.

One Nation did not deny Mamet was a member earlier this month. But last week, when questions were raised about Mamet condemning criminal charges against National Socialist Network leaders, One Nation claimed Mamet’s membership had lapsed.
