World.title: ASX set to dip as Wall Street drifts; Nvidia, Qantas results ahead
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip as Wall Street drifts; Nvidia, Qantas results ahead Stan Choe Updated August 27, 2026 — 6:35am ,first published 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market drifted through a quiet day of trading after a report said inflation was a touch worse last month than economists expected. Yields in the bond market, home to some of Wall Street’s biggest recent worries, edged higher following the data. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and remains near its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent. Wall Street is eagerly awaiting the latest numbers from Nvidia. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set for a flat start, with futures at 6.10am AEST pointing to a dip of 7 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Wednesday. Reporting season continues with Qantas and Wesfarmers among companies due up. Stocks made relatively few big moves ahead of the latest earnings report from the market’s most influential company, Nvidia, which arrived after trading ended for the day. Expectations were high once again for the chip giant, whose tremendous growth in profit because of the artificial-intelligence boom has made it the largest stock by value in the US market.



After soaring for years, AI stocks have become shakier on worries that their prices shot too high and that demand for chips may fizzle out if AI does not produce as much profit as hoped. Related Article Consulting Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract Strong profit growth across US companies broadly has been the main reason the US stock market has run to records this year. Abercrombie & Fitch leaped 35.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The retailer also raised its forecast for earnings over the full year and for how much cash it will send to investors by buying back shares of its own stock. J.M. Smucker climbed 4.3 per cent after likewise reporting sweeter results than expected for the spring. The seller of Folgers coffee and Smucker’s jams also raised its forecast for profit over the full year.



On the losing end of Wall Street was Intuit, even though the company behind TurboTax, Credit Karma and QuickBooks topped analysts’ profit expectations in the latest quarter. It fell 3.2 per cent after giving a forecast for profit growth of nearly 25 per cent in its upcoming fiscal year, which fell short of analysts’ expectations. Outside of earnings reports, Meta Platforms added 1.1 per cent after agreeing to pay up to $US18 billion ($24 billion) and to add child-safety measures to Facebook and Instagram to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by states across the country. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 1.58 to 7,675.70 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113.52 to 53,463.88, and the Nasdaq composite fell 21.10 to 26,130.20. In the bond market, which has been home recently to some of Wall Street’s strongest action, Treasury yields ticked higher following updates on inflation and economic growth. Yields had shot upward through the summer on worries about high inflation and the US government’s growing and gargantuan debt, among other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited.



The latest update on inflation released Wednesday said that the measure the Federal Reserve has historically preferred to use sat at 3.7 per cent last month. That was the same rate of inflation as in June and slightly worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected, according to FactSet. It remains far worse than the 2 per cent goal the Fed has set. Growth in spending by US consumers, which is the main engine of the economy, slowed at the same time. The overall economy grew at a 1.5 per cent annual pace in the spring, according to a revised estimate of its performance, the same amount as the government’s first estimate. It all helped Treasury yields squiggle up and down before the 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.65 per cent from 4.64 per cent late Tuesday. Traders didn’t change their forecasts much for what the Federal Reserve will do with its main interest rate in the short term, and they are betting on a nearly three-in-four chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at least once by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.



One of the factors that’s worsened inflation this year is higher oil prices, though they’ve come down recently. Related Article Updated

Supermarkets Woolworths doesn’t need Ooshies effect to beat Coles, says CEO The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, continued to swing Wednesday on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. It dropped as low as $US84.56 before settling at $US86.94. That’s down 0.4 per cent from the day before and from $US94 at the end of last week. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.6 per cent for two of the bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Be yourself but look like everyone else’: Imelda Staunton on younger people’s dilemma
World.content:
CultureMoviesFilm ‘Be yourself but look like everyone else’: Imelda Staunton on younger people’s dilemma Stephanie Bunbury August 27, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s such fun to be able to tell Imelda Staunton, who became famous as an actress quite late in life – when she was nearly 50 – that I first saw her on stage in 1986. She was playing the titular Fair Maid of the West in a revival by the Royal Shakespeare Company, with Sean Bean and Pete Postlethwaite as wingmen; her character was an innkeeper of enormous energy, storming back and forth on a bare stage, pint-sized but hugely funny. Like many Australian tourists, we had just bought tickets for whatever was playing in Stratford that night. “I don’t know who she is,” my companion said afterwards, “but she’s fantastic.” Staunton’s fantastic talent stopped being a niche discovery in 2004, when she was awarded a BAFTA for her central performance as a backstreet abortionist in Mike Leigh’s Vera Drake. The film itself won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, was then nominated for several awards, then was nominated for an Oscar. This, Staunton had never imagined. The film was rejected before it went to Venice by the Cannes festival, which convinced her that nobody would ever see it. Instead, she was scooted to a new level of celebrity. Imelda Staunton as the no-nonsense ex-wife to Bill Nighy’s drunken maestro in & Sons. Being Oscar-nominated opened the door to the world of Harry Potter, for which she was asked to play the repellent Dolores Umbridge, a sugar-frosted serpent of a woman always dressed in pink. So convincing was she in her malevolence, encapsulated by a high-pitched giggle that she made Umbridge’s catchphrase, that she became something of an internet hate figure. After which, of course, she played the Queen in The Crown. What she really admired in the Queen, she told Vogue in a long interview, was her commitment. “[She] was the last bastion of, ‘I’ve said I would do this’. That’s over now, that’s gone. Someone who would turn up, come rain or come shine … not in any way comparing, but if you agree to do eight shows a week, you do eight shows a week. I don’t care if you’re tired.” They were filming the series when Elizabeth II died; she was “inconsolable” with grief for the woman whose life she was inhabiting. Four years later, the real Elizabeth II and Staunton’s evocation of this uniquely Stoic figure have almost merged into one.



Like her late Majesty, Staunton always seems to be working. We are on Zoom to discuss & Sons, in which she plays the no-nonsense ex-wife Isabel to Bill Nighy’s drunken, dilapidated maestro of the modern novel, holed up in his stately pile with a pantry full of whisky and a mysteriously omnipresent Czech housekeeper, Gerde (Anna Geislerová). Living with him, yearning to be free, is his youngest son Andy (Noah Jupe), reputedly the result of an affair that dealt the death blow to his marriage. Staunton and Nighy as ex-spouses in the feature film & Sons. He and Isabel already had two sons – now about 30 and floundering in life – when she left him. Richard (Johnny Flynn) is a sometime-screenwriter with a history of substance abuse, while Jamie (George MacKay) is a would-be documentary maker who has picked Dad as his obvious subject. Both are guiltily aware of leeching off Dad for a leg-up. They would prefer to keep their distance, but Dyer gathers all three sons to bid them farewell, convinced that he is close to death. Isabel also attempts to distance herself from this performance, but the elderly sparring partners still have one fight left in them: a clash of firecracker intensity described by one critic as “two black-belts each at the top of their game”. The plot hinges on a bizarre reveal, but this is possibly less important than the film’s reflections on family, parenthood, fame and failure. Legacy and inheritance weigh heavily on the Dyer boys. “Well, of course, it’s the male ego,” Staunton says. “Let’s face it, it’s called & Sons. It would have been interesting if there’d been a daughter in there. “But it touches on wanting to live your life over again as a better person, the fact that someone wants to recreate themselves in someone else, rather than letting that someone else be themselves. I think that in today’s society, a lot of people want to be like other people. We’re told: ‘be yourself, but plump up your lips, get your cheeks stuffed and look the same as everyone else’. For young people, I think, the pressure to look a certain way is unbearable.”



Staunton, you feel, has never tried to look like anyone else. What for? She has five Olivier awards – the top awards in London theatre – to her credit. She has been married for more than 40 years to Jim Carter, who she met in 1982 when they were both cast in Guys and Dolls, their difference in height played for laughs. They were married the following year; the longest they have been apart was three weeks in 2008, when she was shooting Ang Lee’s Taking Woodstock in the US. They both vowed that wouldn’t happen again. “We take our life more seriously than our jobs,” she told Vogue. “Of course, we both take [the job] very seriously. But you go, what’s the most important thing here? That I play another part? Or that we go on a very nice holiday, or that we have that time in the garden?” Staunton as Queen Elizabeth II in the final season of The Crown. Netflix Their daughter, Bessie, is also an actor; she and her mother appeared together in a successful revival of George Bernard Shaw’s Mrs Warren’s Profession, playing mother and daughter. Clearly, the Carter-Staunton family hasn’t gone through the same mill of anxiety as the Dyers in & Sons, perhaps because they looked the issue squarely in the face. “It’s a difficult thing for the child of two actors to try and forge their own path,” Staunton says. “And we’ve talked about this, the three of us. When we did the play together, I sort of thought, ‘oh God, is this a good idea?’ And I still don’t know if it was. What I do know is that we had an amazing time doing it.” It is a plus, she says, that Bessie takes after her dad: she’s 175 centimetres tall. “I quite like that she looks nothing like me,” Staunton says. “She’s everything I could never be. And she’s got a bit of a producer’s hat – she’s very good at bringing people together – and she’s written a short film. So she does other things. I’m very glad she’s more of her own person than I thought she might be.” She just had to hold back from checking during rehearsals that Bessie had brought her lunch. “I thought: ‘No, back off Imelda. She can do her own lunch’. But doing the acting together was wonderful.”

World.title: Apple set to unveil foldable iPhone next month
World.content:
Apple will hold its biggest product introduction of the year on September 9 (US time), kicking off the tenure of new chief executive officer John Ternus.

The event will take place at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, and be livestreamed on its website, the company said on Wednesday (US time). The tagline for the gathering is “Surprise and shine,” according to invitations sent to media.

John Ternus faces a steep challenge in the new role, as the industry gears up for immense change spurred by artificial intelligence. Bloomberg

Apple is poised to unveil new versions of the products that account for most of its revenue. This September event will be especially critical, as the company will use it to introduce its first foldable iPhone, entering a market dominated by Samsung.

As the iconic iPhone nears the 20th anniversary of its introduction, the new foldable design marks the biggest single change to the product’s look. The device will be about the size of a standard passport, and it will open up to reveal a screen roughly the size of a small iPad.

World.title: Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet
World.content:
With Australian politics and media more fractured than ever, this long-running ABC series is serving up just what we need.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On February 22, 2012, in an upbeat double-act, then-Liberal frontbencher Christopher Pyne and former Howard government minister Amanda Vanstone teamed up as subjects on the first episode of Kitchen Cabinet. They were the game guinea pigs for an idea tailored to the skills of the host, Canberra press-gallery journalist and enthusiastic baker Annabel Crabb. Vanstone, recently returned from her ambassadorship in Rome, made tomato pasta; Pyne, a self-confessed clueless cook, barbecued a couple of steaks; Crabb provided a Persian love cake. And an enduring homegrown format was born. Related Article Australian TV Albanese and Taylor both said yes to Annabel Crabb, but one pollie is holding out “For as long as I’ve written about politics,” Crabb explained in the opener, “I’ve noticed that you can always get more out of people if you sit down to eat with them. Even the most disciplined politician will soften if there’s food and wine involved. The very best way to get to know someone is in their own kitchen.” Much has changed in the social and political climate and in the media between the initial, six-episode season and the recently concluded eighth series. In that time, Kitchen Cabinet has become one of the staples of the ABC’s light-entertainment line-up. Yet, from the start, there have been brickbats: that it’s soft and doesn’t pose tough questions; and that it’s a PR gift for the guests. One 2015 episode, in which then-social services minister Scott Morrison cooked a Sri Lankan curry but wasn’t grilled about his previous policies as immigration minister, drew notable heat. More recently, the critical chorus has included the complaint that the show is old, tired and past its use-by date. Scott Morrison on Kitchen Cabinet with Crabb in 2015, an episode which was heavily criticsed by some viewers. Yet, in these fractured and often-febrile times, we need what this show serves up more than ever. The perspective that it presents on our politicians is different from that available elsewhere. The charges that it’s soft overlook its attributes. And, importantly, it presents a view of politicians as people like us: with homes and families and formative experiences. As well as kitchens. Removed from the combat of political contest, separated from the soundbites and scripted press calls, the subjects are presented as human beings.



Maybe how they cook a curry is irrelevant to how they do their jobs, but having a fuller appreciation of who they are is beneficial. That’s a valuable perspective because the world is overloaded with ugly and dismaying examples of what happens when we fail to see those with whom we might disagree, or even actively oppose, as people rather than targets. And the accounts from politicians – especially women – attest to the vile threats and abuse that result from this mindset. Over the years, I’ve rarely seen an episode of Kitchen Cabinet that didn’t tell me something I didn’t know about its guest or portray the pollie serving the meal – some nervously, some smoothly assured – in an unexpected and illuminating light. Crabb and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese outside The Lodge in episode one of the new season of Kitchen Cabinet. ABC Perhaps, for some viewers, the generally convivial nature of the interactions masks their productive candour. The show set out to be conversational, not confrontational, and it was never intended to be 7.30, Insiders or, back in the day, Lateline or Q&A. It complements the news and current-affairs programs, it’s not endeavouring to duplicate them. Editor's pick Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s Beyond cheesy publicity stunts – think babies, hard-hats or high-vis vests – politicians are typically seen through a narrow lens: attack or defence positions, policy statements. Maybe how they cook a curry is irrelevant to how they do their jobs, but having a fuller appreciation of who they are, and why they do what they do, is beneficial.



In recent years, mistrust of political leaders and major parties has escalated; changes in media have allowed the audience more latitude to choose the type of information that they wish to receive amid an unceasing news cycle. As social media and streaming services have mushroomed, heritage media has haemorrhaged. Meanwhile, the rising popularity of podcasts has presented a new arena for politicians – although the recent “melongate” controversy demonstrates its potential pitfalls, even for a seasoned player like the Prime Minister. Albanese and Nikki Osborne on the controversial Bush Deep podcast that aired in July. Bush Deep Podcast It’s understandable that pollies and their minders might view some of these newer options as attractive, a way to reach those who no longer bother with broadcast networks and ideally, to connect with younger voters. But it’s also a niche audience and arguably one that has the participants preaching to the choir, while Kitchen Cabinet, screening in primetime on the national public broadcaster and then freely available on ABC iview, offers broader possibilities. It’s no cakewalk though, and charges that the show goes soft on its subjects can be unfair. The atmosphere isn’t antagonistic – although it can get tense – and probing questions are posed. This season, for example, Crabb quizzes Opposition Leader Angus Taylor about his statements on Insiders about “taking people from bad countries”. “Be very careful with this,” he cautions, clearly tensing up. “I am being,” she responds. “Long interview, full of context.” The exchange is framed in strained smiles, but the sensitivity of the subject flashes like a warning light. Crabb with Angus Taylor at his family farm outside Goulburn in the new season of Kitchen Cabinet. Jewish Labor MP Josh Burns is asked how he and his partner, Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell, navigate their relationship given their differing views on the Middle East. Nationals deputy leader Darren Chester is asked how voters can differentiate between his party and Pauline Hanson’s when its former leader, Barnaby Joyce, defected to One Nation.



After she identifies the way in which Muslims are often simplistically regarded as a homogeneous group, Greens deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi is asked, “When you hear commentary about how Muslim people think or what their characteristics are as a group in the parliament, what does that feel like as a workplace?” Faruqi describes how she’s marginalised and how her religion is denigrated by colleagues: “In which other workplace would even a skerrick of this be tolerated?” she asks, radiating anger and pain. Crabb and deputy Greens leader Mehreen Faruqi on Kitchen Cabinet. ABC Beyond the dialogue, there are also the insights that come from seeing someone on their home turf. I still remember the 2013 episode with Labor MP Jenny Macklin and her meticulously arranged, readily accessible spice drawer, a clear indication of a person who organises things efficiently. The same year, SA independent senator Nick Xenophon prepared taramasalata and tzatziki in his office kitchen before taking Crabb to a local Greek cafe, where he grilled octopus. Explaining his failure to invite her to his home, he said that he lives alone and his house is “pretty messy”. So we saw a man married to his work, keen to for the opportunity to explain it and endeavouring to contort himself into the requirements of the format. Crabb and Ricky Muir in 2015. The 2015 episode with Victorian senator Ricky Muir, from the micro Australian Motoring Enthusiast Party, had him cooking trout and vegetables over a campfire in front of a bush cabin near his home and speaking with more common sense than much of his portrayal in the media had allowed. That the show offers these glimpses, creating impressions that become indelible, is a notable asset. Part of its value for me has been that I’ve regularly come away from an episode with a grudging respect for someone about whom I’d previously had only unkind thoughts.

World.content:

A great movie never gets old. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Binge right now. Don’t have Binge? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+. Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy (2004) The stupidity is glorious and unchecked in this Will Ferrell comedy, where he plays a pompous 1970s newsreader who has an identity crisis when he falls in love with Christina Applegate’s capable new co-anchor. Will Ferrell as Ron Burgandy in Anchorman. Anora (2024) Filmmaker Sean Baker brought his sharp, sardonic feel for the marginalised into the mainstream with this Academy Award best picture winner about a Brooklyn stripper (Mikey Madison) who marries the wayward son of an unimpressed Russian oligarch.



Babe (1995) Fantastical, storybook sweet and a plea for kindness, this now beloved Australian family film celebrates an upstart piglet who yearns to do the farm work of a sheepdog. It’s a winning tale, tinged by a smidge of unavoidable reality. Babe. Back to the Future (1985) One of the great enduring Hollywood pleasures, this witty, inclusive science-fiction comedy stars Michael J. Fox as the teen who finds himself in the past, upending his parents’ courtship. Inventive, funny and family-friendly. Wendi McLendon-Covey, Rose Byrne, Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy, Maya Rudolph and Ellie Kemper In Bridesmaids. Bridesmaids (2011)



Starting with co-writer Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy and Rose Byrne, this showcase of comic actresses delivers an unhinged but also insightful exploration of female friendship as preparations for a wedding run amok. Casino (1995) Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci reunited for this real-life mob saga about the Mafia associates – plus a scintillating Sharon Stone – who spin out of control when given the run of Las Vegas. Sumptuous, bloody filmmaking. Cate Blanchett in Elizabeth. Elizabeth (1998) In her international breakthrough, Cate Blanchett is a translucent centrepiece who must sacrifice her own desires to survive a murderous 16th-century campaign to reach and retain England’s contested throne. Power is depicted with elegant brutality. Gallipoli (1981)



Starring an impossibly young Mel Gibson and Mark Lee as athletic rivals turned World War I comrades, Peter Weir’s compelling war film reveals how the horrors of trench warfare helped form Australia’s national identity. Gladiator (2000) Ridley Scott updated the swords-and-sandals genre from the 1950s to the age of computer-generated imagery, with a defiant Russell Crowe as the fallen Roman general seeking vengeance on his imperial foes by fighting his way to Colosseum glory. Russell Crowe as Maximus in Gladiator. Reuters Hanna (2011) As much a maximal action invocation as a twisted European fairytale, Joe Wright’s coming-of-age thriller stars a teenage Saoirse Ronan as an avenging innocent sent by her fugitive father (Eric Bana) to kill his CIA adversary (Cate Blanchett). In the Name of the Father (1993)



Still fiercely contentious on both sides, this biographical drama is nonetheless one of Daniel Day Lewis’ defining roles, playing a young Northern Irish man falsely convicted by the British government for a terrorist attack. It’s Complicated (2009) Nancy Meyers gracefully aged the romantic comedy into fifty-something abandon, with a masterful Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin as the divorced parents who have an unexpected affair. Steve Martin, and perfect decor, complete the equation. Florence Pugh, Saoirse Ronan and Emma Watson in Little Women. AP Little Women (2019) Greta Gerwig’s resonant, restructured take on an American literary standard, brought to life by an outrageously stacked ensemble cast, is a deeply felt portrait of 19th-century dilemmas and decisions for a quartet of sisters. World.title: This transport hub could hold the key to Melbourne’s megacity future
World.content:
Use the interactive map to see how many more people could live in your suburb by 2101 as we explore the idea of redirecting the booming population to urban transport hubs and regional towns.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Victoria’s population grows by about one person every four minutes and 40 seconds. Factoring in births, deaths, international and interstate migration, and the fact most of these people will live in Melbourne, Victoria’s capital is well on the way to becoming a megacity of more than 10 million people by 2101. To put that in perspective, in the lifetime of a baby born today, Melbourne would need to absorb the population of two Perths. It’s a confronting reality that puts us on a course matching the likes of New York, Moscow and Shanghai, as about 2000 newcomers make Melbourne their home every week. If Melbourne continues to allow the city’s footprint to expand, Wallan, Whittlesea, Cranbourne South, Sunbury and Eynesbury would see the biggest population boost by 2101. However, if we focus growth into established areas, some heritage streetscapes in the city’s inner east will be lost and industrial land around our port, in West Melbourne and Port Melbourne, would have to be transformed into residential hubs.



Population and housing projections from Johnny Barnard, founder of the National Forecasting Program at demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (.id), and commissioned by The Age, show the areas of metropolitan Melbourne that would see the biggest population increases. Use the interactive map above to see how your suburb could change. This week, The Age has explored the dilemma that housing almost 5 million extra residents, in 2 million more dwellings, would create for the city. In October, The Age and the University of Melbourne will host Melbourne Assembly, a three-day forum bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. However we choose to grow Melbourne, a city with a growth rate higher than that of most developed countries, poses challenges for all levels of government and the city’s residents. Today we ask: Are there alternatives to the way we are handling the growth? Can we do better, and if so, how? Megacity blues More than seven in 10 Australians live in six state capitals, a phenomenon influenced by the country’s colonial history and the “top-down” establishment of port-dominated settlements that once reported back to imperial London.



European fear of our vast desert interior further marked the coastal capitals as the places to be. In that sense, the evolution of our cities has been less organic than in many other countries. Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne Assembly These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million Melburnians do not have a direct say in the size and growth of their city. The federal government is responsible for immigration levels and neither it nor state governments have population policies that dictate how big our cities should be. Our cities are left to cope with the influx of people as best we can. While acknowledging the demands and challenges of rapid growth, most planners believe allowing Melburnians to dictate the overall size of the city, would give existing residents too much authority and future residents none.



“It’s not a good idea,” says Pat Fensham, Victorian president of the Planning Institute of Australia, pointing to the experience of New South Wales in 2000. Then-premier Bob Carr sought to slow the growth of his capital, bemoaning that his government could not keep up with the infrastructure needed to service a booming population. It was a call famously interpreted as Sydney being “full”. Planners back the development of major transport hubs such as Broadmeadows, where the population could rise by more than 50 per cent by 2101. Luis Enrique Ascui “Carr declared Sydney full soon after the 2000 Olympics and stalled infrastructure investment for a growing city,” says Fensham. “It has taken two decades of freeway and metro line building, et cetera, since he left to get close to catching up and addressing some of the damage done.” So, if we don’t pull up the drawbridge, what do we do? Back to the future of regionalisation Under the “populate or perish” ethos of post-WWII, Australians didn’t stress too much about where all the people would go.



We just kept adding detached single-level housing onto cities that spread into the vast Australian expanse. But by the 1960s, commentators such as Robin Boyd, author of The Great Australian Ugliness, were scathing of our sprawling suburbs, and politicians such as Gough Whitlam had grown concerned that services and infrastructure were not keeping up with our car-dependent frontiers. Whitlam’s alternative was to decentralise, proposing the Commonwealth proactively help build and service centres around the country – such as Albury/Wodonga on the Victorian, NSW border – as part of a wider push for regional planning and government. While Labor’s demise in 1975 put a dampener on decentralisation, the idea is regaining momentum amid growing concern about our capitals as megacities. “It once seemed far-fetched to decentralise, but it is arguably a better model than the megacity option,” says Dr Elizabeth Taylor, a senior lecturer in urban planning and design at Monash University. She stresses, however, that revisiting the idea requires big federal commitment, including to the long-elusive dream of fast rail linking eastern coast capitals and regional centres.

One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts pictured with party colleagues Pauline Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and David Farley. Alex Ellinghausen

World.title: ASX set to dip as Wall Street drifts; Nvidia, Qantas results ahead
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip as Wall Street drifts; Nvidia, Qantas results ahead Stan Choe Updated August 27, 2026 — 6:35am ,first published 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market drifted through a quiet day of trading after a report said inflation was a touch worse last month than economists expected. Yields in the bond market, home to some of Wall Street’s biggest recent worries, edged higher following the data. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and remains near its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent. Wall Street is eagerly awaiting the latest numbers from Nvidia. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set for a flat start, with futures at 6.10am AEST pointing to a dip of 7 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Wednesday. Reporting season continues with Qantas and Wesfarmers among companies due up. Stocks made relatively few big moves ahead of the latest earnings report from the market’s most influential company, Nvidia, which arrived after trading ended for the day. Expectations were high once again for the chip giant, whose tremendous growth in profit because of the artificial-intelligence boom has made it the largest stock by value in the US market.



After soaring for years, AI stocks have become shakier on worries that their prices shot too high and that demand for chips may fizzle out if AI does not produce as much profit as hoped. Related Article Consulting Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract Strong profit growth across US companies broadly has been the main reason the US stock market has run to records this year. Abercrombie & Fitch leaped 35.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The retailer also raised its forecast for earnings over the full year and for how much cash it will send to investors by buying back shares of its own stock. J.M. Smucker climbed 4.3 per cent after likewise reporting sweeter results than expected for the spring. The seller of Folgers coffee and Smucker’s jams also raised its forecast for profit over the full year.



On the losing end of Wall Street was Intuit, even though the company behind TurboTax, Credit Karma and QuickBooks topped analysts’ profit expectations in the latest quarter. It fell 3.2 per cent after giving a forecast for profit growth of nearly 25 per cent in its upcoming fiscal year, which fell short of analysts’ expectations. Outside of earnings reports, Meta Platforms added 1.1 per cent after agreeing to pay up to $US18 billion ($24 billion) and to add child-safety measures to Facebook and Instagram to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by states across the country. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 1.58 to 7,675.70 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113.52 to 53,463.88, and the Nasdaq composite fell 21.10 to 26,130.20. In the bond market, which has been home recently to some of Wall Street’s strongest action, Treasury yields ticked higher following updates on inflation and economic growth. Yields had shot upward through the summer on worries about high inflation and the US government’s growing and gargantuan debt, among other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited.



The latest update on inflation released Wednesday said that the measure the Federal Reserve has historically preferred to use sat at 3.7 per cent last month. That was the same rate of inflation as in June and slightly worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected, according to FactSet. It remains far worse than the 2 per cent goal the Fed has set. Growth in spending by US consumers, which is the main engine of the economy, slowed at the same time. The overall economy grew at a 1.5 per cent annual pace in the spring, according to a revised estimate of its performance, the same amount as the government’s first estimate. It all helped Treasury yields squiggle up and down before the 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.65 per cent from 4.64 per cent late Tuesday. Traders didn’t change their forecasts much for what the Federal Reserve will do with its main interest rate in the short term, and they are betting on a nearly three-in-four chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at least once by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.



One of the factors that’s worsened inflation this year is higher oil prices, though they’ve come down recently. Related Article Updated

Supermarkets Woolworths doesn’t need Ooshies effect to beat Coles, says CEO The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, continued to swing Wednesday on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. It dropped as low as $US84.56 before settling at $US86.94. That’s down 0.4 per cent from the day before and from $US94 at the end of last week. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.6 per cent for two of the bigger moves. World.title: ‘Be yourself but look like everyone else’: Imelda Staunton on younger people’s dilemma
World.content:
CultureMoviesFilm ‘Be yourself but look like everyone else’: Imelda Staunton on younger people’s dilemma Stephanie Bunbury August 27, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s such fun to be able to tell Imelda Staunton, who became famous as an actress quite late in life – when she was nearly 50 – that I first saw her on stage in 1986. She was playing the titular Fair Maid of the West in a revival by the Royal Shakespeare Company, with Sean Bean and Pete Postlethwaite as wingmen; her character was an innkeeper of enormous energy, storming back and forth on a bare stage, pint-sized but hugely funny. Like many Australian tourists, we had just bought tickets for whatever was playing in Stratford that night. “I don’t know who she is,” my companion said afterwards, “but she’s fantastic.” Staunton’s fantastic talent stopped being a niche discovery in 2004, when she was awarded a BAFTA for her central performance as a backstreet abortionist in Mike Leigh’s Vera Drake. The film itself won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, was then nominated for several awards, then was nominated for an Oscar. This, Staunton had never imagined. The film was rejected before it went to Venice by the Cannes festival, which convinced her that nobody would ever see it. Instead, she was scooted to a new level of celebrity. Imelda Staunton as the no-nonsense ex-wife to Bill Nighy’s drunken maestro in & Sons. Being Oscar-nominated opened the door to the world of Harry Potter, for which she was asked to play the repellent Dolores Umbridge, a sugar-frosted serpent of a woman always dressed in pink. So convincing was she in her malevolence, encapsulated by a high-pitched giggle that she made Umbridge’s catchphrase, that she became something of an internet hate figure. After which, of course, she played the Queen in The Crown. What she really admired in the Queen, she told Vogue in a long interview, was her commitment. “[She] was the last bastion of, ‘I’ve said I would do this’. That’s over now, that’s gone. Someone who would turn up, come rain or come shine … not in any way comparing, but if you agree to do eight shows a week, you do eight shows a week. I don’t care if you’re tired.” They were filming the series when Elizabeth II died; she was “inconsolable” with grief for the woman whose life she was inhabiting. Four years later, the real Elizabeth II and Staunton’s evocation of this uniquely Stoic figure have almost merged into one.



Like her late Majesty, Staunton always seems to be working. We are on Zoom to discuss & Sons, in which she plays the no-nonsense ex-wife Isabel to Bill Nighy’s drunken, dilapidated maestro of the modern novel, holed up in his stately pile with a pantry full of whisky and a mysteriously omnipresent Czech housekeeper, Gerde (Anna Geislerová). Living with him, yearning to be free, is his youngest son Andy (Noah Jupe), reputedly the result of an affair that dealt the death blow to his marriage. Staunton and Nighy as ex-spouses in the feature film & Sons. He and Isabel already had two sons – now about 30 and floundering in life – when she left him. Richard (Johnny Flynn) is a sometime-screenwriter with a history of substance abuse, while Jamie (George MacKay) is a would-be documentary maker who has picked Dad as his obvious subject. Both are guiltily aware of leeching off Dad for a leg-up. They would prefer to keep their distance, but Dyer gathers all three sons to bid them farewell, convinced that he is close to death. Isabel also attempts to distance herself from this performance, but the elderly sparring partners still have one fight left in them: a clash of firecracker intensity described by one critic as “two black-belts each at the top of their game”. The plot hinges on a bizarre reveal, but this is possibly less important than the film’s reflections on family, parenthood, fame and failure. Legacy and inheritance weigh heavily on the Dyer boys. “Well, of course, it’s the male ego,” Staunton says. “Let’s face it, it’s called & Sons. It would have been interesting if there’d been a daughter in there. “But it touches on wanting to live your life over again as a better person, the fact that someone wants to recreate themselves in someone else, rather than letting that someone else be themselves. I think that in today’s society, a lot of people want to be like other people. We’re told: ‘be yourself, but plump up your lips, get your cheeks stuffed and look the same as everyone else’. For young people, I think, the pressure to look a certain way is unbearable.”



Staunton, you feel, has never tried to look like anyone else. What for? She has five Olivier awards – the top awards in London theatre – to her credit. She has been married for more than 40 years to Jim Carter, who she met in 1982 when they were both cast in Guys and Dolls, their difference in height played for laughs. They were married the following year; the longest they have been apart was three weeks in 2008, when she was shooting Ang Lee’s Taking Woodstock in the US. They both vowed that wouldn’t happen again. “We take our life more seriously than our jobs,” she told Vogue. “Of course, we both take [the job] very seriously. But you go, what’s the most important thing here? That I play another part? Or that we go on a very nice holiday, or that we have that time in the garden?” Staunton as Queen Elizabeth II in the final season of The Crown. Netflix Their daughter, Bessie, is also an actor; she and her mother appeared together in a successful revival of George Bernard Shaw’s Mrs Warren’s Profession, playing mother and daughter. Clearly, the Carter-Staunton family hasn’t gone through the same mill of anxiety as the Dyers in & Sons, perhaps because they looked the issue squarely in the face. “It’s a difficult thing for the child of two actors to try and forge their own path,” Staunton says. “And we’ve talked about this, the three of us. When we did the play together, I sort of thought, ‘oh God, is this a good idea?’ And I still don’t know if it was. What I do know is that we had an amazing time doing it.” It is a plus, she says, that Bessie takes after her dad: she’s 175 centimetres tall. “I quite like that she looks nothing like me,” Staunton says. “She’s everything I could never be. And she’s got a bit of a producer’s hat – she’s very good at bringing people together – and she’s written a short film. So she does other things. I’m very glad she’s more of her own person than I thought she might be.” She just had to hold back from checking during rehearsals that Bessie had brought her lunch. “I thought: ‘No, back off Imelda. She can do her own lunch’. But doing the acting together was wonderful.”

World.title: Apple set to unveil foldable iPhone next month
World.content:
Apple will hold its biggest product introduction of the year on September 9 (US time), kicking off the tenure of new chief executive officer John Ternus.

The event will take place at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, and be livestreamed on its website, the company said on Wednesday (US time). The tagline for the gathering is “Surprise and shine,” according to invitations sent to media.

John Ternus faces a steep challenge in the new role, as the industry gears up for immense change spurred by artificial intelligence. Bloomberg

Apple is poised to unveil new versions of the products that account for most of its revenue. This September event will be especially critical, as the company will use it to introduce its first foldable iPhone, entering a market dominated by Samsung.

As the iconic iPhone nears the 20th anniversary of its introduction, the new foldable design marks the biggest single change to the product’s look. The device will be about the size of a standard passport, and it will open up to reveal a screen roughly the size of a small iPad.

World.title: Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet
World.content:
With Australian politics and media more fractured than ever, this long-running ABC series is serving up just what we need.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On February 22, 2012, in an upbeat double-act, then-Liberal frontbencher Christopher Pyne and former Howard government minister Amanda Vanstone teamed up as subjects on the first episode of Kitchen Cabinet. They were the game guinea pigs for an idea tailored to the skills of the host, Canberra press-gallery journalist and enthusiastic baker Annabel Crabb. Vanstone, recently returned from her ambassadorship in Rome, made tomato pasta; Pyne, a self-confessed clueless cook, barbecued a couple of steaks; Crabb provided a Persian love cake. And an enduring homegrown format was born. Related Article Australian TV Albanese and Taylor both said yes to Annabel Crabb, but one pollie is holding out “For as long as I’ve written about politics,” Crabb explained in the opener, “I’ve noticed that you can always get more out of people if you sit down to eat with them. Even the most disciplined politician will soften if there’s food and wine involved. The very best way to get to know someone is in their own kitchen.” Much has changed in the social and political climate and in the media between the initial, six-episode season and the recently concluded eighth series. In that time, Kitchen Cabinet has become one of the staples of the ABC’s light-entertainment line-up. Yet, from the start, there have been brickbats: that it’s soft and doesn’t pose tough questions; and that it’s a PR gift for the guests. One 2015 episode, in which then-social services minister Scott Morrison cooked a Sri Lankan curry but wasn’t grilled about his previous policies as immigration minister, drew notable heat. More recently, the critical chorus has included the complaint that the show is old, tired and past its use-by date. Scott Morrison on Kitchen Cabinet with Crabb in 2015, an episode which was heavily criticsed by some viewers. Yet, in these fractured and often-febrile times, we need what this show serves up more than ever. The perspective that it presents on our politicians is different from that available elsewhere. The charges that it’s soft overlook its attributes. And, importantly, it presents a view of politicians as people like us: with homes and families and formative experiences. As well as kitchens. Removed from the combat of political contest, separated from the soundbites and scripted press calls, the subjects are presented as human beings.



Maybe how they cook a curry is irrelevant to how they do their jobs, but having a fuller appreciation of who they are is beneficial. That’s a valuable perspective because the world is overloaded with ugly and dismaying examples of what happens when we fail to see those with whom we might disagree, or even actively oppose, as people rather than targets. And the accounts from politicians – especially women – attest to the vile threats and abuse that result from this mindset. Over the years, I’ve rarely seen an episode of Kitchen Cabinet that didn’t tell me something I didn’t know about its guest or portray the pollie serving the meal – some nervously, some smoothly assured – in an unexpected and illuminating light. Crabb and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese outside The Lodge in episode one of the new season of Kitchen Cabinet. ABC Perhaps, for some viewers, the generally convivial nature of the interactions masks their productive candour. The show set out to be conversational, not confrontational, and it was never intended to be 7.30, Insiders or, back in the day, Lateline or Q&A. It complements the news and current-affairs programs, it’s not endeavouring to duplicate them. Editor's pick Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s Beyond cheesy publicity stunts – think babies, hard-hats or high-vis vests – politicians are typically seen through a narrow lens: attack or defence positions, policy statements. Maybe how they cook a curry is irrelevant to how they do their jobs, but having a fuller appreciation of who they are, and why they do what they do, is beneficial.



In recent years, mistrust of political leaders and major parties has escalated; changes in media have allowed the audience more latitude to choose the type of information that they wish to receive amid an unceasing news cycle. As social media and streaming services have mushroomed, heritage media has haemorrhaged. Meanwhile, the rising popularity of podcasts has presented a new arena for politicians – although the recent “melongate” controversy demonstrates its potential pitfalls, even for a seasoned player like the Prime Minister. Albanese and Nikki Osborne on the controversial Bush Deep podcast that aired in July. Bush Deep Podcast It’s understandable that pollies and their minders might view some of these newer options as attractive, a way to reach those who no longer bother with broadcast networks and ideally, to connect with younger voters. But it’s also a niche audience and arguably one that has the participants preaching to the choir, while Kitchen Cabinet, screening in primetime on the national public broadcaster and then freely available on ABC iview, offers broader possibilities. It’s no cakewalk though, and charges that the show goes soft on its subjects can be unfair. The atmosphere isn’t antagonistic – although it can get tense – and probing questions are posed. This season, for example, Crabb quizzes Opposition Leader Angus Taylor about his statements on Insiders about “taking people from bad countries”. “Be very careful with this,” he cautions, clearly tensing up. “I am being,” she responds. “Long interview, full of context.” The exchange is framed in strained smiles, but the sensitivity of the subject flashes like a warning light. Crabb with Angus Taylor at his family farm outside Goulburn in the new season of Kitchen Cabinet. Jewish Labor MP Josh Burns is asked how he and his partner, Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell, navigate their relationship given their differing views on the Middle East. Nationals deputy leader Darren Chester is asked how voters can differentiate between his party and Pauline Hanson’s when its former leader, Barnaby Joyce, defected to One Nation.



After she identifies the way in which Muslims are often simplistically regarded as a homogeneous group, Greens deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi is asked, “When you hear commentary about how Muslim people think or what their characteristics are as a group in the parliament, what does that feel like as a workplace?” Faruqi describes how she’s marginalised and how her religion is denigrated by colleagues: “In which other workplace would even a skerrick of this be tolerated?” she asks, radiating anger and pain. Crabb and deputy Greens leader Mehreen Faruqi on Kitchen Cabinet. ABC Beyond the dialogue, there are also the insights that come from seeing someone on their home turf. I still remember the 2013 episode with Labor MP Jenny Macklin and her meticulously arranged, readily accessible spice drawer, a clear indication of a person who organises things efficiently. The same year, SA independent senator Nick Xenophon prepared taramasalata and tzatziki in his office kitchen before taking Crabb to a local Greek cafe, where he grilled octopus. Explaining his failure to invite her to his home, he said that he lives alone and his house is “pretty messy”. So we saw a man married to his work, keen to for the opportunity to explain it and endeavouring to contort himself into the requirements of the format. Crabb and Ricky Muir in 2015. The 2015 episode with Victorian senator Ricky Muir, from the micro Australian Motoring Enthusiast Party, had him cooking trout and vegetables over a campfire in front of a bush cabin near his home and speaking with more common sense than much of his portrayal in the media had allowed. That the show offers these glimpses, creating impressions that become indelible, is a notable asset. Part of its value for me has been that I’ve regularly come away from an episode with a grudging respect for someone about whom I’d previously had only unkind thoughts.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A great movie never gets old. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Binge right now. Don’t have Binge? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+. Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy (2004) The stupidity is glorious and unchecked in this Will Ferrell comedy, where he plays a pompous 1970s newsreader who has an identity crisis when he falls in love with Christina Applegate’s capable new co-anchor. Will Ferrell as Ron Burgandy in Anchorman. Anora (2024) Filmmaker Sean Baker brought his sharp, sardonic feel for the marginalised into the mainstream with this Academy Award best picture winner about a Brooklyn stripper (Mikey Madison) who marries the wayward son of an unimpressed Russian oligarch.



Babe (1995) Fantastical, storybook sweet and a plea for kindness, this now beloved Australian family film celebrates an upstart piglet who yearns to do the farm work of a sheepdog. It’s a winning tale, tinged by a smidge of unavoidable reality. Babe. Back to the Future (1985) One of the great enduring Hollywood pleasures, this witty, inclusive science-fiction comedy stars Michael J. Fox as the teen who finds himself in the past, upending his parents’ courtship. Inventive, funny and family-friendly. Wendi McLendon-Covey, Rose Byrne, Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy, Maya Rudolph and Ellie Kemper In Bridesmaids. Bridesmaids (2011)



Starting with co-writer Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy and Rose Byrne, this showcase of comic actresses delivers an unhinged but also insightful exploration of female friendship as preparations for a wedding run amok. Casino (1995) Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci reunited for this real-life mob saga about the Mafia associates – plus a scintillating Sharon Stone – who spin out of control when given the run of Las Vegas. Sumptuous, bloody filmmaking. Cate Blanchett in Elizabeth. Elizabeth (1998) In her international breakthrough, Cate Blanchett is a translucent centrepiece who must sacrifice her own desires to survive a murderous 16th-century campaign to reach and retain England’s contested throne. Power is depicted with elegant brutality. Gallipoli (1981)



Starring an impossibly young Mel Gibson and Mark Lee as athletic rivals turned World War I comrades, Peter Weir’s compelling war film reveals how the horrors of trench warfare helped form Australia’s national identity. Gladiator (2000) Ridley Scott updated the swords-and-sandals genre from the 1950s to the age of computer-generated imagery, with a defiant Russell Crowe as the fallen Roman general seeking vengeance on his imperial foes by fighting his way to Colosseum glory. Russell Crowe as Maximus in Gladiator. Reuters Hanna (2011) As much a maximal action invocation as a twisted European fairytale, Joe Wright’s coming-of-age thriller stars a teenage Saoirse Ronan as an avenging innocent sent by her fugitive father (Eric Bana) to kill his CIA adversary (Cate Blanchett). In the Name of the Father (1993)



Still fiercely contentious on both sides, this biographical drama is nonetheless one of Daniel Day Lewis’ defining roles, playing a young Northern Irish man falsely convicted by the British government for a terrorist attack. It’s Complicated (2009) Nancy Meyers gracefully aged the romantic comedy into fifty-something abandon, with a masterful Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin as the divorced parents who have an unexpected affair. Steve Martin, and perfect decor, complete the equation. Florence Pugh, Saoirse Ronan and Emma Watson in Little Women. AP Little Women (2019) Greta Gerwig’s resonant, restructured take on an American literary standard, brought to life by an outrageously stacked ensemble cast, is a deeply felt portrait of 19th-century dilemmas and decisions for a quartet of sisters. Lurker (2025)

World.title: This transport hub could hold the key to Melbourne’s megacity future
World.content:
Use the interactive map to see how many more people could live in your suburb by 2101 as we explore the idea of redirecting the booming population to urban transport hubs and regional towns.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Victoria’s population grows by about one person every four minutes and 40 seconds. Factoring in births, deaths, international and interstate migration, and the fact most of these people will live in Melbourne, Victoria’s capital is well on the way to becoming a megacity of more than 10 million people by 2101. To put that in perspective, in the lifetime of a baby born today, Melbourne would need to absorb the population of two Perths. It’s a confronting reality that puts us on a course matching the likes of New York, Moscow and Shanghai, as about 2000 newcomers make Melbourne their home every week. If Melbourne continues to allow the city’s footprint to expand, Wallan, Whittlesea, Cranbourne South, Sunbury and Eynesbury would see the biggest population boost by 2101. However, if we focus growth into established areas, some heritage streetscapes in the city’s inner east will be lost and industrial land around our port, in West Melbourne and Port Melbourne, would have to be transformed into residential hubs.



Population and housing projections from Johnny Barnard, founder of the National Forecasting Program at demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (.id), and commissioned by The Age, show the areas of metropolitan Melbourne that would see the biggest population increases. Use the interactive map above to see how your suburb could change. This week, The Age has explored the dilemma that housing almost 5 million extra residents, in 2 million more dwellings, would create for the city. In October, The Age and the University of Melbourne will host Melbourne Assembly, a three-day forum bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. However we choose to grow Melbourne, a city with a growth rate higher than that of most developed countries, poses challenges for all levels of government and the city’s residents. Today we ask: Are there alternatives to the way we are handling the growth? Can we do better, and if so, how? Megacity blues More than seven in 10 Australians live in six state capitals, a phenomenon influenced by the country’s colonial history and the “top-down” establishment of port-dominated settlements that once reported back to imperial London.



European fear of our vast desert interior further marked the coastal capitals as the places to be. In that sense, the evolution of our cities has been less organic than in many other countries. Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne Assembly These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million Melburnians do not have a direct say in the size and growth of their city. The federal government is responsible for immigration levels and neither it nor state governments have population policies that dictate how big our cities should be. Our cities are left to cope with the influx of people as best we can. While acknowledging the demands and challenges of rapid growth, most planners believe allowing Melburnians to dictate the overall size of the city, would give existing residents too much authority and future residents none.



“It’s not a good idea,” says Pat Fensham, Victorian president of the Planning Institute of Australia, pointing to the experience of New South Wales in 2000. Then-premier Bob Carr sought to slow the growth of his capital, bemoaning that his government could not keep up with the infrastructure needed to service a booming population. It was a call famously interpreted as Sydney being “full”. Planners back the development of major transport hubs such as Broadmeadows, where the population could rise by more than 50 per cent by 2101. Luis Enrique Ascui “Carr declared Sydney full soon after the 2000 Olympics and stalled infrastructure investment for a growing city,” says Fensham. “It has taken two decades of freeway and metro line building, et cetera, since he left to get close to catching up and addressing some of the damage done.” So, if we don’t pull up the drawbridge, what do we do? Back to the future of regionalisation Under the “populate or perish” ethos of post-WWII, Australians didn’t stress too much about where all the people would go.



We just kept adding detached single-level housing onto cities that spread into the vast Australian expanse. But by the 1960s, commentators such as Robin Boyd, author of The Great Australian Ugliness, were scathing of our sprawling suburbs, and politicians such as Gough Whitlam had grown concerned that services and infrastructure were not keeping up with our car-dependent frontiers. Whitlam’s alternative was to decentralise, proposing the Commonwealth proactively help build and service centres around the country – such as Albury/Wodonga on the Victorian, NSW border – as part of a wider push for regional planning and government. While Labor’s demise in 1975 put a dampener on decentralisation, the idea is regaining momentum amid growing concern about our capitals as megacities. “It once seemed far-fetched to decentralise, but it is arguably a better model than the megacity option,” says Dr Elizabeth Taylor, a senior lecturer in urban planning and design at Monash University. She stresses, however, that revisiting the idea requires big federal commitment, including to the long-elusive dream of fast rail linking eastern coast capitals and regional centres.

World.title: 'Something went seriously wrong': Answers on Moa Point to be released next week
World.content:
Calls for more transparency around Moa Point sewage disaster Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The local government minister says findings from a crucial investigation into the Moa Point disaster will be released to the public next week.

About 14 billion litres of raw sewage has spilled into the city's south coast since the plant catastrophically failed and flooded on 4 February, nearly seven months ago.

Power was shut off at the plant for months, raw, screened sewage has been pumped close to the shore at Tarakena Bay in heavy rain, and businesses in the area say they have lost thousands due to the loss of foot traffic, surfing and diving.

Local government minister Simon Watts confirmed late on Wednesday that the final report from a Crown Review Team investigating the disaster was on his desk.

He said he would carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations, before releasing it next week.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little said he expected the final report to be critical of Wellington City Council - but would not provide further detail.

"It's not surprising there will be adverse findings," he said.

"Something went seriously wrong at Moa Point sewage treatment plant, there will be criticisms - and we just now need to know what those are in the final version of the report, which I expect the minister will release in a matter of weeks."

He said the council had seen an interim report and provided feedback so it was factually accurate.

That interim report was expected to be released by July.

But Watts decided to withhold its release, citing advice from the Crown Review Team that doing so could prejudice legal investigations.

In that advice, released under the Official Information Act, Crown Review chair Raveen Jaduram advised Watts not to release the interim report, saying it contained potentially adverse findings and recommendations against Wellington City Council and Wellington Water.

"The Crown Review team believes providing these stakeholders (and potentially other related parties) further opportunities to respond to the interim report would be consistent with its terms of reference requirement to undertake its work in a manner consistent with natural justice."

Jaduram also said the interim findings could change before the final report, and might prejudice legal investigations.

Rongotai MP Julie Anne Genter said she was very pleased the final report will be released, and would be keen to read it - along with other Wellingtonians.

The community wanted accountability, she said.

"The public has repeatedly asked for there to be more transparency around this process and it's very frustrating six months after the disaster happened, that we still really don't have any clear answers."

Lyall Bay resident Tania Slater said her daily life had changed dramatically from the sewage spill.

"I was part of a swimming group...every morning we would go in rain, hail or shine, but yeah, only half the group goes in now, the really hardy ones, but some of us can't... for health reasons, I just can't be exposing myself to fecal matter."

Scott Hodgkinson was a kayak fisherman, but he had also stopped that. The couple were thinking of moving away from the suburb.

"I'm a kayak fisherman who can't fish out there anymore, I'm a surfer who doesn't surf out there anymore, We don't even walk on the beach anymore, Tania swims everyday, or used to, so...it's hideous," he said.

Both were calling for answers over how the failure occurred.

"Our rates are rising and our taxes are rising, so yes, we have a right to know what's happening...this is our home, we need to know what's going on," Slater said.

Wellington City Council has so far paid $116,684 for expenses for the four-member Crown Review Team, and Tiaki Wai has paid $222,812 for the review team's expenses and costs.

Tiaki Wai - which has taken over from Wellington Water - has told RNZ it is on track to fix the plant to the extent it will stop spewing raw sewage into the sea by February 2027.

World.title: Two dead, others injured in Far North crash
World.content:
Two people have died and others are injured following a multi-vehicle crash in the Far North.

In a statement, police said emergency services were called to Oruru Road near Jason Road in Peria at 8pm on Wednesday.

"Sadly, two people were located deceased at the scene.

"Two others were transported to hospital, one in a critical condition and one with serious injuries."

Police had closed the road while a Serious Crash Unit examination took place but has since reopened.

World.title: Man charged with human trafficking accused of deceiving staff recruited from overseas
World.content:
A man charged with human trafficking and migrant exploitation is accused of deceiving staff recruited from overseas by promising them they would be paid for all hours they worked.

One of the staff - who was recruited from India - is alleged to have been paid 36 hours per week despite working a minimum of 54 hours.

The man, listed as a company director, is also accused of failing to pay staff for working public holidays, inciting staff to breach conditions of work visas and altering employment agreements to reduce the pay rates.

RNZ earlier revealed a Christchurch man, who has interim name suppression, faced 35 charges under the Crimes Act and Immigration Act.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Immigration New Zealand (INZ) earlier confirmed the charges, which relate to 11 complainants, include allegations of "trafficking in persons and migrant exploitation".

Court documents seen by RNZ reveal the man, aged in his 50s, faces three charges of arranging, organising or procuring the recruitment of a person into New Zealand "knowing that recruitment involved one or more acts of deception".

Two of the complainants were from India, and the third from Saudi Arabia.

The court documents say the defendant recruited them knowing that the terms and conditions of their employment would be "materially different" from what was promised verbally and in their individual employment agreement "namely that all hours he worked would be paid by the employer".

The man also faces charges of supplying information to an immigration officer knowing that it was false or misleading, inciting or procuring people to breach the conditions of their work visas, and failing to pay minimum wage.

He also faces two charges of obtaining by deception by altering the original terms of an employment agreement to reduce pay rates.

One court document says that between November 2020 and June 2022 the man is accused of employing at least five people before their visas were approved.

INZ national manager of investigations Jason Perry earlier told RNZ the charges related to the alleged exploitation of 11 people.

"Trafficking in persons and migrant exploitation are serious offences that can have a significant impact on victims. INZ is committed to identifying, investigating and prosecuting this offending where there is sufficient evidence to do so."

Perry said the charges followed a "complex investigation" by INZ's immigration compliance and investigations team.

"As the matter is now before the courts, we are unable to make any further comment on the allegations, evidence, or the defendant at this time.

World.title: Starship Hospital defers less urgent cases to cope with 'flood' of kids with flu symptoms
World.content:
Starship Children's Hospital is deferring less urgent cases to cope with a "flood" of very young children in hospital with flu symptoms.

Doctors say the free under-fives flu vaccine announced for next year cannot come soon enough and will save lives.

University of Auckland professor of paediatric population health, Cass Byrnes, works as a respiratory specialist at Starship.

The hospital treated children from around the country but was having to put a temporary stop to some of them coming, she said.

That was because, firstly, there were not enough beds for everyone and, secondly, they did not want those children to catch flu in hospital.

There was no treatment for the virus itself but the children in hospital often needed support for serious symptoms, she said.

"Including supporting feeding, supporting with oxygen, or on occasion needing even more intensive respiratory support. It's... scary for the child and scary for the parents."

Children in this year's outbreak were quite commonly presenting with non-respiratory symptoms like headaches, digestive problems and very high fever, she said.

Byrnes said she could not be more relieved to see the vaccine funded for under-fives.

It would save lives - but it would also prevent some children from developing breathing conditions later - sometimes long after the flu had gone, she said.

It needed to come with a publicity campaign, because parents of the small group of under-fives who were currently entitled often did not realise, she said.

"And also starting [a campaign] early enough so people get a chance to have a think about or see the campaign two or three times in a row before thinking, 'Absolutely - I need to get along there and get a vaccination.'"

Currently children under five could get a free vaccine if they had previously been hospitalised with a respiratory disease or had another serious condition.

Pharmac estimated about 260,000 more children would be able to be vaccinated for free from April next year.

Official statistics showed children under five were far more likely to be hospitalised or end up in intensive care with flu-like symptoms than any other age group.

Very infectious strain

Porirua GP Dr Bryan Betty, former chair of General Practice NZ, said he was now "running a full-time respiratory clinic separating respiratory patients from non-respiratory", and requesting all patients who come in wear masks, following a "huge upswing in viral influenza A".

Dr Bryan Betty. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"It's very infectious. So, it's no more serious than normal flu, except it's the number of people who are going to get it is a lot larger - and it's a numbers game."

It was hitting Pasifika very hard, Betty said, adding that elderly, pregnant women and people with comorbidities such as diabetes and heart disease were also susceptible.

"If you haven't had a vaccination, it is still absolutely worthwhile going and getting the vaccination. This flu season is very late. We think it is going to run right through into spring. It is not too late to go and get a vaccination."

If you were already sick, stay home was his advice, if possible.

World.title: Weather: Highways closed as rain and snow trigger warnings
World.content:
Severe weather conditions have forced the closure of some highways in the South Island, with motorists urged to reconsider travel.

State Highway 73 was closed between Springfield and Otira because of snow, with rockfalls also reported in the area.

SH94 from Te Anau to Milford Sound remained closed because of the avalanche risk.

Area warnings were in place for flooding on State Highway 6 from Makarora to Fox Glacier and from Lake Wahapo to Harihari on the West Coast.

Looking east along State Highway 8 towards Burkes Pass township in the Mackenzie Basin. NZTA Waka Kotahi

MetService issued road snowfall warnings for the Crown Range Road, Milford Road and the Lewis, Lindis, Arthur's and Porters Passes.

"The winter storm slowly weakens as it moves onto central New Zealand, followed by showery westerlies across the South Island," MetService said in its severe weather outlook.

Heavy rain warnings were in place for Westland and the Canterbury lakes and rivers about and south of Arthur's Pass, while a heavy snowfall warning was issued for Canterbury High Country south of the Rangitata River, and Otago north of Arrowtown to Ranfurly.

MetService said the snow could cause damage to trees and powerlines, stress livestock and disrupt travel.

"If you do have to travel, maybe consider having a go bag in your car, just in case you get trapped," MetService meteorologist Braydon White told RNZ on Wednesday.

Police are urging caution to motorists, saying while there have been no serious crashes reported, there is heavy rainfall across the area.

"We want to remind the public to drive to the conditions."

Drivers are reminded to slow down, increase following distance, exercise patience and never drive impaired or distracted.

River flows in Canterbury were expected to remain high through to Friday.

World.title: Government can reverse growing number of children in poverty, retired paediatrician says
World.content:
Launch of manifesto to reduce child poverty Morning Report Download MP3 6m

A retired paediatrician says changes to government policy can reverse the growing number of children in poverty.

Child Poverty Action Group has released a manifesto calling for cross-party support to reduce the number of children living in material hardship.

The group's CEO Lyn Amos told Morning Report child poverty was a "political choice" and urged for all parties to make policy changes.

StatsNZ figures show the number of children in material hardship rose by 47,500 between 2022 and 2025.

The manifesto's lead author, emeritus professor Innes Asher said most political parties agreed in 2018 to halve the number of children in poverty by 2028, "instead it's gone up".

"They've been pulled down into material hardship at a very time that we had a pact in 2018, the Child Poverty Reduction Act, when we all agreed that it should be halved by 2028 to six percent, and it's gone up now to 14 percent."

That meant one in seven children were living in poverty, she said, but the impact was more pronounced for some groups, with one in four tamariki Māori, one in three Pacific children, and one in four disabled children living in material hardship.

The Child Poverty Action Group said poverty persisted because of failures in the labour market, housing, health and disability, education, welfare and tax settings.

It said these were down to political choices and all parties needed to be held accountable.

One in seven children are living in poverty, the manifesto says. Supplied/ Unsplash - Providence Doucet

The group's manifesto laid out "practical" policy changes it wanted all political parties to take up, Asher said.

The policy change that would bring the fastest and greatest change would be to replace Working For Families with one simple child tax credit that reached all children in low- and middle-income families, and didn't hinge on their parents' benefit status, she said.

The Court of Appeal found in 2013 that the current In Work Tax Credit discriminated against children of parents on benefits and caused material harm to families, she said.

"Yet there's been no government that's had the courage to change it. It doesn't require courage, it requires sense to change it."

The manifesto showed child poverty was estimated to cost New Zealand between $13.5 and $18 billion a year in avoidable demands on health, education, social support, and justice.

It said there was a reduction in child proverty rates between 2019 and 2022 - after the Child Poverty Reduction Act became law.

Asher said at the time there was a families package, the best start policy, and benefits were fully indexed.

"So those are the things that helped and those things have been taken away or reduced.

"We know that government policies have driven this child poverty crisis and therefore government policy changes can turn it round," she said.

"We're wanting cross-party support for this manifesto as a pathway for a better future for our country."

The manifesto said nearly 170,000 children were living in material hardship at June 2025, and more than 350,000 children were in financially insecure households.

'We can't afford not to do it'
