CPAG chief executive Lyn Amos told Morning Report the country had gone in the wrong direction when it came to reducing child poverty.

"Not well at all. The goal [in] 2028 is 6 percent living in material hardship, well we have been going in the wrong direction...we're absolutely going back wards"

She referenced decisions made in the 1991 budget which Amos said resulted in child poverty doubling.

"That's from state housing being sold off, benefits being slashed, wages being suppressed... so once again, we can use policy to, um, to find the solutions."

Amos said the group challenged all political parties to commit to the solutions outlined in the manifesto.

She said this also included actions such as raising minimum wage, building social housing, free GP visits up to the age of 18 and during pregnancy, increasing the child disability allowances and fees free early childhood education centres.

World.title: Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown disappointed with National's 'nonsense' reason to reject bed tax
World.content:
Mayor of Auckland on bed tax, city deal, rates cap Morning Report Download MP3 8m

With just 10 weeks until the general election, Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown says National is "panicking" it is going to lose the city's support - and making mistakes in the process

The government also blindsided councils this week with legislation to restrict rates rises to 4 percent a year.

Auckland Minister Simon Watts told RNZ on Wednesday the wording in the city deal would be changed and alternatives to a bed levy looked into.

Brown said he briefly met with Watts on Wednesday, but did not have a lot to say.

"I just said 6'good morning'. I mean, we have a beer together and he's not a bad guy and he's very uncomfortably pushing the company line from National at the moment," Brown told Morning Report on Thursday.

"I'll just wait until the election's over.. It's an election period and they're panicking, and so we'll wait till afterwards and see what happens.

"But at the moment it's a bit disappointing. The city deal was one of their slogans - it wasn't my idea, but I thought we'd have a go at it and we've honoured it and we'll continue to honour our side of it."

Brown said ruling out the accommodation levy would not help National's reelection chances.

"The public understand the bed night levy better than the National MPs do. It's not a tax. I mean, you don't pay it unless you get in a hotel. And the people of Auckland - which is the third of New Zealand - are already here."

Luxon said National did not want to put extra costs on Kiwis. Brown said this was "nonsense" as the 2.5 percent levy was "peanuts" and besides, accommodation providers doubled room rates when events were on.

"I'm not interested in an alternative. I mean, alternatives have to come from the taxpayer - and the taxpayers and the ratepayers are the same people, actually. I don't know if they've noticed that, but they are."

Brown said whoever was in government after 7 November, they would probably come back around to the idea.

"Why wouldn't you want to get on with a third of New Zealand? Particularly it's a third of New Zealand who decides. who the government is. This is where the elections are won and lost and I'm quite good at winning elections in Auckland. I won by 100,000 votes last time. I don't know if anyone noticed that."

Wayne Brown and Christopher Luxon. Supplied

Cap on taxes?

As for the rates cap, Brown said this year's rise in Auckland of nearly 8 percent was to pay for its share of the City Rail Link costs, and next year's was slated to be 3.5 percent, already below the 4 percent limit.

"They collect 10 times as much as tax as [councils] take as rates… Why don't you put a cap on taxes?"

World.title: Tonga-born All Black Saula Ma'u eager for more after dream debut
World.content:
Tonga-born All Black prop Saula Ma'u made his debut in the black jersey in South Africa on Wednesday morning (NZT) and says he is eager for more top international matches.

Ma'u was called up as an injury replacement last week, and took the field with 20 minutes to go at Ellis Park and helped the All Blacks come from 35-17 down to winning the match 41-35.

Emotional and fighting back tears post-match, Ma'u told reporters he was over the moon and would savour the "unreal" moment for life.

"I was talking to this guy before, like a couple weeks ago, I was back at home playing for Otago, and then two weeks later, I'm playing for the All Blacks," the Havelu village native from Tongatapu said.

"It just feels amazing, unreal, because obviously there was always a goal of mine to one day to play for the All Blacks.

"Just coming into camp last week, just feels crazy to be in that environment. The boys been making me feel welcome. The coaches just getting me up to speed, and yeah, it's a dream come true. And then obviously, I I want more of it."

Ma'u, born on 29 April 2000, left Tonga when he was 15 and enrolled at Auckland Grammar.

His pathway took him through Otago, where in 2021 he made the team for the National Provincial Championship (NPC), before a call up to the Highlanders in 2022.

He has been with the franchise since and was in the thick of things during the NPC over the last three weeks.

Last week, he jetted to South Africa to join the All Blacks on 'The Greatest Rivalry' tour as a replacement for fellow prop Ollie Norris.

On Wednesday morning, he came off the bench to make his debut, in front of vocal Lions fans at Ellis Park, stating his first taste of international rugby in the black jersey was a tough one.

"It was a bit hard, tougher compared to Super Rugby," Ma'u said.

"Just the speed, and obviously that's what Renz (Dave Rennie) is hard on, it's our work ethic, and yeah, just working hard."

Ma'u said the scrum contests were tough, and he watched the Lions push and dismantle the All Blacks scrums a few times from the bench, before getting his chance to lock horns with them when his turn came.

"Well, we're just trying to focus on us, what we're doing, with how we're prepping throughout the week,' he said.

"We're just training hard, working like many connections with hookers, back five, yeah. Scrum came good though. Came good at the end of the game.

"Credit to the to the back five and the work we did throughout the week, and obviously Jason (Jason Ryan) has been making us work hard in our scrums, like watching videos of the other team, making sure we're ready for what's coming on game day."

Officially All Blacks no 1242, said he just hoped he made his family and village proud before he broke down in tears.

"I just want to say thank to the Heavenly Father for the blessings he gave me to wear the black jersey," he said.

"Obviously my friends and families back home, my partner, Mum and Dad, and then yeah, just grateful for the coaching staff for the All Blacks for allowing me and giving me a chance to represent my family and my friends, and my village back home.

"Hopefully I have made them proud."

Ma'u formed a strong front row combination with fellow substitutes Bradley Slater and Xavier Numia as the All Blacks maintained a perfect record in South Africa tour.

Meanwhile, fellow Pasifika heritage players Emoni Narawa and Rieko Ioane scored a double each in the win against the Lions, while Noah Hotham got a try.

The match-day 23 also featured Tongan heritage player Richie Mounga making his return to the All Blacks since 2023.

The side was captained by veteran Blues captain and Samoan heritage player Patrick Tuipulotu.

World.title: De Minaur to head home for Davis Cup tie against Poland
World.content:
Australia's top men's singles player Alex de Minaur will come home to lead the nation's latest Davis Cup challenge in Brisbane next month.

Australia will play Poland at Pat Rafter Arena on September 19 and 20, days after de Minaur's run at the US Open at Flushing Meadows.

Australia, currently number eight in Davis Cup rankings and 28-time champions, will need to beat Poland in the World Group tie to advance to the Davis Cup qualifiers next year.

Davis Cup tennis returns to Brisbane The countries will face off in a 2026 World Group I tie at the Pat Rafter Arena on September 19 and 20.

"There is nothing quite like representing the green and gold and to do it at home makes it even more special," de Minaur said in a Tennis Australia statement.

"We know what's at stake against Poland and we will be going out there with one goal – to get the win and put ourselves back into the qualifiers.

"We love playing in front of the Aussie fans and we will be ready to fight for every point."

The rest of the team will be named soon.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Alex loves playing for Australia. Having him lead the team in Brisbane is a huge boost," Australian coach Lleyton Hewitt said.

"He has had some incredible Davis Cup performances for us over the years and I know how much it means to him to represent his country.

"We have got a tough tie ahead of us against Poland, but playing at home gives us a great opportunity."

The tie will be the second time the two nations have played each other in Davis Cup. Australia beat Poland 4-1 in Warsaw in 2013.

World.title: How Rosie Fordham leads the way in a race 'everybody comes out for'
World.content:
Even at the other end of a phone, Rosie Fordham gives the impression of someone containing an enormous amount of energy.

The 24-year-old, from New South Wales, has just finished waxing her skis when she speaks to ABC Sport, preparing the tools of her trade as Australia's leading cross-country skier.

Even that relatively mundane activity is described with an effusiveness that positively fizzes down the line.

We probably shouldn't be surprised.

Cross-country skiing is the ultimate full-body workout, maximising muscles in both upper and lower body and exacting a relentless aerobic demand on anyone who takes part.

It is, without question, a discipline that is among the most gruelling of all physical endeavours the human body can partake in.

Cross-country skiing is hard. (Getty Images: NCAA/Brett Wilhelm)

Add in generally inhospitable, sub-zero temperatures and exposed, high-altitude conditions and you've got yourself a challenge that is not for the faint of heart.

Anyone who competes at any level in this sport is supremely fit in a way that few can genuinely comprehend — and intensely self-motivated to succeed.

Fordham is the best cross-country skier Australia has ever produced.

Last year she became the first Australian to ever win a medal in an international cross-country skiing event, claiming silver in the 10-kilometre interval skating race at the FIS U23 World Ski Championships.

She has since claimed a number of top-20 finishes in the intensely competitive FIS World Cup, and achieved Australia's highest-ever finish at a Winter Olympics by finishing 29th in the 50km mass start event in Val di Fiemme.

"It's awesome to be a part of it," Fordham tells ABC Sport from the Australian ski fields.

"I think in previous years, or even when I started skiing … you just never really heard about cross-country skiing when I was a junior.

"We were definitely kind of left out of a lot of the coverage.

"But now, being able to back it up with good results so people can see that we are legitimate contenders in such gruelling and very traditional winter sports has been pretty cool."

Rosie Fordham says the good results Australian cross-country skiers are achieving is helping grow the sport. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

Australia's 2026 Winter Olympics was its most successful of all time, with Aussie athletes winning six medals in Milano-Cortina; three golds, two silvers and a bronze across freestyle skiing and snowboarding disciplines.

Olympic medallists Jakara Anthony, Cooper Woods, Josie Baff, Scotty James, Dani Scott and Matt Graham all earned their time in the limelight after such brilliant success in Livigno's alpine paradise.

And in the face of such sensational return, it might be easy to sniff at top-30 finishes elsewhere as not being deserving of praise.

But that is far from a fair stance to take.

Snow Australia president Daniel Bosco said he was "really proud" of what the Australians had achieved in both alpine and Nordic skiing events.

"The success we've had with the cross-country teams is outstanding; unheard of," he told ABC Sport in Livigno during those Games.

Rosie Fordham led the Australian cross-country ski team to a hugely impressive performance in Milano-Cortina. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"It's funny, I mean, the Australian public and most people who aren't connected to the sport probably look at a 29th place finish and think, 'Oh well, we're not that competitive.'

"But to me that is just such an awesome outcome.

"Let's go back 20 years and look at maybe freestyle and some of the other park and pipe disciplines that were just starting to develop. We probably felt we weren't that competitive back then in those sports either.

"But we dreamt big and we achieved. Who knows what's possible for these cross-country and alpine teams."

That admiration is shared by the higher-profile medal winners as well.

"You talk to people who are winning World Cups and things in aerials and moguls and they're like, 'Oh, you guys do this crazy thing', 'you're so fit' and 'it's awesome what you do,'" Fordham said.

"So, I guess, just hearing that and seeing that people seem to care a little bit more about endurance sports in general and winter sports has been pretty cool."

Kangaroo Hoppet

The Kangaroo Hoppet was run for the 32nd time. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

One of the most visible representations of the popularity of endurance sports on the Australian winter sport scene is the enduring appeal of the Kangaroo Hoppet.

The race's roots are in the establishment of the Birkenbeiner Nordic Ski Club in 1977 in Mount Beauty, Victoria, which began a 21km long-distance race around Falls Creek into the Bogong High Plains wilderness area.

In 1989, the club bid to join the Worldloppet global series of ski marathons by hosting a 42km version of the event, with the newly christened Kangaroo Hoppet becoming the first Southern Hemisphere event in the series in 1991.

Taking place annually on the third Saturday in August, the Kangaroo Hoppet showcases a huge range of abilities and, despite challenging snowfall conditions, this year's 32nd edition was completed with 730 skiers across three events.

In the men's race, Olympians Lars Young Vik and Seve De Campo tore off around the course, with Young Vik claiming victory for the first time, while Bentley Walker-Broose finished third.

Lars Young Vik claimed victory ahead of fellow Olympian Seve de Campo. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

Fordham claimed victory in the women's race for the second year in a row, ahead of Milano-Cortina Olympian Maddie Hooker and rising biathlon competitor Isabella Moon.

Just by competing through, Fordham was reminded how much support there was for the sport in Australia.

"It's a cool race," Fordham said of the Hoppet.

"The first time I did it was last year and I honestly didn't know that there was that many people who cared about cross-country skiing in Australia.

"Everybody comes out for the Hoppet. I've never seen that many people on skis in one place and it's pretty cool to get everybody on the course.

Rosie Fordham is two from two at the Kangaroo Hoppet. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

"Normally you do a two-lap course so you'll be passing and lapping people and they would know your name and cheer for you by name. This year we did a shortened course so we did four laps of a smaller course and these people are out there racing, they're skiing pretty hard and working really, really hard, and they are still cheering for the top-tier athletes, they know all our names.

"I think that it's easy to forget that there's a whole community back home that are actually watching the races and not just forgetting that we exist.

"When we're overseas, you don't usually hear from them or remember that people are really interested.

"It's cool to remember, I guess, that people do care back home and they are like quite invested in how we do.

"It's pretty awesome to just be a part of the community."

Interschools driving the next generation

Australia has long punched above its weight from a participation point of view in winter sport, even if that may come as a surprise to those who rarely venture to the alpine regions.

Australia is developing a core group of cross-country skiers. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling)

Snow Australia notes that 109 Australian Winter Olympians have passed through the interschools program, which now sees more than 7,000 high school students compete annually across a huge range of disciplines.

"It is so amazing to see that 31 members of the Milano Cortina Australian team have come from the interschools pathway," said Wendy Olsen, Snow Australia's national event coordinator.

"It inspires the new generation of snow-sport athletes, to see Olympians grow so far from the same position they are standing in today.

"It goes to show just how important these first competition experiences truly are."

Fordham is one of the Winter Olympians who found the sport through that experience. It turned the promising long-distance runner into one of the world's best long-distance skiers.

"I was downhill skiing as a kid and then found cross-country skiing through interschools at year eight," Fordham said.

"I like that it combines the endurance from running, but also the being in the mountains and skiing from downhill skiing. So it's kind of a perfect combo."

You never know where the next Olympic skier is going to come from. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

This year, Fordham was helping coach her former school and got another taste of how opportunity can strike for some young skiers.

"It's pretty awesome," Fordham says of the interschools.

"I think, without it, we definitely wouldn't have the interest in snow sports that we do in Australia.

"It's just an excuse to try everything. I was coaching my old school last week and one of the kids that does alpine skiing, he won the cross-country race in year six.

"I was like, 'Did you even know that you could win a cross-country race?' and he says, 'Oh, yeah, I guess I won.' That's just crazy.

"We find a lot of talent just by having them enter the race because they think, 'That's a bit of fun, I'll try it out.'

"It is a way to find people who love the sport and also people who are really good at it, just because they do it for fun with their friends, which I think is pretty amazing to have something like that."

Long-term goals for Utah

Rosie Fordham has her sights set on improving her Olympic performances. (Getty Images: VOIGT/Grega Valancic)

School is out for Fordham now though, the 2026/27 season representing the first year she will be a full-time athlete after she graduated from the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

It means heading to Lillehammer for a stint training with the Great Britain squad ahead of a full tilt at the World Cup season and World Championships in Falun, Sweden.

"It's quite exciting to be based in Europe for a bit … to be done with uni and not having to go back and forth between the US and Europe, racing and taking exams and all sorts, while racing for college as well.

"It'll be nice to focus fully on the World Cup and the World Championships."

Of course, the longer-term goals remain focused on Olympic Games, with Utah in 2034 a particularly intriguing one.

"In the women's side of the sport, the best are the ones that sort of stick around the longest," Fordham said.

"Just looking at the women's side and on the World Cup, usually there's some young athletes that can break through but most of the time it's the late 20s, early 30s that are really succeeding, just with a bigger base and that they've built more.

"I'm definitely looking forward to the next three years and then I would really like to race in Utah in seven years.

"That's actually really exciting for me because it's one of the places that I've had a lot of breakthrough races.

Rosie Fordham won two NCAA titles at the Utah Olympic course earlier this year. (Getty Images: NCAA/Brett Wilhelm)

"I had a fourth at US Nationals there, then my first college podium was there and then just this year I won two NCAA titles at that exact race course.

"That course has a special place in, like, my career, so I would love to make it that far.

"But in the short term, World Champs this year and then the next Olympic Games in France and just trying to build on fitness and technique and then make some gains to be able to push up from where I've been.

"I have the highest finish at World Cup, World Champs and Olympics of an Australian ever, but I don't see that as the ending. I'd like to be better than I was last year, and the year before.

"Even though I currently have the highest-placed results, I want to make them even higher."

World.title: Para swimming champion matched by her dog in gold medal winning feats
World.content:
It is not often a dog is as accomplished as its owner on the sporting stage, but Para swimmer Jenna Jones's Australian shepherd, Luna, is the exception.

"She's my best friend. Honestly, we have the same personality, which is scary sometimes," Jones told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

The duo competes in a sport called rally, where a handler and dog walk a course and are tested on obedience and agility. And like her owner, Luna is a gold medallist.

"It builds our bond together and we're in talks of ambassadorship [as a] runway model for Luna, except she's turning into a dog model," Jones said.

Loading Instagram content

Whatever sporting glory awaits Luna, Jones still holds the upper hand, recently securing gold in the women's 100 metre S13 freestyle at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, alongside bronze in the 50m freestyle.

It was her first major individual title, ten years after she made her international debut as a 15-year-old at the Rio Paralympics.

The Glasgow experience now has her hungry to taste more at this week's Para Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in California.

"That was such an incredible experience, something I guess people only dream of and still riding the high of that definitely," she said.

"And it definitely gives me so much confidence going into Pan Pacs.

"But the thing I think I'm looking forward to the most is, we have so many rookies on this team and I'm so excited to watch them all debut."

Jones will be one of the senior members of the team at this week's Para Pan Pacs in California.

Jones, originally from the Blue Mountains in NSW but now based on the Sunshine Coast, was diagnosed with a rare degenerative eye disease when she was in kindergarten.

"I'm so lucky that I got into sport at such a young age," she said.

"It taught me how to move my body and showed me how to trust my body, which has given me so much confidence in myself, in turn has given me so much independence in my life.

"Being in this swimming environment, I've met so many incredible people that will be my best friends for the rest of my life and it's opened me up to so many incredible opportunities like this.

"So I'm just so grateful for all of it and I love every second of it."

The 25-year-old is currently studying for a diploma at university and hopes to eventually complete a counselling degree.

As a two-time Paralympian and one of the senior members of the team, she admitted it can be tough juggling study and her sporting career.

But when she reflects on her younger self breaking records in her first national championships, there is an overwhelming sense of pride.

"I think as an athlete it's so common not to sit and smell the roses when you're in your career," she said.

"Thinking about little 13-year-old me breaking those records, she would be so proud of where I am today."

World.title: Nikita Tszyu says Ben Mahoney 'edged' thrilling Gold Coast draw
World.content:
Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

Incredibly, Tszyu said after the fight that he felt Mahoney edged it and should have been given the win.

"I gave the fight to Ben, honestly," Tszyu said in the ring.

"Maybe one or two rounds more, but I can't be a judge. It was a close fight, but I thought he edged it."

Moments later, Tszyu walked back those comments, saying he was emotional and over-critical at himself.

"I think it was just the emotions," Tszyu said.

"I saw myself stopping him. Not being able to get it, that was just a bit emotional for me.

"I'm a huge critic inside the ring to myself."

He did note that it was the toughest fight of his career: "What do you think?" he said when asked.

The judges scored the fight wildly differently, with Phillip Holiday awarding the fight to Tszyu, 117-111 Sabrina Kerr going the other way and scoring 113-115 to Mahoney, while Carl Zappia scored it a 114-114 draw.

"I don't want to talk down on Nikita and his team, but I do believe I won that fight," Mahoney said.

Ben Mahoney took the fight to Nikita Tszyu in the contest. (Supplied: Main Event)

Mahoney was lifted into the air by his team at the conclusion of the fight, clearly believing he had done enough, and stood on the corner waving at his home crowd before the decision was read out.

The fight was desperately even, with Mahoney more active, while Tszyu delivered more power punches.

Both men were marked after the fight, with Tszyu particularly bruised at the press conference.

Regardless of the result, the number five and number seven ranked super welterweights in the IBF both delivered a terrific performance in front of a thoroughly engaged crowd.

The prize for the winner was a chance to face British fighter Josh Kelly for the IBF world title.

A draw somewhat ends those plans for the moment and, with neither fighter seemingly keen to meet in a rematch, it appears the world title ambitions of both may have to wait.

On the undercard, Cal Peters delivered another sensational result, beating Blake Wells by eighth round stoppage to move to 9-0 and win the IBF Pan Pacific middleweight title.

Peters, a 2024 Olympian and silver medallist at the 2022 Commonwealth Games,

"Those country boys, they're just built different," Peters said.

"I was hitting him with some good shots to the head and he just wouldn't go down."

Kirra Ruston beat Saundre Simmons by first round TKO to move to 10-0, much to the disgust of the Bermudan fighter and his corner.

Koen Mazoudier also kept his hopes of meeting Jermall Charlo by beating Sam Beck by majority decision in a tense contest, while heavyweights Brandon Grach and Ike Pluto started the main card off in fine fashion, with Grach winning by split decision.

Follow all the action live from the Gold Coast Convention Centre.

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"If I didn't think the Giants would finish top-four next year, I wouldn't stay," Greene said.

"One thing I want to do with them is win a flag and that's the best thing I could do ever in footy.

"I could win two or three (premierships) somewhere else [but] it wouldn't be as good as one at the Giants."

Greene has played 282 games for GWS, including the club's first AFL game in 2012.

AAP

World.title: Time to 'recalibrate': Olympic figure skating champion Liu to miss season
World.content:
Olympic gold medallist figure skater Alysa Liu has said she will sit ​out the upcoming season to fine-tune her technique but reassured fans she would return to the sport.

Liu became ​the first ‌American woman since 2002 to capture Olympic gold in women's singles at this year's Milano ‌Cortina Games, where she also helped ⁠the United States to gold in ‌the team event.

"I ​always want to ‌challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote in a social media post, ​adding ‌that she would take time to "recalibrate".

Loading Instagram content

"It's important to me that my sport ⁠reflects my personal ‌growth.

"So fear not, I'll ‌be back, and in the meantime I'll be ‌rooting for my teammates near and far."

In an interview with ‌NBC ​Sports on Tuesday, ⁠Liu said she was planning to work on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything" during her break from competition and ⁠intended to return in the 2027-28 season.

Winter Olympics live blog Alysa Liu becomes the first American woman to win singles figure skating gold in 24 years, completing her comeback after retiring in 2022 when she was only 16 years old.

"I just felt this ‌was ‌right. So I'm trusting my ​instincts," she said.

The announcement marks the latest change in a roller-coaster career for Liu, who arrived at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics and finished sixth.

She won bronze at the world titles a few months later before "retiring" from the sport at the age of 16, saying that skating "takes up your whole life, almost".

When she returned to skating she had a new look, with bleached stripes in her hair and a frenulum piercing — and a new approach and confidence that saw her win the world title in 2025 before gold at Milano Cortina.

Liu said her new approach to her sport and to life was more important than results.

Now she leaves to dream it all up again.

Reuters / ABC

World.title: Hird has chance to finally deliver true unity Essendon seeks
World.content:
When new Essendon coach Mark McVeigh was flanked by president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts at his introductory press conference on Wednesday, there was a clear theme emanating from the day: unity.

Unity is the thing Essendon has strived for, and failed to find, for the last two decades as it has cycled through players, coaches and administrators in a bid to end an infamous finals drought.

Welsh hopes that by hiring McVeigh he is able to kill two birds with one stone.

McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite Mark McVeigh and Andrew Welsh are set to approach James Hird about a role at the club after he was overlooked to return as the senior coach for a second time.

The process to find its next coach acted as a litmus test for Essendon to actually show it had changed as a club after years of saying it with no actions to follow.

When Brad Scott was ousted midway through the season and James Hird launched his candidacy on national TV in the same week, the consensus was that Hird's return to the Bombers coaches box was a fait accompli.

The lack of belief or trust in Essendon as a sporting organisation left candidates pulling out, believing the club's trumpeted 'process' was actually a sham designed to deliver Hird the role.

It proved to be anything but, as Hird himself revealed after being beaten by McVeigh, leaving both he and Essendon at a potentially pivotal crossroads.

This rejected bid to be Essendon's coach is completely different to Hird's last rejection, when he finished second behind Brad Scott.

James Hird (centre) was left on the outside looking in when Brad Scott (left) won Essendon's coaching race in 2022. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire)

There was something symbolic in Hird, one of Essendon's favourite sons, being beaten out by Scott, a nemesis of his from the Brisbane Lions heyday.

Scott winning the coaching race was reminiscent another occasion where he'd famously got one over Hird, overpowering the under-cooked then-Essendon skipper on the wing during a key period in the 2001 grand final.

Scott, having arrived from the AFL and being selected by an independent panel, appeared a choice that was an aggressive attempt to get away from the fabric of Essendon.

Scott's regime brought a lot of change, and while his decisions may eventually age well, they left Essendon's diehards feeling more disillusioned with every loss that followed.

Andrew Welsh (left) and Mark McVeigh (right) are keen for Hird to return to the club in an official capacity. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Hird wasn't exactly forbidden from returning to Essendon while Scott was in charge, but he also wasn't welcomed with open arms.

This time around is different as both McVeigh and Welsh prepare to launch full-court presses to get Hird back through the doors, just not as the coach.

While the knock on Hird's coaching bid was his lack of experience in a recent AFL coaches box, what cannot be disputed is his knowledge of the game.

If Hird is able to get past the itch of being the coach, he could prove to be an incredible asset as either a football boss, or as a developmental coach. The opportunities are endless, given Essendon has basically wiped out its entire football department.

James Hird (left), Dean Solomon (centre) and Mark McVeigh (right) have the opportunity to link up under one roof again. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Having held the belief that McVeigh would have come with him had he been successful, as he also pledged to do in 2022, Hird now has the chance to repay the favour.

Welsh has hinted at Essendon bolstering its football department with key appointments in the coming months as it looks to surround McVeigh with a strong staff. It could do worse than bringing Hird back into the fold.

It is notable that Hird, while not receiving the job he wanted, mentioned he has experienced healing during the process in the form of mending fences with individuals he had fallen out with over the club's supplements scandal.

Hird is smart enough to know what his decision from this point on has the potential to do to his beloved club.

As Essendon desperately seeks unity, Hird's return would guarantee it, and he knows that. It is hard to see him turning his back on Essendon to try and coach elsewhere, even if that means he never gets to coach again.

At the front of Hird's mind will be two scenarios: winning Essendon's next premiership, but not as the coach, or winning a premiership elsewhere as the coach. He must figure out which of those will make him happiest.

The benefits of the McVeigh hire are two-fold for Essendon.

He has spent significant time in the coaches' boxes of two teams that have enjoyed deep September runs, albeit without winning the whole lot.

Loading Instagram content

McVeigh's history of working with both the Allies and the Swans Academy was a major selling point given Essendon's list demographic.

Critics suggesting McVeigh's hire was simply a case of jobs for mates were disrespectful to both his decade of coaching reps as well as Welsh's ability to be a professional.

Contrary to all the hysteria about Essendon only hiring "Essendon people", McVeigh is the first Essendon person to be hired as the club's senior coach since Hird's departure in 2015.

The coaches that have followed Hird — John Worsfold, Ben Rutten and Scott — have all enjoyed success at other clubs like McVeigh has, but lacked an ability to truly connect with the club and its fans.

That is McVeigh's superpower. He connects, and he connects with all generations.

It was not by accident that the club filmed McVeigh being greeted at The Hangar by Ken Fraser, the captain of Essendon's 1965 premiership side.

It was also not by accident that both McVeigh and Welsh continually referenced the goal for Essendon to be "one club", making a pointed note to invest in the club's AFLW program.

McVeigh even appeared on a podcast with some of Essendon's biggest content creators from outside the club, a stark difference from Scott, who gave off the vibe of an untouchable CEO fans could never really connect with, rather than your friendly local head coach.

Matthew Lloyd (centre) has indicated he would potentially join McVeigh (left) and Welsh (right) back at Essendon. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

It is no surprise that McVeigh's arrival has already seemingly caused a change in tune from both Hird and fellow Essendon icon, Matthew Lloyd.

Since his retirement at the end of 2009, Lloyd has mostly stayed away from the club while becoming one of the AFL's most prominent media figures.

Lloyd is uncompromising when it comes to his views on Essendon, annoying segments of the club's fanbase who wonder why he has not stepped in to help fix the problems he keeps highlighting.

As McVeigh's appointment grew closer, Lloyd curiously changed his tune and said he would like to go back to club land.

It would be no surprise to see him in an official role at Essendon in the coming years as McVeigh builds out his staff.

All of this brings us back to Hird and Essendon's seemingly never-ending quest to find unity.

The basic pitch from Hird's supporters is that he is the only one who can truly bring unity back to what has been a broken club.

The pitch just missed one thing.

Who says Hird can only bring unity as Essendon's coach?

World.title: Pogačar's sensational solo attack squeezes Vuelta rivals dry
World.content:
Four days is all it took for Tadej Pogačar to end the Vuelta a España as a meaningful contest, the Slovenian great once again riding away from the peloton to win solo and establish a massive lead over the rest of the field.

It has been 32 years since Tony Rominger led a grand tour from start to finish when he won the 1994 Vuelta.

But with yet another thrilling display of daring, Pogačar put himself in pole position to emulate the Swiss rider and become just the ninth man to lead a three-week race from start to finish.

Superlatives have long been superfluous when writing about this Slovenian superstar.

Things that should not be possible are made to look routine.

When he hits the front of a race as the road goes into the mountains, the rest of the pack knows that their only chance is to ride at their own tempo.

Any attempt to fly too close to this generation's greatest star will surely send their hopes of finishing the race crashing to the ground, like Icarus.

As soon as Tadej Pogačar is in this position, that's likely to be the last the peloton sees of him. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Pogačar took off with just over 50 kilometres remaining of the 104.8km circuit around Andorra la Vella to claim yet another dominant victory.

Decathlon CMA CGM put the power down at the bottom of the Collada de Beixalis climb, the second mountain of the day, and ripped the peloton to shreds.

Australian Jay Vine led the charge in support for the Slovenian's UAE Emirates XRG team, but with the pace already high, Pogačar upped his rate to burst clear.

Decathlon's Austrian leader Felix Gall tried to match Pogačar's pace in the initial throes of his attack.

However, the Austrian, as so many riders have discovered before him, could barely hold the double-world champion's wheel and quickly dropped off before being joined by the rest of the favourites.

"The pace was already super fast on the throttle right from the base [of the climb]," Pogačar told media after the race.

"When Jay let me pass him on Decathlon's wheel, I knew: 'OK, I don't want to get isolated from all those general classification contenders, because otherwise they'll all gang up on me.'

"I tried to attack on the climb. When I saw that I could open up a gap, I just hoped I could hold on until the finish. It worked out.

"It was really tough, but it's a wonderful feeling."

Tadej Pogačar is irresistable. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Pogačar's lead extended to over 3 minutes at one stage before he rolled home to win by 2 minutes and 39 seconds from Jarno Widar, with Gall third.

The 50km attack was his longest in a grand tour, bettering the 43km solo victory he launched in the Pyrenees last month at the Tour de France.

It is another remarkable performance from the Slovenian to add to the extraordinary wins that have become so normal it is expected of him.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Tadej Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

With two key objectives to come this season, the World Championships road race in Canada falls just two weeks after the Vuelta's conclusion, with the Giro di Lombardia a further two weeks after that, Pogačar may now be able to take things easier through the next two-and-a-half weeks of racing in Spain.

The 27-year-old's lead in the general classification now stands at 3 minutes and 21 seconds, with four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič sitting second.

"To be honest, any lead is a bonus," Pogačar said.

"This is fantastic, because now I can head into the coming days with peace of mind and a lot of confidence.

"We're taking it day by day and staying focused. Hopefully, after this stage, the pressure will ease up a bit."

Pogačar is also a comprehensive leader in the points and king of the mountains classifications.

Wednesday's fifth stage is a hilly 173.3km ride from Falset Costa Daurada to Terres de l'Ebre in Spain's north east.

Tech.title: All the ways Instagram and Facebook are changing for teens
Tech.content:
A non-personalized feed option: In four months, Facebook and Instagram must give teens the “reasonably accessible” option of a default feed that isn’t personalized by Meta’s recommendation engine. Meta will occasionally send teens reminders about this option, and parents will also be able to set it as their child’s default setting.

Age assurance: Meta has agreed to ramp up efforts to identify and apply restrictions to underage users on the platform. Under the settlement, Meta must either continue to develop its own age assurance standard or adopt a third-party option. The method must evaluate whether a user is under 13, so they can be removed from the platform, or identify if someone is aged 13 to 17, in which case they would receive teen account protections. New users who haven’t yet been evaluated by Meta’s system will receive teen protections by default. Meta must also adhere to data minimization policies, implement a process for users to appeal their status as a minor, and have its age assurance system reviewed by an independent auditor.

Two-hour time limit: Teens will only be able to use Instagram and Facebook — cumulatively — for two hours per day, unless the limit is turned off by a parent. Meta will apply the time limit not only across both apps, but across a user’s alternate account if it detects one. As noted in the settlement agreement, time spent consuming videos or audio more than 22 minutes long, messaging, or using an app’s settings won’t count toward the limit, which will reset at 12AM each day.

Persistent prompts: Within four months, Meta is required to show teens prompts every 15 minutes that they continually scroll on Instagram and Facebook to prevent “excessive, mindless, or unintended” usage. The platforms will also send prompts after 60 minutes and 90 minutes. An example of the notification included in the settlement shows a message saying, “You’ve scrolled for a while. Try exploring something new,” with a prompt for users to view content related to other topics and to review their algorithm. Parents can change this setting to be less or more restrictive.

Nighttime restrictions: Meta will block teens from accessing most of Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6AM. During this time, teens can’t post on either platform or view feeds, stories, reels, or scroll through their Explore page. Teens will still be able to access messaging features and account settings at night, and parents, again, can adjust the setting.

Muted notifications during the school day: Teens won’t receive push notifications by default between 8AM and 3PM, except for “direct messages and alerts about their account security or safety,” unless the setting is changed by a parent.

Toggle off autoplay: Teens will get the option to turn off autoplay, which means they’ll have to tap or swipe their screen to view content, rather than Instagram or Facebook playing it as soon as it appears on their screen.

No more visible likes: Facebook and Instagram will begin hiding the number of likes and reactions on teens’ posts by default, and will stop showing them on other posts as well.

Tech.title: Being a mom is hard — the heat is making it harder
Tech.content:
It’s 8:52 AM and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 Celsius) where I live in Southern California. My husband just came back from a morning outing with our four-month-old. “How was the botanic garden?” I ask him. “It was okay. It was just too hot,” he tells me. I didn’t expect us to spend so much of our son’s first summer cooped up inside, hiding from the heat.

As I write this, an extreme heat warning for my area is glaring at me from my phone, effective for at least the next three days. “Dangerously hot conditions with high temperatures up to 110 [degrees Fahrenheit] expected,” my weather app warns me. “Stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of the sun.”

As I write this, an extreme heat warning for my area is glaring at me from my phone.

It’s the sort of warning more kids are growing up with as global average temperatures climb. Around the world, 560 million children under the age of 10 are experiencing at least one additional month of heat stress each year as a result of climate change, according to a new study published in the journal Science Advances.

“I hope that this increases public awareness that climate change is a problem that is already happening today, that’s already affecting us,” says Rosa Pietroiusti, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel. “It’s affecting the health of the most vulnerable.”

Pietroiusti’s team used an international standard for moderate heat stress, days when taking protective measures like rest breaks are recommended to prevent heat-related illness. The threshold is set at a WetBulb Globe Temperature of 28 degrees Celsius (82.4 F), a measure that takes heat, humidity, wind speed, and cloud cover into account. Thanks to advances in climate attribution science, they were able to assess the number of days crossing that threshold and how many of those heat stress days were added by climate change.

They found that children are disproportionately exposed to dangerous heat, as compared to older age categories. Climate change has led to at least one additional month of heat stress for 43 percent of all kids in the 0-9 age group — 560 million little ones. That’s nearly triple the number of people aged 60-69 exposed to the same amount of climate-induced heat stress.

That’s due to even more socio-political inequity at a global scale; the highest increases in heat stress due to human-caused climate change take place in countries in the Global South that have contributed least to the fossil fuel pollution raising temperatures. These countries have younger populations, and they also tend to have less access to air conditioning or infrastructure designed to withstand extreme weather events. And if countries blow past the targets they agreed upon in the Paris climate accord, the number of children under the age of 10 that are exposed to an extra month of heat stress rises to 650 million with just 2 degrees Celsius of global warming, the new study finds.

Heat in particular can sneak up on you because it doesn’t always arrive with the same public safety warnings as a big storm might. And yet it’s a leading cause of weather related deaths globally, according to the World Health Organization. Heat stress can lead to dehydration, heat stroke, and eventually organ failure.

Babies and kids are even more susceptible than most adults. Their small bodies have a higher surface area-to-body mass ratio that makes it easier for them to overheat. Think of a small ice cube melting in the sun compared to a big block of ice. Babies’ sweat glands are still developing, making it even harder for them to regulate their body temperature. They’re totally dependent on adults to take life-saving precautions, like staying hydrated.

Heat-related illness is preventable as long as a kid can find a place to stay cool. And we can stop summers from getting even hotter than they already are today by turning to energy sources like solar and wind that don’t emit planet-heating pollution.

There are already plenty of ways the heat makes being a new mom even harder than it needs to be. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that parents avoid taking babies outside for long stretches whenever the ‘feels like’ temperature reaches higher than 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32.2 Celsius). With this summer’s heatwaves, that meant that my family was mostly stuck indoors from about 11:00 in the morning or earlier until past sunset.

My son typically loves walks outside, and spending time outdoors can be especially beneficial for a parent’s mental wellbeing postpartum. I hate that it’s not even safe to explore his grandparents’ backyard after a certain time. Sometimes there’s a doctor’s appointment or groceries to grab midday. That often means blasting the AC to cool down a sweltering car while we wait in a hot parking lot.

As irritating as this all is, I’m one of the lucky parents with a car and air conditioning at home. We had a taste of what it would be like without AC when we lost power one hot July afternoon. Power outages have grown longer in the US as extreme weather has become more common. Heatwaves can trigger blackouts because of electricity demand peaks when people blast the AC, or when utility companies preemptively shut off power lines to keep them from sparking wildfires.

Regardless of the weather, breastfeeding is hard!

My family packed up to head to grandma’s house to stay cool, and to save the stash of breastmilk in the freezer (thankfully the lights came back on just before we were about to leave). I calculated, and had the milk gone bad, that would amount to about 20 hours of my time pumping (much of it during sleepless nights) down the drain. I didn’t know this until I was about to become a mom, but newborns shouldn’t drink water. So they might feed more frequently to hydrate. Breastfeeding parents are often thirsty because you’re losing fluid to your baby, even more so in the heat.

Regardless of the weather, breastfeeding is hard! Being a parent is hard! Being a kid gets tough, too. That’s what makes lazy summer days at the beach, and having other outdoor adventures so important. It’s supposed to be an escape, and prime time for core memory-making.

Before my baby was born in April, I daydreamed about us lounging at the beach this summer. I couldn’t imagine his face yet, but I could picture those tiny toes in the sand. My son and I did manage to make it to the ocean. A baby’s skin is too sensitive for sunscreen until about 6 months old, so he wore his little blue bucket hat for a short walk along the pier. My husband took a quick video of us when I attempted to take him out of the stroller to gaze over the water. He scowls and fusses when the bright sun hits his eyes. “This is too much?” I ask him. “This is too much.”

Tech.title: Google’s new AI transcription edits out your ‘ums’ and ‘ahs’
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google has updated Gemini Audio with new transcription capabilities that automatically detect specialized jargon and more than 85 languages. Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is a new addition to the Gemini family that follows the launch of 3.5 Live Translate, and comes as we’re still waiting for Google to release the Gemini 3.5 Pro model that it promised to roll out in June.

Google says that 3.5 Transcribe “represents a major advancement from our previous transcription model, Chirp 3,” especially regarding multilingual performance and wording error rates. The transcription model allows users to “edit naturally with just your voice,” according to Google, and can automatically format text and remove filler words like “um” and “uh.”

Users can provide a customized vocabulary to the model, allowing 3.5 Transcribe to automatically adapt transcription to unique spelling requirements and specialized jargon to prevent those words from being edited manually. It can also attribute speech for up to three speakers in pre-recorded audio, alongside providing word-level timestamps.

Alongside 3.5 Transcribe, Google also said that 3.5 Live and 3.5 Live Experimental updates will be coming to Gemini Audio today that build on the existing speech recognition tech powering Gemini’s voice chat mode. After we published this story, Google then reached out to say these additional models arent being launched yet, and didn’t provide a new launch date. According to the information Google previously provided, Gemini 3.5 Live is better at handling mid-sentence interruptions, language recognition, and live visual processing, while Gemini 3.5 Live Experimental goes further by narrating its progress step by step in real time while it tackles reasoning on more complex tasks.

Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is rolling out starting today in English for all macOS Gemini app users, and the Rambler dictation feature on Android in select countries and languages. It’s also available for developers in public preview in the Gemini API via AI Studio and Antigravity. Google says that Chrome support is coming soon.

Update, August 26th: Google also mentioned two Gemini 3.5 Live and 3.5 Live Experimental in information provided to The Verge prior to publication, but now says that only 3.5 Transcribe is being announced today.
